examContext: SY0-701 may use CIRT and CSIRT interchangeably; recognize both refer to the internal team that executes the incident response plan.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is named the lead of her company's newly formed CIRT, and she writes the on-call rotation so a qualified responder is always reachable within fifteen minutes of an alert. When a malware infection is detected at 2 a.m., the rotation ensures someone begins containment immediately rather than waiting until morning.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants a designated internal group with clear roles and an on-call rotation to immediately respond to detected security incidents. What is this group commonly called?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: A nonprofit organization that publishes the CIS Critical Security Controls and CIS Benchmarks, which are widely adopted, prioritized best-practice guidelines and configuration standards for securing operating systems, applications, and network devices.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize CIS Benchmarks as a common source for secure configuration baselines, also called hardening guides, referenced when auditing or hardening systems, often used alongside STIG and NIST guidance.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria needs to harden a fleet of newly provisioned Linux servers before they go into production. Maria applies the CIS Benchmark for the specific Linux distribution, disabling unnecessary services and enforcing secure configuration settings that align with an industry-recognized baseline.
detail.quizQuestion: A systems administrator needs an industry-recognized, prioritized set of configuration guidelines to harden a newly deployed Linux server before production use. Which resource should the administrator consult?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A CMDB is a centralized repository that stores information about an organization's IT assets, their configurations, and the relationships between them. It supports change management and helps identify the potential impact of proposed changes or incidents.
examContext: SY0-701 connects CMDB to asset and change management; know it tracks configuration items and their dependencies, helping teams assess the blast radius of a change or incident.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team maintains a CMDB that maps every application to the specific servers, databases, and network devices it depends on. When a critical patch requires rebooting a shared database server, Sam quickly queries the CMDB to see every downstream application that will be affected and schedules a maintenance window accordingly.
detail.quizQuestion: Before applying a patch to a shared server, an administrator wants to quickly identify every application and service that depends on it. Which tool should they consult?

definition: A CMS is a software platform used to create, manage, and publish digital content, such as a website, without requiring users to write code directly. Popular CMS platforms are frequent attack targets because outdated plugins, themes, or core software can introduce serious vulnerabilities.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CMS platforms in the context of web application vulnerabilities and patch management; remember that unpatched CMS plugins/extensions are a very common real-world attack vector requiring regular vulnerability scanning.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya runs a vulnerability scan on the company's public website and finds the CMS is running a plugin with a known SQL injection flaw three versions out of date. She schedules an emergency update and adds the CMS to the automated patch-management cycle so plugin versions no longer silently drift out of date.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan of a company's public-facing website reveals an outdated plugin on its content management system with a known remote code execution flaw. What should be the immediate next step?
quizOptions: A) Ignore it since the website is not a critical system
B) Apply the vendor patch or update the plugin promptly
C) Take down the WAF protecting the site
D) Disable HTTPS until the next scheduled maintenance window

definition: COOP is the process of planning how an organization's essential functions will continue during and after a disruptive event, such as a natural disaster or cyberattack. It overlaps closely with business continuity planning but is especially associated with government and critical-function continuity requirements.
examContext: SY0-701 groups COOP with BCP and DRP as resilience and recovery planning concepts; know that COOP focuses on keeping essential operations running during a disruption, which is closely related to but distinct from disaster recovery, which focuses on restoring systems afterward.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan helps a county government agency draft a COOP document identifying which services (like emergency dispatch) must keep running no matter what, and lines up an alternate site and backup staff for each one. When a flood knocks out the primary building, the agency keeps dispatch running from the pre-designated alternate site within the hour.
detail.quizQuestion: A government agency wants to ensure its essential public services keep functioning during and immediately after a major disruption, rather than focusing on restoring IT systems afterward. Which planning discipline most directly addresses this?

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: COPE is a mobile device deployment model where the organization owns and manages the device but allows the employee to also use it for personal purposes. It gives IT more control than BYOD while still offering employees some personal flexibility.
examContext: SY0-701 compares COPE, BYOD, and CYOD; know COPE devices are company-owned, giving IT full management rights, unlike the employee-owned BYOD model.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company issues COPE smartphones to the sales team, fully managed through MDM but allowing employees to install personal apps and browse freely during off hours. Because the devices are corporate-owned, Alex can enforce full-disk encryption and push security patches without needing employee consent for each change.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants full management control over mobile devices, including enforced encryption and patching, while still letting employees use the devices personally. Which deployment model fits best?

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: Contingency planning is the broad discipline of preparing alternative actions an organization will take when normal operations are disrupted, encompassing business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response as subsets. It ensures the organization isn't caught improvising during a crisis.
examContext: SY0-701 treats contingency planning as the umbrella term under which BCP, DRP, and incident response plans all sit; if a question asks for the broadest term covering "what to do when things go wrong," CP is often the intended answer.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is tasked with building out the organization's overall contingency planning program, so he creates a hierarchy of documents: a business continuity plan for operations, a disaster recovery plan for IT systems, and an incident response plan for security events, all under one contingency planning framework. This structure ensures each specific plan is tested and nothing falls through the cracks.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants one overarching framework that encompasses its business continuity plan, disaster recovery plan, and incident response plan as components. What is this overarching framework called?

definition: The CPU is the primary processor that executes instructions in a computer system. In security, CPU features like virtualization extensions and secure enclaves support protections such as trusted execution environments and hardware-based isolation.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CPU-level security features or vulnerabilities, such as hardware support for virtualization or side-channel exploits affecting processor caches.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan enables CPU-based virtualization extensions on the hypervisor hosts so each virtual machine runs in a properly isolated hardware-enforced boundary. This prevents a compromised VM from easily accessing memory belonging to another tenant VM on the same physical host.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud provider wants to ensure that virtual machines belonging to different customers on the same physical host cannot access each other's memory. Which component provides the hardware-level isolation needed?

definition: A CRC is a checksum algorithm used to detect accidental changes to data during transmission or storage. It catches corruption efficiently but, unlike a cryptographic hash, offers no protection against intentional tampering by a skilled attacker.
examContext: SY0-701 tests whether you know CRC is for detecting accidental data corruption, not a secure integrity control against malicious tampering, which instead requires a cryptographic hash like SHA or HMAC.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's network team notices a high rate of CRC errors on a specific switch port and traces it to a faulty cable causing bit corruption during transmission. Replacing the cable resolves the errors, illustrating that CRC is designed to catch this kind of accidental physical-layer corruption rather than deliberate tampering.
detail.quizQuestion: A network interface reports a high number of frame checksum failures, which engineers trace to a damaged cable. What type of error-checking mechanism detected this corruption?

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

definition: A CRL is a list published by a Certificate Authority identifying digital certificates that have been revoked before their scheduled expiration, such as due to key compromise. Clients check the CRL, or use the faster OCSP method, to avoid trusting a revoked certificate.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts CRL with OCSP: a CRL is a periodically downloaded list that can be stale, while OCSP provides real-time revocation status for a single certificate.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization discovers that a server's private key was exposed in a misconfigured backup, so he immediately has the CA revoke the associated certificate and publish the update to the CRL. Clients that check the CRL before the certificate's natural expiration date will now refuse to trust it.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's private key is compromised and they need to ensure clients stop trusting the associated certificate immediately, even though it has not yet expired. What should the CA do?
quizOptions: A) Wait for the certificate to expire naturally
B) Publish the certificate's serial number to a CRL (or OCSP responder)
C) Reissue the same certificate with a new expiration date
D) Disable DNS for the domain

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: A voluntary framework published by NIST that organizes cybersecurity activities into core functions, including Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover, to help organizations assess and improve their security posture.
examContext: SY0-701 expects familiarity with the NIST CSF core functions as a common language for describing an organization's security maturity, often contrasted with prescriptive, mandatory standards like PCI DSS.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is asked to benchmark the organization's security program against an industry standard and chooses the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Chen maps existing controls to the Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover functions, revealing that the company has strong protective controls but weak detection capability.
detail.quizQuestion: A CISO wants a flexible, outcome-based framework to assess maturity across core security functions like Identify, Protect, and Detect, rather than a rigid checklist of required controls. Which framework should the CISO adopt?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A CSIRT is the formal team responsible for coordinating an organization's response to security incidents, from detection through recovery and lessons learned. It is the most commonly used term for this function in both enterprise practice and the exam.
examContext: SY0-701 frequently uses CSIRT as the standard term for the incident response team; know its responsibilities span the full incident response lifecycle, not just technical remediation.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's CSIRT runs a post-incident lessons-learned meeting after containing a phishing-driven breach, documenting that the initial alert was missed for six hours due to an alert-fatigue issue in the SIEM. They adjust alert thresholds afterward, directly reducing detection time for the next similar incident.
detail.quizQuestion: After a security incident is fully resolved, a team meets to document what worked, what failed, and how detection time can be improved. Which phase of the incident response lifecycle does this represent?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: The CSO is the senior executive responsible for the organization's overall security strategy, which may include both physical security and information/cyber security depending on the company's structure. The CSO sets security policy direction and represents security risk to the rest of executive leadership.
examContext: SY0-701's governance objective expects you to know that executive roles like the CSO (sometimes split into a CISO for cyber-specific duties) own ultimate accountability for security risk decisions and policy approval.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security team presents a risk register showing several unaddressed high-severity findings, and the CSO uses that report to secure additional budget and headcount from the board. With executive backing from the CSO, Maria's team hires two more analysts to close the remediation backlog.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team needs executive-level buy-in and budget approval to address a backlog of high-risk findings. Which role is most directly responsible for championing security risk to the rest of the executive leadership?

definition: A CSP is a company that offers cloud computing services such as infrastructure, platforms, or software over the internet, like AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. Security responsibilities are divided between the CSP and the customer according to a shared responsibility model that varies by service type.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests the shared responsibility model: in IaaS the customer manages more of the stack, while in SaaS the CSP manages nearly everything except data and access.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team assumes their CSP automatically encrypts all stored data, but an audit reveals that encryption at rest for their storage buckets was actually an opt-in setting they never enabled. She updates the configuration and documents the shared responsibility boundary clearly for the rest of the team going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: A company assumes its cloud provider automatically secures all configuration settings for its storage service, but an audit finds a publicly exposed bucket. Whose responsibility was the misconfiguration under the shared responsibility model?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: A CSR is a message sent to a Certificate Authority to request a digital certificate, containing the applicant's public key and identifying information. The CA validates the request and issues a signed certificate in response.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the order of operations: generate a key pair, create a CSR, submit it to a CA, then receive the signed certificate back.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam generates a new public/private key pair for a web server and creates a CSR containing the server's domain name and organization details. He submits the CSR to a public CA, which verifies domain ownership and returns a signed certificate that Sam installs on the server.
detail.quizQuestion: What must an administrator generate and submit to a Certificate Authority in order to obtain a new digital certificate for a web server?

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: CSRF is a web attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into submitting an unwanted request to a site where they're already logged in, exploiting the trust that site places in the user's browser session. Anti-CSRF tokens embedded in forms prevent this by verifying the request genuinely originated from the legitimate site.
examContext: SY0-701 tests CSRF as distinct from XSS: CSRF abuses the trust a site has in an authenticated user's browser, while XSS abuses the trust a user has in a site's content; know anti-CSRF tokens as the standard mitigation.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria discovers that her banking application's fund-transfer form has no hidden token, meaning a malicious webpage could silently submit a transfer request using a logged-in victim's session cookie. She adds a unique anti-CSRF token to the form that the server validates on submission, blocking forged cross-site requests.
detail.quizQuestion: A malicious website contains hidden code that automatically submits a password-change form to a banking site in the background while a victim, who is already logged into their bank, happens to visit it. What type of attack is this?

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A CSU is a hardware device that connects a company's internal digital network to an external WAN circuit (often paired with a DSU), terminating the line and providing diagnostics and signal conversion. It sits at the network's demarcation point with the telecom provider.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CSU/DSU as part of WAN connectivity and the network demarcation point; know it sits between the customer's router and the carrier's line, a boundary that matters when troubleshooting whose responsibility a connectivity failure is.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam is troubleshooting an intermittent WAN outage and traces the problem to the CSU at the network's demarcation point rather than the internal router. Because the CSU is owned by the carrier, Sam opens a ticket with the ISP instead of trying to fix it internally, saving hours of wasted effort.
detail.quizQuestion: A network outage is traced to a device sitting exactly at the boundary between the company's internal network and the carrier's WAN line. Which device marks this demarcation point?

definition: Counter Mode (CTR, sometimes written CTM) turns a block cipher into a stream cipher by encrypting successive values of an incrementing counter and XORing the result with the plaintext. It allows blocks to be encrypted and decrypted in parallel, making it fast for high-throughput applications.
examContext: SY0-701 may list CTM alongside GCM, CBC, and ECB as cipher modes; remember that counter mode's parallelizability makes it popular in high-speed network encryption, and that GCM combines counter mode with built-in authentication.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya needs to encrypt a very high-throughput data feed between two data centers and chooses a cipher running in Counter Mode specifically because it can encrypt multiple blocks in parallel across CPU cores. This lets the link sustain full line-rate speed without the encryption becoming a bottleneck.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineer needs a block cipher mode that allows multiple blocks of a large data stream to be encrypted in parallel for maximum throughput. Which mode is best suited for this requirement?

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: The CTO is the senior executive responsible for an organization's overall technology direction and innovation strategy, often focused on product and engineering technology choices rather than day-to-day IT operations. The CTO works alongside the CIO and CSO to ensure new technology adoption doesn't outpace security review.
examContext: SY0-701's governance objective expects you to distinguish the CTO's technology-strategy focus from the CIO's IT-operations focus and the CSO's security focus, since exam scenarios sometimes test which executive owns a particular type of decision.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's engineering team wants to adopt a new third-party API for the company's flagship product, and the CTO requires a security review to be completed before approving the integration. The CTO's insistence on involving the security team early catches a data-handling issue before the API ever reaches production.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineering department wants to adopt a new technology platform for the company's core product. Which executive role is typically most responsible for setting the strategic direction on this kind of technology adoption decision?

definition: CVE is a standardized naming system that assigns unique identifiers to publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities, making it easier to reference and track them consistently across tools and organizations. Each CVE entry typically includes a description and references to patches or advisories.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs CVE with CVSS (severity scoring) and NVD (the database hosting CVE details); know a CVE ID follows the format CVE-YEAR-NUMBER.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's vulnerability scanner flags a web server and references CVE-2023-44487 in its report, letting him quickly look up the exact flaw, affected versions, and available patch. Because the identifier is standardized, every tool in his stack references the same vulnerability consistently.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan report references a specific identifier in the format CVE-2024-XXXXX so that analysts across different tools can agree on exactly which flaw is being discussed. What does this identifier system provide?
quizOptions: A) A numeric severity score from 0 to 10
B) A standardized reference for a publicly known vulnerability
C) A list of revoked certificates
D) A record of configuration items

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: CVSS is a framework for rating the severity of a vulnerability on a scale from 0 to 10, based on factors like attack vector, complexity, and impact. It helps organizations prioritize which vulnerabilities to patch first.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to interpret a CVSS score range, such as 9.0-10.0 being Critical, to prioritize remediation; know it's a scoring framework, not a vulnerability database itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team has fifty open vulnerabilities but limited patching time this week, so she sorts them by CVSS score and tackles the 9.8-rated remote code execution flaw first, deferring a 3.1-rated low-impact information disclosure issue. This prioritization ensures the most exploitable risk is closed first.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team has limited time to patch multiple vulnerabilities and needs an objective way to decide which to fix first. Which framework should they use to rank severity?

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: A community-developed catalog of common software and hardware weakness types, such as buffer overflows or improper input validation, that serves as a standardized classification system for describing security vulnerabilities at the root-cause level.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CWE alongside CVE; remember that CVE identifies specific known vulnerabilities in specific products, while CWE categorizes the underlying type of weakness, the root cause, that can lead to vulnerabilities.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya is reviewing a static code analysis report that flags a function as vulnerable to CWE-89, SQL Injection. Priya uses the CWE classification to understand the root-cause weakness pattern and trains developers to use parameterized queries to eliminate that entire class of defect across the codebase.
detail.quizQuestion: A code scanning tool flags a vulnerability and references a standardized weakness category describing improper neutralization of special elements used in SQL commands, rather than a specific product vulnerability. Which classification system is the tool using?

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: CYOD is a mobile device deployment model where employees select a device from a company-approved list, which the organization then owns or manages. It balances user choice with the ease of IT support and security standardization.
examContext: SY0-701 differentiates CYOD, which offers choice from an approved, company-owned list, from BYOD (any personal device) and COPE (company-issued with personal use allowed).

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's IT department offers new hires a choice of three approved smartphone models under a CYOD program, all pre-enrolled in MDM before being handed out. This lets employees pick a device they like while ensuring IT only has to support a small, consistent set of hardware configurations.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to limit the variety of mobile hardware it must support while still giving employees some choice in their device. Which deployment model fits best?

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: DAC is an access control model where the owner of a resource decides who is granted access and what permissions they have. It's flexible but can lead to inconsistent security since individual users control permissions rather than a central policy.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts DAC, where the resource owner decides access, with MAC's system-enforced labels and RBAC's role-based assignments; know DAC is the default model in most file systems like Windows NTFS.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam creates a shared folder on a file server and, as its owner, grants read-write access to two colleagues directly through the file properties dialog. Because this is DAC, Sam personally controls who can access the folder rather than a central security team setting the policy.
detail.quizQuestion: A file owner independently decides to grant a coworker read access to a document stored on a shared drive, without going through a central security policy. Which access control model does this represent?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: A DBA is the person responsible for managing, maintaining, and securing an organization's databases, including configuring access permissions, performance tuning, and backups. Because DBAs often hold powerful privileged access to sensitive data, their accounts are a high-value target and a key focus of least-privilege and separation-of-duties controls.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference the DBA role in the context of privileged account management and separation of duties; remember that DBA accounts should be covered by just-in-time or just-enough access policies and session auditing like any other privileged account.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex, the DBA for a healthcare application, is required to request temporary elevated access through the company's privileged access management tool instead of holding standing admin rights to the patient database at all times. This just-in-time approach means Alex's full database privileges are only active during an approved maintenance window, not around the clock.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to reduce the risk posed by its database administrators holding permanent, always-on elevated privileges to sensitive data. Which control would most directly address this?
quizOptions: A) Giving the DBA a stronger password
B) Requiring just-in-time privileged access through a PAM solution
C) Allowing the DBA to share one shared admin account with the help desk
D) Removing all logging on the database server

definition: A DDoS attack floods a target system or network with traffic from many compromised devices, known as a botnet, simultaneously overwhelming its resources and making services unavailable to legitimate users. It's distinguished from a simple DoS attack by its distributed, multi-source nature.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DDoS mitigation strategies like traffic scrubbing, rate limiting, and content delivery networks; know the 'distributed' element comes from a botnet of many infected hosts across different networks.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's e-commerce site goes offline during a flash sale after receiving traffic from tens of thousands of distinct IP addresses simultaneously, far more sources than any single attacker could control directly. He enables a cloud-based scrubbing service that filters the botnet traffic before it reaches the origin server, restoring availability within minutes.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application becomes unavailable after being flooded with traffic originating simultaneously from tens of thousands of different IP addresses around the world. What type of attack is most likely occurring?

items.name: DoS vs DDoS
items.detail: DoS comes from a single source; DDoS is distributed across many compromised devices (a botnet), so it cannot be stopped by blocking one IP.

items.name: Volumetric
items.detail: Saturates bandwidth (UDP or ICMP floods).

items.name: Protocol
items.detail: Exhausts connection-state resources, such as a SYN flood against a firewall or server's state table.

items.name: Application layer
items.detail: Low bandwidth but expensive requests (HTTP floods, Slowloris) that tie up the web application.

items.name: Amplification
items.detail: A small spoofed request makes a third-party server (open DNS, NTP or memcached) send a much larger reply to the victim.

items.name: Reflection
items.detail: The attacker spoofs the VICTIM's IP as the source so that innocent servers send their responses to the victim, hiding the real attacker.

items.name: Defenses
items.detail: Rate limiting, CDN or scrubbing services, SYN cookies, WAF, RTBH (remotely triggered black hole) routing, and over-provisioned capacity.

definition: DEP is an operating system security feature that marks certain memory regions as non-executable, preventing malicious code injected into those regions, such as via a buffer overflow, from running. It works alongside ASLR as a core memory-exploit mitigation.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs DEP with ASLR as OS-level exploit mitigations; know DEP specifically blocks code execution from data-only memory regions like the stack or heap.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security baseline enforces DEP on every workstation, so when a malicious document attempts to execute shellcode it had injected into a data buffer, the operating system blocks the execution attempt outright. The exploit fails even though the buffer overflow vulnerability itself was never patched.
detail.quizQuestion: An exploit successfully overflows a buffer and injects shellcode, but the operating system prevents that injected code from ever executing because of where it resides in memory. Which protection is responsible?

definition: DES is a legacy symmetric block cipher with a 56-bit key that is now considered cryptographically weak and can be broken by brute force with modern computing power. It has been replaced by AES for virtually all modern security uses.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize DES, and its variant 3DES, as deprecated or weak algorithms that should not be used in new systems, in contrast to the current standard, AES.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan finds a legacy payment application still encrypting card data with DES due to code written over two decades ago. He flags it as a critical finding in the security assessment, since the 56-bit key can now be brute-forced in hours, and schedules a migration to AES.
detail.quizQuestion: A legacy application is found encrypting sensitive data with a 56-bit key algorithm that modern hardware can brute-force in a practical amount of time. Which algorithm is most likely in use?

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

definition: A key exchange algorithm that allows two parties to establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel without ever transmitting the key itself, forming the mathematical foundation for many secure communication protocols.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange algorithm, not an encryption or signing algorithm, and that it underlies protocols like IPsec and TLS; also know it is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks unless combined with authentication.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex is designing a VPN configuration and needs two endpoints to agree on a session encryption key without ever sending that key across the network. Alex configures the IPsec tunnel to use Diffie-Hellman key exchange so both sides derive the same shared secret independently, keeping the key itself off the wire entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: Two systems need to establish a shared symmetric encryption key over a public, untrusted network without ever transmitting the key itself. Which type of algorithm accomplishes this?

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and other network configuration settings, like DNS servers and the default gateway, to devices joining a network. A rogue DHCP server can redirect clients to malicious DNS servers or gateways as part of a man-in-the-middle attack.
examContext: SY0-701 may test DHCP snooping as a switch security feature that blocks rogue DHCP servers from handing out malicious configuration information to clients on the network.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya notices several workstations receiving IP configurations that point to an unfamiliar DNS server not managed by IT. She traces it to a rogue DHCP server an employee accidentally connected to the network and enables DHCP snooping on the switches so only the authorized server's responses are trusted going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: Several workstations begin resolving company domain names to incorrect IP addresses after receiving network configuration from an unauthorized device plugged into a switch port. Which switch security feature would have prevented this?

definition: DHE is a key exchange method that generates a brand-new, temporary Diffie-Hellman key pair for every session instead of reusing the same key pair repeatedly. This provides perfect forward secrecy, meaning that even if a key is later compromised, past encrypted sessions remain safe.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize DHE and its elliptic-curve variant ECDHE as the mechanisms that provide forward secrecy in TLS handshakes, a key differentiator from static/non-ephemeral key exchange.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the company's web servers to prefer TLS cipher suites that use DHE for key exchange instead of static RSA key exchange, specifically to gain forward secrecy. Months later, when an old server's private key is exposed during a breach, previously captured encrypted traffic still cannot be decrypted because each session used its own ephemeral key.
detail.quizQuestion: A security architect wants to ensure that if a server's private key is ever compromised in the future, previously captured encrypted TLS sessions still cannot be decrypted. Which key exchange property should the TLS configuration require?
quizOptions: A) A key exchange that provides forward secrecy, such as DHE
C) A longer-lived session key reused across connections

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: DKIM is an email authentication method that adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages, allowing the receiving mail server to verify the message wasn't altered in transit and actually came from the claimed sending domain. It works alongside SPF and DMARC to reduce email spoofing and phishing.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DKIM, SPF, and DMARC as the three complementary email-authentication protocols; DKIM specifically focuses on message integrity and sender verification through a digital signature in the email header.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures DKIM signing on the company's outbound mail server so every email is cryptographically signed with a private key, and publishes the matching public key in DNS. When a competitor's mail server receives a forged email claiming to be from Chen's company, the DKIM signature check fails and the message is flagged as suspicious.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants receiving mail servers to be able to cryptographically verify that an email's content was not altered in transit and genuinely originated from an authorized server for their domain. Which email security protocol provides this signature-based verification?

items.name: A / AAAA
items.detail: Map a hostname to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

items.name: CNAME
items.detail: An alias that points one name at another name.

items.name: MX
items.detail: Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.

items.name: NS
items.detail: Names the authoritative name servers for the zone.

items.name: PTR
items.detail: Reverse lookup: IP address to hostname.

items.name: TXT
items.detail: Free-form text. Used for domain verification and for email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).

items.name: SOA
items.detail: Start of authority: zone metadata such as the serial number and refresh timers.

items.name: SRV
items.detail: Locates a service, giving host and port.

items.name: DNSSEC
items.detail: Signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity (defeats cache poisoning). It does NOT encrypt queries.

items.name: DoH / DoT
items.detail: DNS over HTTPS / TLS: encrypt DNS queries for privacy.

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: A DLL is a file containing code and data that multiple programs can use simultaneously on Windows systems. Attackers exploit DLL injection or DLL hijacking to run malicious code within the context of a legitimate, trusted process, helping it evade detection.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DLL injection as a technique where malicious code is loaded into a legitimate process's memory space to inherit its permissions and evade security tools watching for suspicious standalone processes.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's EDR tool flags that a trusted system process has loaded an unsigned library from a temporary folder, a classic sign of DLL injection. Investigation reveals malware was using this technique to run its code under the identity of a legitimate Windows process, avoiding suspicion from basic process monitoring.
detail.quizQuestion: Malware runs its malicious code inside the memory space of a legitimate, trusted Windows process in order to evade detection and inherit that process's permissions. Which technique is being used?

definition: DLP is a set of tools and policies that detect and block unauthorized transmission or exposure of sensitive data, such as credit card numbers or personal information leaving the network via email or USB. It enforces data handling policy automatically rather than relying on user discretion.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DLP's role in preventing data exfiltration, including scanning outbound email and removable media transfers for sensitive patterns like PII or payment card data.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys a DLP solution that scans all outbound email for patterns resembling Social Security numbers and credit card numbers. When an employee accidentally attaches a spreadsheet full of customer PII to an external email, the DLP system automatically blocks the send and alerts the security team.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee accidentally attempts to email a spreadsheet containing customer credit card numbers to an external address, but the message is automatically blocked before it leaves the network. Which control is responsible?

expansion: Domain Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance
definition: DMARC is an email security policy standard that tells receiving mail servers what to do when a message fails SPF or DKIM checks (such as quarantine or reject it) and provides reporting back to the domain owner about authentication failures. It ties SPF and DKIM together into an enforceable, monitored policy.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM by adding enforcement (reject/quarantine/none) and reporting; a common exam distinction is that SPF/DKIM verify, while DMARC decides what happens on failure and reports back to the sender domain.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam publishes a DMARC record for the company's domain set to "reject," so that any email failing both SPF and DKIM checks is blocked outright instead of just flagged. Within weeks, the DMARC aggregate reports reveal a third party had been spoofing the company's domain for phishing, and the policy was already stopping those messages from reaching victims.
detail.quizQuestion: A company has SPF and DKIM configured but still receives reports of attackers successfully spoofing its domain in phishing emails that reach external recipients. Which protocol should be added to specify and enforce what receiving servers should do with messages that fail those checks?

definition: A DMZ is a network segment that sits between an internal trusted network and an untrusted external network, like the internet, hosting public-facing servers such as web or mail servers. It limits the exposure of the internal network if a public-facing server is compromised.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize the DMZ as a buffer zone protected by firewalls on both sides, isolating internet-facing services from the sensitive internal LAN.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria redesigns the network so the public web server sits in a DMZ bounded by two firewalls, one facing the internet and one facing the internal LAN. When the web server is later compromised through a vulnerability, the attacker cannot pivot directly into the internal network because the second firewall blocks unauthorized traffic between the zones.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants its public-facing web server to be reachable from the internet while ensuring that a compromise of that server does not directly expose the internal corporate network. Where should the web server be placed?
quizOptions: A) In a DMZ between two firewalls
B) Directly on the internal LAN
C) On the same VLAN as the domain controllers
D) Behind no firewall at all

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

definition: DNAT is a technique that rewrites the destination IP address of incoming packets, commonly used to forward external traffic to an internal server hosted behind a firewall or router. It allows a public-facing service to use a private internal IP address.
examContext: SY0-701 may differentiate DNAT, which translates inbound destination addresses, often for port forwarding to internal servers, from standard NAT/PAT used for outbound traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures DNAT on the perimeter firewall so that traffic arriving on the public IP's port 443 is automatically forwarded to an internal web server's private address. External users never see or need to know the internal addressing scheme used behind the firewall.
detail.quizQuestion: A firewall needs to forward inbound traffic arriving at a public IP address to a specific internal server using a private address. Which technique accomplishes this?

items.name: Static NAT
items.detail: One-to-one fixed mapping between a private and a public address. Used to publish an internal server.

items.name: Dynamic NAT
items.detail: Private addresses are mapped to a pool of public addresses on demand.

items.name: PAT (NAT overload)
items.detail: Many private hosts share ONE public IP, distinguished by port numbers. What home routers do.

items.name: DNAT / port forwarding
items.detail: Destination NAT: rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so an outside client can reach an internal service.

items.name: Security note
items.detail: NAT hides internal addressing but is NOT a firewall; it provides no real protection by itself.

definition: DNS translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses that computers use to locate each other on a network. Because it is foundational to how users reach websites, DNS is a frequent attack target for poisoning, hijacking, and tunneling.
examContext: SY0-701 covers DNS attacks like cache poisoning and tunneling for data exfiltration, along with the DNSSEC mitigation that adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya notices unusually large and frequent DNS queries to an external domain from a single workstation, which turns out to be malware using DNS tunneling to exfiltrate stolen data past the firewall. She blocks the domain and implements DNS query monitoring to catch similar behavior going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: A workstation is sending an abnormally high volume of unusual DNS queries to a single external domain, and a packet capture reveals encoded data hidden within the queries. What technique is most likely being used?
quizOptions: B) DNS tunneling for data exfiltration

definition: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records, allowing resolvers to verify that responses have not been tampered with and genuinely originate from the authoritative source. It protects against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning attacks.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DNSSEC provides integrity and authentication for DNS data but does not encrypt DNS queries themselves, a separate concern addressed by protocols like DNS over TLS.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables DNSSEC on his organization's domain so resolvers can cryptographically validate that DNS responses for the company's website truly came from the authoritative name server. A later attempted cache-poisoning attack against an ISP's resolver fails because the forged response doesn't carry a valid signature.
detail.quizQuestion: A domain owner wants to ensure that resolvers can verify DNS responses for their domain have not been forged or tampered with in transit. Which technology should they deploy?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.
