definition: An FPGA is a reconfigurable integrated circuit that can be programmed after manufacturing to perform custom hardware functions, including cryptographic acceleration. In security, FPGAs are used in HSMs and specialized devices for high-performance, hardware-based cryptographic operations.
examContext: SY0-701 mentions FPGAs in the context of hardware-based cryptographic acceleration and embedded or ICS security, offering reconfigurable flexibility that fixed-function chips lack.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's team builds a hardware security appliance using an FPGA to perform AES encryption at line speed for a high-throughput network link. Because the FPGA is reprogrammable, the team later updates it to support a new cipher mode without replacing the physical hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineering team needs a hardware chip capable of accelerating cryptographic operations at high speed, with the flexibility to be reprogrammed later for a new algorithm. Which component fits this need?
quizOptions: D) A standard CPU without acceleration

definition: FRR is a biometric accuracy metric measuring how often a system incorrectly denies access to a legitimate, authorized user. A high FRR frustrates real users with repeated failed scans, so it must be balanced against the false acceptance rate, which measures how often impostors are wrongly let in.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know FRR alongside FAR and the crossover error rate as the key metrics for evaluating biometric authentication system accuracy and tuning its sensitivity threshold.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company rolls out fingerprint scanners at the data center entrance, but employees complain they're frequently denied entry even with a valid fingerprint. Chen realizes the scanner's sensitivity is tuned too aggressively, producing a high false rejection rate, and adjusts the threshold to reduce legitimate users being turned away while still catching impostors.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees at a secure facility report that the biometric fingerprint scanner frequently denies access to legitimate, authorized staff even when they scan their correct finger. Which metric describes this specific problem?

items.name: Fingerprint
items.detail: Cheap and widely accepted, but can be fooled by lifted prints or fakes unless liveness detection is used.

items.name: Retina
items.detail: Scans the blood-vessel pattern at the back of the eye. Very accurate but intrusive, so uncommon.

items.name: Iris
items.detail: Scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Accurate and stable over a lifetime, and less intrusive than retina.

items.name: Facial recognition
items.detail: Convenient, but affected by lighting and angle, and spoofable with photos or masks without liveness checks.

items.name: Voice
items.detail: Affected by noise and illness; spoofable with recordings or deepfakes.

items.name: Vein / palm
items.detail: Maps the pattern of blood vessels; difficult to forge.

items.name: Gait
items.detail: A behavioral biometric based on how a person walks.

items.name: FRR (Type I)
items.detail: False Rejection Rate: a LEGITIMATE user is wrongly denied. Hurts usability.

items.name: FAR (Type II)
items.detail: False Acceptance Rate: an IMPOSTOR is wrongly allowed in. This is the dangerous one for security.

items.name: CER / EER
items.detail: Crossover (Equal) Error Rate: the point where FAR equals FRR. The LOWER the CER, the more accurate the system.

definition: FTP is a protocol for transferring files between a client and server over a network, but it transmits data, including credentials, in plaintext by default. It should be replaced by secure alternatives like FTPS or SFTP in any security-conscious environment.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize FTP as insecure, unencrypted, and running on port 21, and to prefer FTPS or SFTP instead; a classic distractor tests whether you know FTP alone offers no encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's network capture tool reveals plaintext usernames and passwords being transmitted every time a legacy application connects to a file server over FTP. She migrates the application to use SFTP instead, immediately eliminating the credential exposure without changing the underlying file transfer workflow.
detail.quizQuestion: A packet capture reveals that usernames and passwords are visible in plaintext whenever a legacy application transfers files to a server. Which protocol is most likely responsible?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: FTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption to traditional FTP, securing the authentication and data transfer between client and server. It should not be confused with SFTP, which is a completely different protocol built on SSH.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the distinction between FTPS, which is FTP wrapped in TLS/SSL, and SFTP, file transfer over SSH; know they are not interchangeable despite the similar names.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's compliance auditor requires encrypted file transfers but the vendor's legacy software only supports traditional FTP commands wrapped in TLS, not SSH. He configures FTPS rather than SFTP, since it layers encryption onto the familiar FTP command structure the vendor software expects.
detail.quizQuestion: A legacy application only supports standard FTP commands but needs to transmit data with TLS encryption rather than switching to an SSH-based protocol. Which option should be configured?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: GCM is a block cipher mode that combines the speed of counter mode encryption with a built-in authentication tag, providing both confidentiality and integrity verification in a single pass. This authenticated encryption design makes it the preferred mode for modern protocols like TLS 1.3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize AES-GCM as a widely used authenticated encryption mode in current TLS cipher suites, valued because it detects tampering as part of encryption rather than requiring a separate integrity check like an HMAC.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria selects AES-GCM for the company's new API encryption standard specifically because it provides both encryption and tamper detection in one operation, removing the need to implement a separate HMAC check. This simplifies the code and closes a gap where a previous implementation forgot to verify integrity at all.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants a single cipher mode that provides both confidentiality and built-in tamper detection without implementing a separate message authentication step. Which mode best satisfies this requirement?
quizOptions: B) Cipher Block Chaining without HMAC
D) ECB with a checksum appended

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: A European Union regulation that governs how organizations collect, process, store, and transfer the personal data of EU residents, granting individuals rights such as data access, correction, and erasure, with significant fines for noncompliance.
examContext: SY0-701 treats GDPR as the primary example of a data privacy regulation with extraterritorial reach, since any organization processing EU residents' data must comply regardless of where the organization is based, and tests awareness of concepts like the right to be forgotten and breach notification timelines.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company processes customer data for European clients, so Sam implements a data mapping process to track where personal data is stored and builds a workflow so EU customers can request deletion of their records within the regulation's required timeframe. This keeps the company compliant and avoids the steep fines GDPR allows regulators to impose.
detail.quizQuestion: A US-based e-commerce company has no physical presence in the EU but sells products to European customers and stores their personal data. Which regulation still applies to this company?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

items.name: Fines
items.detail: Monetary penalties set by regulators (GDPR is the best-known example).

items.name: Sanctions
items.detail: Formal restrictions or penalties, including legal action or being barred from certain activity.

items.name: Reputational damage
items.detail: Loss of customer trust and negative press.

items.name: Loss of license
items.detail: Losing the right to operate, handle payment cards, or practice in a regulated field.

items.name: Contractual impacts
items.detail: Breach of contract, terminated agreements and lost business.

definition: A free, open-source implementation of the OpenPGP standard that provides encryption and digital signing for files, emails, and communications, allowing users to protect confidentiality and verify sender authenticity using public-key cryptography.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize GPG as a practical, widely used tool for implementing PGP-style asymmetric encryption and signing, commonly contrasted with S/MIME as two competing approaches to secure email encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya needs to send a confidential financial report to an external auditor over email without relying on a corporate PKI deployment. Priya uses GPG to encrypt the file with the auditor's public key and digitally sign it with her own private key, so only the auditor can decrypt it and can verify it genuinely came from Priya.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee needs to send an encrypted and digitally signed file to an external partner without either party having access to a shared corporate certificate authority. Which free, open-source tool is commonly used for this?

definition: A GPO is a collection of configuration settings in a Windows Active Directory environment that can be applied to users or computers to enforce security policies, such as password requirements, software restrictions, or screen-lock timeouts. GPOs let administrators centrally push consistent security configurations across thousands of endpoints at once.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPOs as the mechanism for enforcing baseline configurations and hardening settings across Windows domain-joined systems; know it's a centralized policy-enforcement tool, conceptually similar to MDM for mobile devices.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam creates a GPO that forces a 15-minute screen-lock timeout and a minimum 14-character password on every domain-joined workstation in the company. Within one login cycle, every existing machine automatically picks up the new setting without an administrator touching each device individually.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator wants to enforce a consistent screen-lock timeout and minimum password length across every Windows workstation joined to the company's domain, without manually configuring each machine. Which mechanism should be used?
quizOptions: C) An individual local security policy on each PC

definition: GPS is a satellite-based navigation system that provides precise location and time data to compatible receivers, commonly built into mobile devices, vehicles, and asset trackers. In security contexts, GPS data supports geofencing, device-tracking, and geolocation-based access policies, but it can also be spoofed or jammed.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPS in the context of mobile device management features like geofencing and remote-wipe triggers, or as an example of a signal that attackers can spoof to defeat location-based security controls.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the MDM platform to use each company phone's GPS location to automatically trigger a remote wipe if the device leaves the country without authorization. When a sales laptop-replacement phone is mistakenly left in an airport abroad, the geofencing policy wipes its corporate data before anyone can misuse it.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants corporate mobile devices to automatically trigger a security action if they are detected outside an approved geographic region. Which technology provides the location data needed to enforce this geofencing policy?

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: A GPU is a specialized processor originally designed for rendering graphics but now widely used for highly parallel computing tasks, including password cracking and machine-learning workloads. Attackers use GPU clusters to dramatically speed up brute-force and hash-cracking attacks compared to using a CPU alone.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPUs in the context of password-cracking speed and why strong hashing algorithms with built-in work factors (like bcrypt or Argon2) are recommended, since they are specifically designed to resist GPU-accelerated brute-force attacks.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is evaluating the organization's password hashing algorithm and recommends migrating from a fast, unsalted hash to bcrypt specifically because bcrypt's deliberate slowness resists the kind of massively parallel cracking attempts that a GPU cluster can perform. This single change makes a stolen password database far less practical for attackers to crack at scale.
detail.quizQuestion: A security architect is choosing a password hashing algorithm and wants one specifically designed to resist large-scale cracking attempts using GPU clusters. Which property should the chosen algorithm have?
quizOptions: A) High speed with no configurable work factor
C) A deliberately slow, tunable work factor like bcrypt or Argon2

definition: An integrated approach organizations use to align IT and security activities with business goals, manage uncertainty and potential loss, and meet legal and regulatory obligations, often supported by dedicated GRC software platforms.
examContext: SY0-701 uses GRC as an umbrella concept tying together policy, risk management, and regulatory requirements; expect it in the context of security program oversight, where governance sets the rules, risk management evaluates exposure, and compliance verifies adherence.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya is tasked with building a single dashboard that tracks policy exceptions, open risk items, and upcoming audit deadlines for executive leadership. Priya implements a GRC platform that ties these three disciplines together, giving the board a unified view of the organization's overall risk and compliance posture.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants one integrated program that aligns security policy with business objectives, tracks risk treatment decisions, and verifies adherence to regulations like SOX and GDPR. What is this integrated discipline called?

items.name: Fines
items.detail: Monetary penalties set by regulators (GDPR is the best-known example).

items.name: Sanctions
items.detail: Formal restrictions or penalties, including legal action or being barred from certain activity.

items.name: Reputational damage
items.detail: Loss of customer trust and negative press.

items.name: Loss of license
items.detail: Losing the right to operate, handle payment cards, or practice in a regulated field.

items.name: Contractual impacts
items.detail: Breach of contract, terminated agreements and lost business.

items.name: Boards
items.detail: Set strategy and oversee risk at the top of the organization.

items.name: Committees
items.detail: Cross-functional groups such as a security steering committee or a Change Advisory Board (CAB).

items.name: Government entities
items.detail: Regulators and agencies that set legal requirements at local, regional, national and global levels.

items.name: Centralized
items.detail: One authority sets policy for everyone. Consistent, but slower and less tailored.

items.name: Decentralized
items.detail: Business units set their own policy. Flexible, but risks inconsistency.

items.name: Monitoring and revision
items.detail: Policies must be reviewed regularly and updated when laws, threats or the business change.

definition: GRE is a tunneling protocol that encapsulates a wide variety of network layer protocols inside point-to-point links, often used to create VPN tunnels. On its own, GRE provides no encryption, so it's frequently paired with IPsec for confidentiality.
examContext: SY0-701 may test that GRE alone lacks encryption and authentication, making GRE-over-IPsec a common combination when a secure, encrypted tunnel is required.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam sets up a GRE tunnel between two routers to carry a non-IP routing protocol across the internet, but realizes the tunnel traffic is completely unencrypted and readable by anyone capturing it. He wraps the GRE tunnel inside IPsec to add the encryption GRE itself lacks.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineer configures a tunnel to encapsulate multiple protocol types between two sites, but later discovers an attacker can read the tunneled traffic in plaintext. What is the most likely cause?
quizOptions: A) The tunnel is a plain GRE tunnel without IPsec
B) The tunnel is using AES-256
C) The tunnel is using ESP
D) The tunnel is using DNSSEC

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: HA refers to system designs that minimize downtime through redundancy, failover mechanisms, and elimination of single points of failure, ensuring continuous operation. It's a core availability control supporting business continuity goals.
examContext: SY0-701 ties HA to redundancy concepts like clustering, load balancing, and failover; know HA specifically addresses the 'availability' leg of the CIA triad.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya designs a web application with HA in mind, deploying it across two data centers with automatic failover so that if one site loses power, traffic seamlessly shifts to the other. When a storm knocks out power at the primary site, customers never notice any interruption in service.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants its critical web application to remain available even if an entire data center loses power. Which design principle addresses this requirement?

definition: An HDD is a traditional storage device that uses spinning magnetic platters to store data. Proper disposal or sanitization of HDDs, through degaussing, wiping, or physical destruction, is critical to prevent data recovery after decommissioning.
examContext: SY0-701 covers secure data destruction methods for HDDs, including degaussing and multi-pass wiping, which differ from the sanitization methods appropriate for SSD-based media.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company retires a batch of old servers and uses a degaussing device to destroy the magnetic patterns on each HDD before recycling the hardware. An independent audit later confirms none of the drives contain any recoverable data, satisfying the company's data destruction policy.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization is decommissioning old servers and needs to ensure that data on their magnetic storage drives cannot be recovered before the hardware is recycled. Which method is appropriate for this type of media?
quizOptions: C) Reformatting with a quick format

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: A HIDS monitors a single host's system logs, file integrity, and activity to detect signs of a compromise, rather than monitoring network traffic. It complements network-based detection by catching threats that only become visible once they're already running on the endpoint.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to contrast HIDS with NIDS: HIDS watches one host's internal activity (file changes, logs, processes) while NIDS watches network traffic; know that HIDS can detect threats that encrypted traffic might hide from a network sensor.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria deploys a HIDS agent on the company's critical database server to monitor for unauthorized changes to system files and configuration, since encrypted application traffic would otherwise hide malicious activity from network sensors. When an attacker modifies a system binary after gaining a foothold, the HIDS immediately flags the file integrity violation.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker gains access to a server and modifies a system binary to maintain persistence, but all traffic to and from the server remains encrypted. Which type of detection tool is best positioned to catch this activity?

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

expansion: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
definition: A US federal law that establishes national standards for protecting sensitive patient health information, requiring healthcare providers, insurers, and their business associates to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to associate HIPAA with protecting PHI (protected health information) in the healthcare sector, and to know it mandates specific security controls and breach notification requirements distinct from general privacy laws like GDPR.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya works for a hospital IT department rolling out a new patient portal and must ensure all patient records are encrypted at rest and in transit, with access logs retained for audits. Priya configures role-based access so only treating physicians and billing staff can view relevant PHI, satisfying HIPAA's technical safeguard requirements.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital's IT team is designing access controls for a new electronic health records system. Which regulation specifically dictates how they must protect this patient data?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: A HIPS actively monitors and can automatically block malicious activity detected on a single host, such as preventing a suspicious process from executing or modifying protected files. Unlike a HIDS, which only alerts, a HIPS takes real-time preventive action on the endpoint itself.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the detect-versus-prevent distinction: HIDS detects and alerts, HIPS detects and actively blocks; this same detect/prevent pairing also applies to the NIDS/NIPS network-based equivalents.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures HIPS on the finance team's workstations so that any process attempting to inject code into another running process is automatically terminated rather than just logged. During a later malware outbreak, the HIPS blocks the payload's privilege-escalation attempt in real time, stopping the infection before it spreads.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants an endpoint security tool that will automatically terminate a malicious process the moment it attempts to inject code into another process, rather than just generating an alert for analysts to review later. Which type of tool provides this active, automatic blocking?
quizOptions: D) Security information and event management

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

definition: HMAC combines a cryptographic hash function with a secret key to verify both the integrity and authenticity of a message. Unlike a plain hash, HMAC ensures that only someone with the shared secret key could have generated a valid code for the message.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know HMAC provides authentication in addition to integrity, unlike a bare hash such as SHA alone, because it incorporates a secret key into the calculation.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen implements HMAC-SHA256 to sign API requests between two internal services, using a shared secret key known only to both systems. When a request arrives with a valid HMAC, the receiving service knows not just that the message is intact, but that it genuinely came from the trusted sender.
detail.quizQuestion: Two internal systems need to verify that messages exchanged between them have not been altered and were genuinely sent by the authorized partner system, not just anyone who knows the hash algorithm. Which mechanism provides both guarantees?

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

definition: HOTP generates a one-time password using an HMAC function combined with a counter value that increments with each use. Unlike TOTP, the code remains valid until it is used, since it isn't tied to a time window.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts HOTP, which is counter-based and valid until used, with TOTP, which is time-based and expires after a short window; both are common hardware/software token mechanisms for MFA.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria issues hardware tokens using HOTP to field technicians who often work in areas with no reliable clock synchronization, since HOTP codes depend on a counter rather than the current time. Each code remains valid until used, avoiding failed logins caused by clock drift that a time-based token might suffer.
detail.quizQuestion: A company needs one-time password tokens for field workers in locations where device clocks may drift out of sync. Which one-time password mechanism avoids relying on synchronized time?

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant physical device that generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys, performing encryption operations without ever exposing the keys to the host system. It provides a higher level of key protection than software-based key storage.
examContext: SY0-701 references HSMs for secure key management and generation, often in the context of PKI and high-security environments requiring FIPS-validated hardware.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization stores its root CA's private signing key inside an HSM rather than on a general-purpose server's file system. Even if the server hosting the CA software is later compromised, the attacker cannot extract the private key itself because it never leaves the tamper-resistant hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to store a root Certificate Authority's private key in a way that prevents it from ever being extracted, even if the surrounding server is compromised. Which solution should they use?
quizOptions: B) A standard file share with permissions

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: HTML is the standard markup language used to structure and display content on web pages. Improper handling of user-supplied input that gets reflected as HTML is the root cause of cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.
examContext: SY0-701 ties HTML to web application vulnerabilities like XSS, where unsanitized user input is rendered as executable HTML or JavaScript in a victim's browser.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's web application takes a comment field and renders it directly into the page's HTML without sanitizing special characters. An attacker submits a comment containing a script tag, and that malicious HTML executes in every other visitor's browser who views the comment section.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application renders user-submitted comments directly into the page without sanitizing special characters, allowing an attacker's script tag to execute in other visitors' browsers. What is the root cause of this vulnerability?

definition: HTTP is the foundational protocol for transferring web content between clients and servers, but it transmits data in plaintext, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping and tampering. HTTPS adds TLS encryption to address this weakness.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to always prefer HTTPS over plain HTTP; questions often test recognizing unencrypted HTTP traffic as a finding during a security assessment.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan runs a vulnerability assessment and finds that an internal admin portal is still accessible over plain HTTP, exposing login credentials to anyone capturing traffic on the local network. He enforces a redirect to HTTPS and disables port 80 entirely, closing the exposure immediately.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability assessment finds that an internal web portal transmits login credentials without any encryption. Which protocol is most likely in use, and what should it be replaced with?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: HTTPS is HTTP secured with TLS encryption, protecting the confidentiality and integrity of web traffic between a browser and server. It also allows the client to verify the server's identity through its digital certificate.
examContext: SY0-701 ties HTTPS to TLS and certificate validation; know that a padlock icon indicates an encrypted and authenticated connection, though it doesn't guarantee the site's content itself is trustworthy.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria notices that a phishing site uses a valid HTTPS certificate and padlock icon, which fools several employees into trusting it. She trains the team that HTTPS only confirms the connection is encrypted and the certificate is valid, not that the site's owner or content is legitimate.
detail.quizQuestion: Several employees fall for a phishing site because it displays a valid padlock icon in the browser. What does the padlock actually guarantee about the connection?
quizOptions: A) That the site cannot contain phishing content
B) That the site is verified as non-malicious
C) That the site owner has passed a background check
D) That the traffic is encrypted and the certificate is valid, nothing about the site's legitimacy

definition: HVAC systems regulate temperature and humidity in facilities like data centers, which is critical for keeping servers operating within safe environmental thresholds. Increasingly, HVAC systems are networked and controlled by ICS/SCADA components, making them a potential attack target.
examContext: SY0-701 covers HVAC as an environmental control important for data center availability, and notes that network-connected HVAC or ICS systems expand an organization's attack surface.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen discovers the data center's HVAC control system is connected to the same network segment as production servers, with no isolation. He moves the HVAC controllers onto a separate, tightly restricted VLAN after realizing a compromise of the climate control system could overheat and damage servers.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester finds that a data center's climate control system shares a flat network with production servers and has no access restrictions. What is the primary security concern here?
quizOptions: A) There is no concern since HVAC is unrelated to security
B) HVAC systems cannot be networked at all
C) HVAC systems are immune to compromise
D) A compromised HVAC system could be used to damage servers or pivot into the production network

definition: IaaS is a cloud computing model where a provider offers virtualized computing resources like servers, storage, and networking, while the customer manages the operating system, applications, and data. It gives the most control but also the most security responsibility compared to PaaS and SaaS.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS; know that in IaaS, the customer is responsible for OS patching and application security, while the provider secures the physical infrastructure.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company rents virtual servers from a cloud provider under an IaaS model, giving full control over the operating system configuration. When a critical OS vulnerability is disclosed, Alex's team, not the cloud provider, is responsible for patching every affected virtual machine.
detail.quizQuestion: Under a particular cloud service model, the customer is responsible for patching the guest operating system while the provider only secures the physical hardware and hypervisor. Which model is this?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: IaC is the practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes, enabling consistent, repeatable, and version-controlled deployments. Misconfigurations in IaC templates can be replicated at scale across an entire environment.
examContext: SY0-701 frames IaC as both a security benefit, since configurations are consistent and auditable, and a risk, since a single flawed template can propagate vulnerabilities across many systems at once.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya discovers that an IaC template used to provision cloud storage buckets had public read access enabled by a single misconfigured line. Because the template was reused for every new environment, dozens of buckets across the company were exposed until she corrected the template and redeployed.
detail.quizQuestion: A single misconfigured setting in a reusable infrastructure template results in dozens of cloud storage buckets being accidentally exposed to the public. What practice led to this widespread impact?
quizOptions: A) A single isolated human error
C) Infrastructure as Code using a flawed template

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

definition: IAM encompasses the policies, processes, and technologies used to manage digital identities and control what resources they can access. It includes provisioning, authentication, authorization, and deprovisioning throughout the identity lifecycle.
examContext: SY0-701 treats IAM as the overarching discipline covering AAA, SSO, MFA, and RBAC; expect scenario questions about provisioning and deprovisioning accounts under the broader IAM umbrella.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company implements an IAM platform that automatically provisions new-hire accounts with role-appropriate access and immediately deprovisions all access the moment HR marks an employee as terminated. This closes the common gap where former employees retained access for days or weeks after leaving.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to automatically grant role-appropriate access when an employee is hired and immediately revoke all access the moment they leave. Which overarching discipline covers this capability?

definition: ICMP is used by network devices to send diagnostic and error messages, such as those generated by the ping and traceroute utilities. Attackers can abuse ICMP for reconnaissance, like ping sweeps, or denial-of-service attacks such as the ping of death and smurf attacks.
examContext: SY0-701 references ICMP in the context of network scanning and reconnaissance as well as DoS attacks like smurf attacks; know many firewalls rate-limit or block ICMP to reduce this risk.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan notices a flood of ICMP echo requests sweeping sequentially through his company's entire public IP range, a classic reconnaissance technique to discover live hosts. He configures the perimeter firewall to rate-limit ICMP traffic, slowing the scan without breaking legitimate diagnostic tools like ping.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker sends sequential ping requests across an entire IP address range to identify which hosts are alive before launching a targeted attack. What is this reconnaissance technique called?
quizOptions: C) A ping sweep using ICMP

definition: ICS refers to systems that control industrial processes and critical infrastructure, such as power grids, water treatment, and manufacturing equipment. These systems often run legacy, unpatched software and were not designed with modern network security in mind, making them a high-value, high-risk target.
examContext: SY0-701 covers ICS and SCADA security challenges, including legacy protocols and the difficulty of patching live systems, along with the need for network segmentation to isolate OT from IT networks.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's assessment of a water treatment facility finds the ICS controlling chemical dosing is running an operating system that hasn't been patched in six years because downtime isn't an option. Rather than patching live, he recommends strict network segmentation to isolate the ICS from the corporate IT network entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: A water treatment facility cannot patch its process-control systems due to strict uptime requirements, leaving known vulnerabilities unaddressed. What compensating control best reduces the risk?
quizOptions: A) Removing all logging to improve performance
B) Ignoring the vulnerabilities since uptime matters more
C) Connecting the ICS directly to the internet for easier patching
D) Network segmentation isolating the ICS from other networks

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: IDEA is a symmetric block cipher developed as a patented alternative to DES, historically used in early versions of PGP for email encryption. It has largely been superseded by AES in modern systems but may still appear in legacy system discussions.
examContext: SY0-701 may mention IDEA as a legacy symmetric cipher in the history of encryption standards; know it predates AES and was notably used in early PGP implementations, but it is not the current recommended standard.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam is auditing a 20-year-old legacy system and discovers it still relies on the IDEA cipher for encrypting stored files. He flags it for replacement with AES-256, since IDEA is no longer considered a current best-practice algorithm for new deployments.
detail.quizQuestion: During a legacy system audit, an analyst finds a file-encryption module using a symmetric cipher that was historically used in early PGP implementations but has since been superseded by newer standards. Which cipher is most likely in use?

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

definition: An IDF is a smaller wiring closet or cabinet, typically on each floor of a building, that connects local network cabling back to the main distribution frame. IDFs concentrate cable runs and need physical security controls since physical access to network wiring can enable eavesdropping or tampering.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference IDFs as part of facility physical security; know that wiring closets housing IDFs should be locked and access-controlled, since physical access to network infrastructure can bypass many logical security controls entirely.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya conducts a physical security walkthrough and finds an IDF closet on the third floor left unlocked with network switches exposed. She has a keyed lock and access log installed on the closet door so that only authorized network technicians can physically reach the switch ports and patch panels.
detail.quizQuestion: During a physical security audit, an assessor finds an unlocked wiring closet on an office floor containing network switches that connect back to the building's main distribution frame. What is this closet called, and what is the primary risk of leaving it unlocked?
quizOptions: A) A data center; risk of flooding
B) A SCIF; risk of signal leakage
C) A NOC; risk of power loss
D) An IDF; risk of unauthorized physical access to network infrastructure

definition: An IdP is a service that creates, maintains, and authenticates digital identities, then asserts a user's identity to other applications (service providers) so the user doesn't need separate credentials for each one. It is the core component behind federated identity and single sign-on systems like SAML or OIDC.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the IdP's role in federation: the IdP authenticates the user and issues an assertion or token, while the relying party (service provider) trusts that assertion instead of handling credentials itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's cloud applications to trust a central IdP so employees log in once and are automatically authenticated into every connected SaaS tool without re-entering credentials. When a new employee is disabled in the IdP after termination, their access to every federated application is revoked simultaneously.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants employees to authenticate once and gain access to dozens of connected cloud applications without re-entering credentials for each one, and wants disabling one account to instantly cut off access everywhere. Which component is central to achieving this federated single sign-on model?

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: An IDS monitors network or host activity for signs of malicious behavior or policy violations and generates alerts, but unlike an IPS, it does not take action to block the traffic itself. It's a passive, detective control rather than a preventive one.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts IDS, which detects and alerts only, with IPS, which detects and actively blocks; know both can be deployed as network-based (NIDS) or host-based variants.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria deploys an IDS on a span port monitoring a copy of all network traffic, so it can analyze patterns for malicious signatures without sitting inline and risking a bottleneck. When it detects a known exploit attempt, it immediately alerts the SOC, but the traffic itself still reaches its destination since the IDS cannot block it.
detail.quizQuestion: A security appliance monitors a copy of network traffic and generates alerts on suspicious activity, but has no ability to stop the traffic itself. What type of device is this?

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

expansion: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: IEEE is a professional standards organization that develops and publishes many of the technical standards used in networking and security, most notably the 802 family covering Ethernet (802.3), wireless LANs (802.11), and port-based network access control (802.1X). Security+ candidates encounter IEEE standard numbers constantly when discussing wired and wireless networking.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize specific IEEE standards by number, especially 802.1X for port-based NAC/authentication and 802.11 for Wi-Fi security, since questions often reference the standard number rather than spelling out IEEE.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan implements IEEE 802.1X on the office network switches so that any device plugging into a wall jack must authenticate via RADIUS before getting network access, rather than being trusted by default. An unauthorized laptop plugged into an empty conference-room port is denied access because it can't complete the 802.1X authentication.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to require port-based authentication so that any device connecting to a wired switch port must authenticate before being granted network access. Which IEEE standard defines this port-based network access control?

definition: IKE is the protocol used to set up a secure, authenticated channel and negotiate cryptographic keys for an IPsec VPN tunnel. It handles key management so that AH and ESP can use fresh, mutually agreed-upon keys for each session.
examContext: SY0-701 ties IKE to the key-negotiation phase of establishing an IPsec tunnel; know it operates before AH/ESP can encrypt or authenticate the actual traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures two VPN gateways to run IKE phase 1 and phase 2 negotiations, establishing a shared secret key before any IPsec-protected traffic flows between the sites. When the negotiated key's lifetime expires, IKE automatically renegotiates a fresh key without dropping the tunnel.
detail.quizQuestion: Before two VPN gateways can begin exchanging encrypted IPsec traffic, they must first establish a secure channel and agree on cryptographic keys. Which protocol handles this negotiation?

items.name: AH
items.detail: Authentication Header: integrity and authentication of the whole packet but NO encryption. IP protocol 51, and it breaks when NAT rewrites the header.

items.name: ESP
items.detail: Encapsulating Security Payload: encryption plus (optional) integrity and authentication. IP protocol 50. This is what provides confidentiality.

items.name: Transport mode
items.detail: Encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header; typically host-to-host.

items.name: Tunnel mode
items.detail: Encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header; typically gateway-to-gateway (site-to-site VPN).

items.name: IKE
items.detail: Internet Key Exchange: negotiates the security associations and keys (UDP 500; UDP 4500 for NAT traversal).

definition: IM refers to real-time text-based communication applications used in both personal and corporate settings. Unmonitored or unsanctioned IM applications create data loss and malware delivery risks, since messages and attached files can bypass standard email security controls.
examContext: SY0-701 may mention IM as a vector for social engineering and malware delivery that often falls outside traditional email security monitoring and DLP coverage.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya discovers employees using an unsanctioned personal IM app to share files with external contractors, completely bypassing the company's email-based DLP scanning. She rolls out an approved, centrally logged IM platform and updates the AUP to prohibit using unauthorized messaging apps for business data.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees are found sharing sensitive files through a personal messaging app that bypasses the company's email security and DLP scanning entirely. What is the best remediation?
quizOptions: A) Only monitor email and leave IM unmanaged
B) Disable all forms of digital communication
C) Ignore it since IM is outside the security scope
D) Provide an approved, monitored IM platform and update policy to prohibit unauthorized apps

definition: IMAP is an email retrieval protocol that keeps messages synchronized on a central server, allowing access from multiple devices simultaneously. Unencrypted IMAP transmits credentials and message content in plaintext, so it should always be used with TLS.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know IMAP, typically port 143 or 993 with TLS, as a mail retrieval protocol, contrasted with SMTP for sending mail and POP3 for simple download-and-delete retrieval.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures the company's mail clients to connect using IMAP over TLS on port 993 instead of the legacy unencrypted port, ensuring that both credentials and message content are encrypted. He also confirms that employees' phones and laptops stay in sync showing the same read/unread status across all devices.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants employees to access the same synchronized mailbox, with consistent read/unread status, across both a laptop and a phone. Which protocol enables this centralized synchronization?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: Forensic evidence, such as a malicious IP address, file hash, domain name, or registry key, that suggests a system has been breached or is exhibiting signs of malicious activity, used to detect and investigate security incidents.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know IOCs, such as hashes, IPs, and domains, are the artifacts analysts search for and share via threat intelligence feeds, often in STIX format, to detect known malicious activity across an environment.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen receives a threat intelligence bulletin listing file hashes and command-and-control domains associated with a new ransomware strain. Chen loads these IOCs into the SIEM so any system contacting those domains or containing those file hashes immediately triggers an alert before encryption can spread.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst receives a threat intelligence bulletin listing specific file hashes and domain names associated with a new malware strain, and loads them into the SIEM to trigger alerts if seen on the network. What are these artifacts called?

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Many failed logins from one account or source suggest brute force or spraying.

items.name: Concurrent session usage
items.detail: The same account logged in from several places or devices at once.

items.name: Impossible travel
items.detail: Logins from locations too far apart for the elapsed time, suggesting stolen credentials.

items.name: Blocked content
items.detail: Spikes of blocked connections or filtered downloads, which can reveal malware phoning home or users hitting malicious sites.

items.name: Resource consumption
items.detail: Unexplained CPU, memory, disk or bandwidth use, such as cryptojacking or data exfiltration.

items.name: Resource inaccessibility
items.detail: Services, files or systems suddenly unavailable: DoS, ransomware or a wiper.

items.name: Out-of-cycle logging
items.detail: Log entries or activity at unusual times, such as a batch job or admin login at 3 a.m.

items.name: Missing logs
items.detail: Gaps or deleted logs, a sign that an attacker is covering their tracks.

items.name: Published / documented
items.detail: Known IoCs and attack patterns from threat intelligence, such as a documented IP, hash or domain.

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: IoT describes the broad category of internet-connected physical devices, like smart cameras, thermostats, and sensors, that often have limited processing power and minimal built-in security. These devices commonly ship with default credentials and infrequent patching, making them popular botnet targets.
examContext: SY0-701 covers IoT security weaknesses, including default or weak credentials and lack of patching, and their frequent recruitment into DDoS botnets like Mirai.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's vulnerability scan discovers dozens of smart security cameras on the corporate network still using the manufacturer's default admin password. He isolates all IoT devices onto a dedicated VLAN with NAC enforcement and forces a password change, closing an easy entry point for attackers.
detail.quizQuestion: A security scan reveals that dozens of smart cameras on the network are still using factory-default administrator credentials. What is the best immediate remediation?
quizOptions: A) Change the default credentials and segment the devices onto a restricted network
B) Leave the cameras as-is since they are low-value targets
C) Connect the cameras directly to the internet for remote access
D) Disable logging on the cameras to improve performance

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: IP is the fundamental network-layer protocol responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks, including the internet. Nearly every networking and security concept, from firewalls to VPNs, operates on top of or around IP addressing.
examContext: SY0-701 expects foundational familiarity with IP addressing underlying ACLs, NAT, and firewall rules; know the difference between public and private IP address ranges.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria writes a firewall rule permitting traffic only from a specific internal IP subnet to reach a sensitive database server, blocking every other address by default. When an unauthorized device on a different subnet attempts to connect, its IP address fails to match the rule and the connection is dropped.
detail.quizQuestion: A firewall rule permits traffic to a database server only from a specific internal address range, blocking all other sources. What is this rule filtering on?

definition: An IPS monitors network traffic for malicious activity and automatically takes action to block or prevent it in real time, unlike an IDS, which only alerts. It sits inline with network traffic so it can drop malicious packets before they reach their destination.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts IPS, which is active, inline, and blocks traffic, with IDS, which is passive and alerts only; know an IPS must be placed inline to intercept and stop traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys an IPS inline between the internet router and the internal network so it can automatically drop packets matching a known exploit signature before they ever reach internal servers. During a real attack attempt, the IPS blocks the malicious packets in real time, unlike the passive IDS it replaced.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants malicious traffic matching known exploit signatures to be automatically blocked in real time, not just logged for later review. Which device should be placed inline on the network?

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
