items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: IPsec is a suite of protocols that provides authentication and encryption for IP packets, commonly used to build secure VPN tunnels between sites or remote users. It includes the AH and ESP protocols along with IKE for key management.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know IPsec's two modes, transport and tunnel: tunnel mode encrypts the entire original packet, while transport mode encrypts only the payload.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya sets up a site-to-site VPN using IPsec in tunnel mode so that the original source and destination IP addresses of internal traffic are hidden inside an encrypted outer packet. An attacker intercepting traffic between the two sites sees only the gateway addresses, not the actual internal hosts communicating.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants a site-to-site VPN where the entire original IP packet, including its internal source and destination addresses, is encrypted and hidden inside a new outer packet. Which IPsec mode should be used?

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

items.name: AH
items.detail: Authentication Header: integrity and authentication of the whole packet but NO encryption. IP protocol 51, and it breaks when NAT rewrites the header.

items.name: ESP
items.detail: Encapsulating Security Payload: encryption plus (optional) integrity and authentication. IP protocol 50. This is what provides confidentiality.

items.name: Transport mode
items.detail: Encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header; typically host-to-host.

items.name: Tunnel mode
items.detail: Encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header; typically gateway-to-gateway (site-to-site VPN).

items.name: IKE
items.detail: Internet Key Exchange: negotiates the security associations and keys (UDP 500; UDP 4500 for NAT traversal).

definition: The fourth version of the Internet Protocol, using 32-bit addresses expressed as four decimal octets to identify devices on a network; its limited address space led to the widespread use of NAT and eventually drove adoption of IPv6.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize IPv4's 32-bit addressing and dotted-decimal notation, and to understand that address exhaustion is the primary driver behind both NAT adoption and the transition to IPv6.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is troubleshooting why dozens of internal devices all appear to share one public address when accessing the internet. Chen explains that the organization is using NAT to conserve its limited pool of public IPv4 addresses, translating many internal private addresses to a small number of public ones.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization has only a handful of public addresses but needs internet access for hundreds of internal devices, so it translates many private addresses to a few public ones. This address conservation technique is necessary mainly because of limitations in which protocol?

definition: The successor to IPv4, using 128-bit addresses to provide a vastly larger address space, along with built-in support for features like autoconfiguration and simplified header processing; it was designed partly to eliminate the need for NAT.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know IPv6's 128-bit address space eliminates the address exhaustion problem of IPv4, and that security teams must ensure IPv6 traffic is not silently bypassing firewall rules written only for IPv4, a common misconfiguration.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex audits the firewall rule set after a penetration test reveals an unexpected path into the internal network. Alex discovers the firewall only filters IPv4 traffic, while several hosts have IPv6 enabled by default, allowing attack traffic to bypass the IPv4-only rules entirely over the unmonitored protocol.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration test reveals a bypass path into the internal network because the firewall rule set only filters one version of the Internet Protocol, while hosts have another version enabled by default. Which commonly overlooked protocol was left unmonitored?

definition: IR is the organized approach to detecting, containing, eradicating, and recovering from a cybersecurity incident, followed by a lessons-learned review. It is guided by a predefined incident response plan to ensure a consistent, effective reaction under pressure.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the IR lifecycle phases, preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned; know the order and purpose of each phase.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's team follows their IR process step by step after discovering ransomware: they isolate infected hosts for containment, remove the malware for eradication, restore from clean backups for recovery, and finally document what happened for the lessons-learned review. Following the process in order prevents them from accidentally restoring infected backups.
detail.quizQuestion: During a malware outbreak, a responder isolates infected hosts from the network before attempting to remove the malware. Which phase of incident response does isolating the hosts represent?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: IRC is an older real-time text messaging protocol that, while once used for legitimate chat communities, became widely abused as a command-and-control channel for botnets because it is lightweight, decentralized, and historically under-monitored. Seeing unexpected outbound IRC traffic from an internal host is a classic indicator of compromise.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize IRC traffic on a corporate network as a potential indicator of botnet C2 communication, since legitimate business use of IRC is now rare, making its presence suspicious by default.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's SIEM flags an internal workstation making repeated outbound connections on an IRC port to an unfamiliar external host. Investigating further, he finds the machine is infected with a bot that receives its commands over that IRC channel, and he isolates the host before it can participate in a larger botnet attack.
detail.quizQuestion: A SOC analyst notices an internal workstation is making unusual, repeated outbound connections over an old chat protocol to an external IP address with no legitimate business justification. What does this traffic pattern most likely indicate?
quizOptions: D) A scheduled software update check

definition: A data protection technology that embeds persistent access controls directly into documents and emails, such as restricting printing, copying, or forwarding, so protections travel with the file wherever it goes, even outside the organization's network.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts IRM with DRM: IRM typically protects internal business documents and emails such as contracts and financial reports, while DRM typically protects commercial media content; both enforce persistent, file-bound usage restrictions.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's legal team needs to share a confidential merger agreement with an external law firm but wants to prevent forwarding, printing, or copying the text. Priya applies IRM protection to the document so those restrictions remain enforced no matter where the file is opened, even after it leaves the corporate network.
detail.quizQuestion: A legal team wants to share a confidential document with an external party while ensuring the recipient cannot forward, print, or copy its contents, even after the file leaves the company's network. Which technology enforces this?

definition: An IRP is the documented set of procedures and responsibilities that guide an organization's response to a security incident, ensuring a consistent and timely reaction. It typically defines roles, communication plans, and the steps for each phase of incident response.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the IRP is the written document, while incident response (IR) is the overall process the plan guides; the IRP should be tested regularly through tabletop exercises.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria runs a tabletop exercise simulating a ransomware outbreak, walking the team through the exact steps defined in the IRP. The exercise reveals that the plan never specified who has authority to take production servers offline, so she updates the document before a real incident exposes the gap.
detail.quizQuestion: A tabletop exercise reveals that responders are unsure who has the authority to take a critical server offline during a live incident. Which document should be updated to resolve this ambiguity?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: ISO is an international body that develops and publishes voluntary standards, including ISO 27001 for information security management systems. Organizations often pursue ISO certification to demonstrate a mature, internationally recognized security program to customers and partners.
examContext: SY0-701 references ISO 27001 as a widely recognized security management framework and standard that organizations can be audited and certified against.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company pursues ISO 27001 certification to win a contract with a European client who requires proof of a formal information security management system. The certification process forces the company to formally document policies that had previously only existed informally.
detail.quizQuestion: A potential client requires proof of a certified, internationally recognized information security management system before signing a contract. Which standard should the vendor pursue certification against?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: An ISP is a company that provides organizations and individuals with access to the internet, typically delivering the physical or wireless circuit that connects a network to the broader internet. Availability planning often considers using multiple ISPs for redundant, diverse-path internet connectivity.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference ISP redundancy in the context of high availability and resilience; know that relying on a single ISP is a single point of failure, and some organizations contract with two different ISPs with physically diverse paths to avoid a shared fiber cut taking down both.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's company experiences a multi-hour outage when a single ISP's regional fiber line is cut by construction work nearby. To prevent a repeat, she negotiates a second circuit from a different ISP using a physically separate path into the building, so a single fiber cut can no longer take the whole company offline.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's internet access goes down company-wide after a single construction accident severs one fiber line. What architectural change would best prevent a recurrence of this single point of failure?
quizOptions: A) Adding a second ISP circuit with a physically diverse path
B) Upgrading to a faster connection from the same ISP
C) Switching from DSL to dial-up as a backup
D) Installing a second switch inside the building

definition: An ISSO is the individual responsible for ensuring that a specific information system or program maintains proper security controls and complies with organizational and regulatory security requirements. The role is common in government and federal contracting environments following frameworks like NIST RMF.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference the ISSO role within governance and risk management frameworks, especially in government/federal contexts, as the person accountable for a specific system's day-to-day security compliance posture.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam serves as the ISSO for a federal agency's case-management system and is responsible for ensuring its NIST RMF authorization package stays current. When a new vulnerability threatens the system's authority to operate, Sam coordinates the remediation and documentation needed to maintain its security authorization.
detail.quizQuestion: A federal agency assigns one person accountability for ensuring a specific information system maintains its security controls and keeps its NIST Risk Management Framework authorization current. Which role is this?

definition: The practice of tracking and managing an organization's hardware and software assets throughout their lifecycle, from procurement through disposal, to maintain accurate inventories, control costs, and support security processes like patching and vulnerability management.
examContext: SY0-701 ties ITAM to the security operations domain; accurate asset inventories are a prerequisite for effective vulnerability management and incident response, since you cannot protect or patch what you do not know you have.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex discovers during an incident investigation that several compromised servers were not listed in any inventory system, delaying the response. Alex implements an ITAM program with automated discovery scanning so every device is tracked from procurement to decommissioning, ensuring security teams always know what assets exist and need protection.
detail.quizQuestion: During a security incident, responders discover several compromised servers were never recorded in any inventory system, significantly delaying containment. Which practice, if implemented beforehand, would have prevented this gap?

definition: A widely adopted framework of best practices for IT service management that defines structured processes for incident management, change management, problem management, and service delivery to align IT services with business needs.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference ITIL in the context of formalized change management and incident management processes; know that it is a process framework for running IT operations, not a technical security control itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's organization has an ad hoc, inconsistent process for handling IT incidents and approving system changes. Chen implements ITIL-based change and incident management processes, requiring a documented change advisory review before any production system is modified, which reduces unplanned outages caused by unreviewed changes.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to standardize how it handles incident tickets, problem management, and change approvals across its IT department using an established best-practice framework. Which framework should it adopt?

definition: An IV is a random or pseudo-random value used alongside a key in encryption to ensure that encrypting the same plaintext multiple times produces different ciphertext. Reusing or predicting an IV, as happened in the weak WEP protocol, can seriously undermine encryption security.
examContext: SY0-701 references IV weaknesses in WEP as a classic example of a broken cryptographic implementation; know a proper IV must be unique, and often unpredictable, for every encryption operation.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security review of legacy Wi-Fi equipment finds it still uses WEP, whose short, frequently reused initialization vectors let attackers statistically recover the encryption key after capturing enough traffic. He replaces the equipment with WPA3-capable hardware that uses a properly managed IV scheme.
detail.quizQuestion: An outdated wireless encryption protocol reuses short initialization vectors frequently enough that attackers can statistically recover the key after capturing sufficient traffic. Which protocol does this describe?

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: A KDC is a trusted third-party service, central to the Kerberos authentication protocol, that issues session tickets and temporary cryptographic keys to clients and servers. It allows parties to authenticate to each other without directly sharing long-term secrets.
examContext: SY0-701 ties the KDC to Kerberos authentication, which underlies Active Directory logins; know the KDC issues ticket-granting tickets that are then used to request individual service tickets.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's Windows domain relies on a KDC running on the domain controller to issue ticket-granting tickets whenever a user logs in. When a user then tries to access a file server, their workstation presents a service ticket obtained from the KDC rather than resending the user's password.
detail.quizQuestion: In a Kerberos-based authentication environment, which component is responsible for issuing the ticket-granting ticket when a user first logs in?

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: A KEK is a cryptographic key used solely to encrypt other keys, such as a data encryption key, rather than encrypting data directly. This key-wrapping approach adds a protective layer so the actual data key is never stored or transmitted in the clear.
examContext: SY0-701 may test the concept of key wrapping and key hierarchies, where a KEK protects a lower-level data encryption key, often within a KMS or HSM.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's cloud storage service encrypts each customer's data with a unique data encryption key, then encrypts that key itself with a KEK stored inside an HSM. If the data encryption key is ever exposed in a backup, it remains useless without also compromising the separately protected KEK.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud provider wants to add an extra layer of protection so that a leaked data encryption key is still useless without a separately secured key. What concept does this describe?
quizOptions: A) Storing all keys in plaintext for convenience
B) Using the same key for everything
C) A key encryption key wrapping the data key

definition: A KMS is a centralized system for generating, storing, distributing, rotating, and revoking cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle. Cloud providers offer KMS services so customers can manage encryption keys for their cloud-stored data without building their own infrastructure.
examContext: SY0-701 ties KMS to proper key lifecycle management, including rotation and revocation; cloud KMS offerings are commonly referenced in cloud security scenarios.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures her cloud provider's KMS to automatically rotate encryption keys for a sensitive database every ninety days without any manual intervention. When a compliance audit asks for proof of key rotation history, the KMS provides a complete, timestamped log.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants cryptographic keys for its cloud database to rotate automatically on a schedule, with a full audit trail, without building custom infrastructure. Which service should it use?

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: L2TP is a tunneling protocol used to create VPN connections, but it does not provide encryption on its own, so it's almost always paired with IPsec to actually secure the tunnel's contents. The combination is commonly referred to as L2TP/IPsec.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know that L2TP by itself provides no encryption or confidentiality, which is why it is always deployed alongside IPsec in practice; a question describing an unencrypted tunneling protocol paired with a separate security protocol is pointing at L2TP/IPsec.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is setting up a legacy VPN solution for a partner organization and discovers that L2TP is configured without IPsec, meaning the tunnel carries traffic without any encryption at all. He enables IPsec alongside L2TP, restoring confidentiality to the VPN tunnel before go-live.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator reviews a VPN configuration and finds it uses only L2TP with no additional security protocol enabled. What is the primary security concern with this setup?
quizOptions: A) L2TP uses outdated SHA-1 hashing
B) L2TP alone does not provide encryption of the tunneled traffic
C) L2TP cannot traverse NAT under any circumstances
D) L2TP requires a hardware token to function

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: A LAN is a network confined to a relatively small physical area, such as an office building or campus, connecting devices so they can share resources and communicate at high speed. Most internal network security controls, like VLANs and NAC, are designed to segment and protect traffic within a LAN.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish a LAN from a MAN/WAN by scope and to understand that LAN segmentation (via VLANs) is a core technique for limiting lateral movement if an attacker compromises one part of the internal network.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen segments the office LAN into separate VLANs for guest Wi-Fi, employee workstations, and IoT devices so that a compromised smart thermostat on the IoT VLAN cannot reach the finance team's workstations. When a vulnerable IoT device is later exploited, the attacker is contained to that one VLAN instead of reaching sensitive systems.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to ensure that if an attacker compromises a smart building device on the local network, they cannot move laterally to reach employee workstations handling sensitive financial data. Which LAN design technique best achieves this containment?
quizOptions: C) Using a single flat network for simplicity

definition: LDAP is a protocol used to query and modify directory services, such as looking up user account and group information stored in Active Directory. Standard LDAP transmits queries and credentials in plaintext unless it is secured.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts plaintext LDAP, typically port 389, with its encrypted counterpart LDAPS on port 636; know LDAP is how applications query directory services like AD.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's application team builds a login feature that queries Active Directory over plain LDAP to validate usernames and passwords, unknowingly sending credentials across the network in cleartext. A network audit catches this and the team switches the connection string to use LDAPS instead.
detail.quizQuestion: An internal application queries Active Directory to validate user credentials, but a packet capture shows the credentials crossing the network unencrypted. What is the most likely configuration issue?
quizOptions: A) The application is using LDAPS instead of LDAP
B) The application is using SAML correctly
C) The application is using Kerberos correctly
D) The application is using plain LDAP instead of LDAPS

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: LDAPS is LDAP encrypted with SSL/TLS, protecting directory queries and credentials from eavesdropping as they travel between a client and directory server. It should always be preferred over plaintext LDAP in production environments.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know LDAPS runs over port 636 and wraps LDAP traffic in TLS, closing the plaintext credential exposure risk present in standard LDAP.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya migrates all directory-integrated applications from port 389 to port 636, enforcing LDAPS for every connection to the company's directory servers. A subsequent penetration test confirms that directory credentials can no longer be captured in plaintext from the network.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to ensure directory service queries and credentials are encrypted in transit rather than sent in plaintext. Which port and protocol combination should they enforce?

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: LEAP is a proprietary wireless authentication protocol developed by Cisco as an early EAP method for Wi-Fi networks, but it has significant known weaknesses, including vulnerability to offline dictionary attacks against its MS-CHAP-based authentication. It has largely been replaced by stronger EAP methods like PEAP and EAP-TLS.
examContext: SY0-701 may include LEAP as an example of a deprecated, insecure wireless authentication protocol that candidates should recognize as a weakness if found in a wireless audit, contrasted with more secure modern EAP variants.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's wireless security audit finds several legacy access points still configured to accept LEAP authentication, a protocol known to be vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks. She disables LEAP across the wireless network and migrates all clients to PEAP, closing a long-standing weakness.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless security audit finds access points configured with an older Cisco-proprietary EAP method known to be vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against its authentication exchange. Which protocol does this describe?

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

definition: MaaS is a cloud-delivered service model in which a third-party provider monitors an organization's infrastructure, applications, or security events remotely, typically through agents or log forwarding to the provider's platform. It allows organizations to outsource continuous monitoring without building and staffing their own full monitoring infrastructure.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference MaaS alongside other XaaS cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) as an example of outsourcing an operational security function to a third party, which introduces third-party risk management considerations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's small IT team cannot staff a 24/7 security operations center, so the company contracts a MaaS provider to continuously monitor server health and security alerts around the clock. When a critical disk-failure warning fires at 2 a.m., the MaaS provider's analyst pages Sam's on-call phone before the drive actually fails.
detail.quizQuestion: A small company cannot afford to staff its own 24/7 monitoring operation but still needs continuous oversight of its servers and security alerts. Which cloud service model would let them outsource this ongoing monitoring function to a third party?

definition: MAC is an access control model where a central authority assigns security labels, like classification levels, to both users and resources, and access is granted only when labels match according to strict, system-enforced policy. Users cannot override or delegate these permissions, unlike in DAC. (Note: on the exam, MAC can also stand for Media Access Control — a network hardware address — or Message Authentication Code — a cryptographic integrity check. Context determines which meaning applies.)
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts MAC, which is strict and label-based and common in military or government systems like SELinux, with the more flexible DAC and role-based RBAC models.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's government client requires a MAC-based system where every file is labeled Confidential, Secret, or Top Secret, and users are cleared to match only specific labels. Even a system administrator with broad technical access cannot grant themselves permission to view Top Secret files without the corresponding clearance label.
detail.quizQuestion: In a government system, a file labeled 'Secret' can only be accessed by a user whose clearance label also matches 'Secret' or higher, a rule that not even the system administrator can override. Which access control model is this?
quizOptions: B) An access control list alone

items.name: Mandatory Access Control
items.detail: An access model where the SYSTEM enforces access using security labels and clearances (Top Secret, Secret...). Users and owners cannot change it. Used in government/military; SELinux is a MAC implementation.

items.name: Media Access Control
items.detail: The 48-bit hardware address burned into a network interface (for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E), used at Layer 2. Related items: MAC filtering, MAC flooding (overflows a switch table), MAC spoofing/cloning, and port security.

items.name: Message Authentication Code
items.detail: A short tag computed from a message and a shared secret key to prove integrity AND authenticity. HMAC and CBC-MAC are examples; it gives no non-repudiation since both sides share the key.

items.name: How to tell which
items.detail: Talking about permissions, labels or clearance: Mandatory. Talking about switches, NICs or address filtering: Media. Talking about message integrity or HMAC: Message Authentication Code.

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: MAM is a set of tools that manage and secure specific applications and their data on a mobile device, without controlling the entire device. It's often used alongside BYOD to protect corporate apps while leaving personal apps and data untouched.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts MAM, which operates at the app level, with MDM, which controls the whole device; MAM is well suited to BYOD scenarios where IT shouldn't manage an employee's entire personal device.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company wants to secure the corporate email app on employee-owned phones without being able to wipe personal photos or install device-wide policies. He deploys a MAM solution that wraps just the email app in a secure container, enforcing encryption and remote wipe only within that app's data.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to enforce encryption and remote wipe capability for a single corporate app on employee-owned phones, without gaining any control over the rest of the personal device. Which solution fits best?

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: A MAN is a network that spans a larger geographic area than a LAN, typically covering a city or metropolitan region, often connecting multiple campus or branch LANs together. It sits between a LAN's building-sized scope and a WAN's much larger, often national or global scope.
examContext: SY0-701 may test your ability to correctly order network scope terms (LAN, MAN, WAN) by size; a MAN connecting multiple offices across a single city is the intended middle-ground answer when a question describes citywide connectivity.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization has three office buildings scattered across the same city and connects them using a metropolitan area network leased from a regional carrier rather than treating each as a separate internet-connected site. This MAN lets all three locations share internal resources, like file servers, as if they were on one larger local network.
detail.quizQuestion: A company has three separate office buildings within the same city and wants to connect them with a private network that spans the whole city but is still smaller in scope than a nationwide WAN. What type of network best describes this connection?

definition: The MBR is the first sector of a storage drive that contains the bootloader and partition table information needed to start the operating system. Because it executes before the OS loads, malware that infects the MBR, known as a bootkit, can be extremely difficult to detect and remove.
examContext: SY0-701 references MBR infections, or bootkits, as a historically significant malware persistence technique that modern UEFI Secure Boot is designed to prevent.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's incident response team finds that standard antivirus scans keep failing to remove a persistent infection that reappears after every reboot. Deeper analysis reveals a bootkit has infected the MBR itself, executing before the operating system or antivirus software even loads, requiring a full disk wipe to remediate.
detail.quizQuestion: A malware infection survives repeated antivirus removal attempts and reappears after every reboot, before the operating system even finishes loading. What type of infection is most likely responsible?

definition: MD5 is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 128-bit hash value, but it has known collision vulnerabilities that make it unsuitable for security-sensitive uses like digital signatures. It may still appear for non-security checksums like verifying accidental file corruption.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize MD5 as a deprecated, collision-prone hashing algorithm that should be replaced with SHA-256 or stronger for any security purpose.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria finds that a legacy application still uses MD5 to hash user passwords before storing them in the database. She flags this as a critical finding, since researchers have demonstrated practical collision attacks against MD5, and migrates the application to a modern salted hashing algorithm.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit finds that an application stores password hashes using an algorithm known to be vulnerable to practical collision attacks. Which algorithm was most likely used?

items.name: MD5
items.detail: 128-bit digest. Broken: practical collision attacks exist, so never use it where security matters. Still seen for quick, non-security file checks.

items.name: SHA-1
items.detail: 160-bit digest. Deprecated: collisions were demonstrated in 2017. Browsers and CAs no longer accept SHA-1 certificates.

items.name: SHA-2 (SHA-256 / SHA-512)
items.detail: The current workhorse family (224/256/384/512-bit digests). SHA-256 is the most common choice for file integrity, certificates and signatures.

items.name: SHA-3
items.detail: Standardized in 2015 using a different internal design (Keccak) from SHA-2. Not a replacement forced by SHA-2 weakness; it is a structurally different fallback.

items.name: RIPEMD
items.detail: Open-design 160-bit hash (RIPEMD-160), an alternative to the SHA family; best known for use in Bitcoin address generation.

items.name: bcrypt / PBKDF2 / Argon2
items.detail: NOT general-purpose hashes: these are deliberately slow password-hashing / key-stretching functions with built-in salting. Use them to store passwords, never plain SHA or MD5.

definition: An MDF is the primary wiring point in a building where external carrier lines and internal cabling converge, typically the central hub that all of a building's IDFs connect back to. It is usually located in a secured central equipment room given its criticality to all network connectivity in the building.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference the MDF as the central point of a building's cabling infrastructure, distinct from the smaller per-floor IDFs; know both require strong physical security since compromising either exposes network cabling to tampering or eavesdropping.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya ensures the MDF room, where the building's internet circuit and all floor IDFs terminate, is protected with badge access, CCTV coverage, and environmental monitoring. When a contractor attempts to access the room without authorization, the badge system denies entry and logs the attempt for review.
detail.quizQuestion: A building's internet circuit from the ISP and all of its per-floor wiring closets converge at one central room. What is this central wiring point called, and why does it warrant strong physical security?
quizOptions: A) An MDF; because compromising it could affect connectivity for the entire building
B) A NOC; because it displays dashboards
C) A SOC; because analysts work there
D) A DMZ; because it faces the internet directly

definition: MDM is software that allows IT administrators to enforce security policies, configure settings, and remotely wipe mobile devices across an organization's fleet. It provides centralized control over device-level security regardless of the ownership model.
examContext: SY0-701 ties MDM to enforcing policies like encryption, passcodes, and remote wipe across BYOD, COPE, and CYOD deployment models.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex enrolls every company-issued phone into an MDM platform that enforces a minimum six-digit passcode and automatic encryption. When a sales director's phone is lost at an airport, Alex remotely wipes the entire device within minutes through the MDM console.
detail.quizQuestion: A company-issued phone is lost at an airport, and IT needs to immediately and remotely erase all data on the device. Which solution provides this capability?

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: An outsourced security service in which a third-party provider monitors an organization's environment around the clock, using a combination of technology and human analysts to detect, investigate, and respond to threats on the customer's behalf.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize MDR as a service model, meaning people plus technology delivered by a vendor, distinct from EDR and NDR which are technology products; useful for organizations lacking in-house 24/7 SOC staffing.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's small IT team cannot staff a 24/7 security operations center to monitor alerts around the clock. Chen contracts an MDR provider that monitors the company's endpoints and network continuously, with human analysts investigating and responding to a late-night ransomware alert before Chen's team even arrives the next morning.
detail.quizQuestion: A small company without a 24/7 in-house security team wants a third-party provider to continuously monitor its environment and have human analysts investigate and respond to threats on its behalf. Which service should it contract?

definition: MFA requires a user to present two or more independent types of credentials, such as something they know, something they have, and something they are, before granting access. It significantly reduces the risk of account compromise even if one factor, like a password, is stolen.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests identifying authentication factors versus attributes; know MFA requires factors from different categories, not just two passwords, which would still be single-factor.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya enables MFA on every employee's email account, requiring a password plus a time-based code from an authenticator app. When an employee's password is later exposed in a third-party data breach, the attacker still cannot log in because they lack the second factor.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee's password is exposed in a data breach, but attackers are still unable to access the corporate email account. What control most likely prevented this?
quizOptions: D) An account lockout policy alone

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: An MFD is an office device that combines multiple functions, such as printing, scanning, copying, and faxing, into a single networked unit. Because MFDs run embedded operating systems, store scanned documents, and sit on the network, they are often an overlooked attack surface and a route to sensitive data left on a hard drive.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference MFDs as an example of embedded/IoT-like devices that are often left unpatched and unmonitored despite storing cached copies of sensitive scanned or printed documents.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security assessment finds the office MFD still uses its default administrator password and has not received a firmware update in over two years. He changes the credentials, applies the latest firmware, and adds the device to the vulnerability-scanning schedule like any other network endpoint.
detail.quizQuestion: A security assessment finds a networked office printer/scanner/copier combo device still using its factory-default administrator credentials and no recent firmware updates. What does this finding represent?
quizOptions: A) An acceptable risk since it's just a printer
B) A compliance requirement that cannot be remediated
C) An overlooked attack surface that needs the same hardening as any network device
D) A false positive specific to scanning tools

definition: An MFP is essentially the same concept as an MFD, a single device combining printing, scanning, copying, and sometimes faxing capabilities, with the terms often used interchangeably. Like any networked embedded device, MFPs need firmware updates, strong admin credentials, and restricted network access to avoid becoming a weak link.
examContext: SY0-701 treats MFP and MFD as interchangeable examples of embedded/network-attached hardware that is frequently overlooked in patch management and asset inventory programs.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex discovers during an asset inventory that the department's MFP was never added to the official IT asset list, meaning it had been silently missing every patch cycle for years. He adds it to the inventory and the automated patch management system so it receives the same regular updates as every laptop and server.
detail.quizQuestion: During an asset inventory review, a networked multifunction printer is found to have been excluded from the official IT asset list and has therefore never received a security patch. What is the most appropriate remediation?
quizOptions: A) Leave it as-is since printers rarely get attacked
B) Disconnect all printers from the network permanently
C) Add the device to the asset inventory and patch management process
D) Replace the device with a non-networked model only

definition: A MITM, or on-path, attack occurs when an attacker secretly intercepts and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they are communicating directly with each other. Techniques like ARP poisoning, rogue access points, and SSL stripping are common ways to position for this attack.
examContext: SY0-701 ties MITM to ARP poisoning, evil twin APs, and SSL stripping; know mutual authentication and certificate validation are key defenses against this attack.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's users connect to a coffee shop's free Wi-Fi, unaware that an attacker has positioned themselves between the users and the access point to intercept traffic. Because the users' VPN client enforces certificate validation, the MITM attempt is detected and the connection is refused rather than silently intercepted.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker on a public Wi-Fi network positions themselves between victims and the access point, silently intercepting and relaying traffic without either party noticing. What is this attack called?

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: ML is a subset of AI in which systems learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed for every scenario. In security, ML powers anomaly-detection tools like UEBA and modern antivirus/EDR engines, but it can also be weaponized by attackers or tricked through adversarial inputs.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference ML as the technology underlying behavioral analytics (UEBA) and next-gen antivirus/EDR detection engines, and may also test awareness that AI/ML systems themselves can be targeted or manipulated (e.g., poisoning training data).

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization deploys a UEBA tool that uses machine learning to baseline each employee's normal login times and data-access patterns. When an account suddenly downloads ten times its usual volume of files at 3 a.m., the ML model flags the behavior as anomalous well before a human analyst would have caught it.
detail.quizQuestion: A security tool learns each user's typical login times, locations, and data access volume, then automatically flags behavior that deviates significantly from that learned baseline. What underlying technology enables this kind of behavioral anomaly detection?

definition: MMS is a mobile telecom standard that allows phones to send messages containing images, video, or audio, extending the older text-only SMS standard. Like SMS, MMS can be abused for phishing-style attacks delivered to mobile devices, sometimes called "smishing" when it includes malicious links or attachments.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference MMS/SMS as a vector for mobile-targeted social engineering attacks; remember that messages arriving through these channels bypass email filtering and security awareness training that focuses only on email-based phishing.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization sees a wave of employees receiving MMS messages containing a malicious link disguised as a shipping notification. Because the company's security awareness training had focused only on email phishing, Sam updates the training to cover SMS/MMS-based smishing attacks on mobile devices.
detail.quizQuestion: Several employees report receiving a multimedia text message with an attached image and a link asking them to verify a package delivery, which turns out to be malicious. What type of attack does this best describe?

definition: An MOA is a formal document between two or more parties outlining a mutually agreed-upon course of action, responsibilities, and resources committed by each party. It is generally more formal and detailed than an MOU.
examContext: SY0-701 groups MOA with other business agreement types like MOU, SLA, and BPA; know an MOA tends to specify more concrete obligations than the less formal, more conceptual MOU.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization signs an MOA with a partner university defining exactly which servers each party will maintain and how security incidents will be jointly reported. Because the MOA spells out concrete responsibilities, there is no ambiguity when a shared system later needs emergency patching.
detail.quizQuestion: Two organizations want a formal document that specifies concrete responsibilities and committed resources for a joint project, more detailed than a simple statement of intent. Which document fits best?

items.name: SLA
items.detail: Service Level Agreement: measurable performance commitments (uptime, response time) between provider and customer, usually with penalties.

items.name: MOU

definition: An MOU is an informal, non-binding document expressing a mutual intent to work together or acknowledge a shared understanding between parties, without the legal weight of a formal contract. It's often used before a formal agreement is drafted.
examContext: SY0-701 tests MOU as a less formal, often non-binding cousin of the MOA and BPA; know it signals intent and understanding rather than enforceable obligations.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company signs an MOU with a potential technology partner to informally agree on exploring a joint security research project before any money or formal contracts are involved. When the partnership later becomes concrete, the two companies replace the MOU with a formal MOA detailing actual responsibilities.
detail.quizQuestion: Two companies want to document a shared, non-binding intention to collaborate before negotiating a formal contract with enforceable obligations. Which document fits this early stage?

definition: MPLS is a carrier WAN technology that speeds up and directs network traffic using short labels instead of complex routing table lookups at every hop, commonly used by enterprises to connect multiple branch offices with predictable performance. It is a private, carrier-managed alternative to routing all site-to-site traffic over the public internet.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference MPLS as a WAN connectivity option for site-to-site links, often compared against SD-WAN as a more modern, flexible alternative with better encryption and centralized control.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company has relied on an expensive MPLS circuit to connect five branch offices, and he evaluates migrating to SD-WAN to gain centralized traffic encryption and more flexible bandwidth allocation at a lower cost. The migration plan keeps MPLS temporarily as a backup path during the cutover to avoid any connectivity gap.
detail.quizQuestion: A company currently connects five branch offices using a traditional carrier-provided WAN technology that routes traffic using labels rather than per-hop routing table lookups, and is considering a more flexible, centrally managed, encrypted alternative. Which legacy technology is currently in use, and which modern technology is being considered as a replacement?
quizOptions: A) MPLS is in use; SD-WAN is being considered
B) VPN is in use; MPLS is being considered
C) SD-WAN is in use; MPLS is being considered
D) LAN is in use; VLAN is being considered

definition: An MSA is a contract that establishes the general terms and conditions that will govern future agreements or transactions between two parties, simplifying subsequent work orders. Specific project details are often later defined in a related statement of work.
examContext: SY0-701 ties MSA to the overarching contract framework under which specific SOWs are executed; know an MSA sets recurring terms so each new engagement doesn't need a full contract renegotiation.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company signs an MSA with a security consulting firm establishing payment terms, confidentiality obligations, and liability limits that will apply to every future project. When a new penetration test is needed six months later, both parties simply sign a short statement of work instead of negotiating an entirely new contract.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to avoid renegotiating payment terms, confidentiality clauses, and liability limits every time it hires the same consulting firm for a new project. Which document should it establish once, upfront?

definition: MSCHAP is Microsoft's proprietary extension of CHAP, adding mutual authentication and stronger password-hashing support for Windows-based remote access. Despite the improvements over plain CHAP, MSCHAPv2 has known cryptographic weaknesses and is often paired with PEAP (as PEAP-MSCHAPv2) to wrap it in a protected TLS tunnel.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know MSCHAPv2 is commonly deployed inside a PEAP tunnel (PEAP-MSCHAPv2) specifically because MSCHAPv2 alone has cryptographic weaknesses that a protected outer tunnel helps mitigate.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's wireless network uses PEAP-MSCHAPv2 so that the MSCHAPv2 authentication exchange, which has known weaknesses on its own, happens inside an encrypted TLS tunnel established by PEAP. This layered approach lets the company keep using its existing Active Directory credentials for Wi-Fi login without exposing them to the known flaws of bare MSCHAPv2.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's wireless authentication wraps an MSCHAPv2 exchange inside an encrypted outer tunnel before transmitting it over the air. Why is this layered design used instead of sending MSCHAPv2 directly?
quizOptions: A) MSCHAPv2 cannot authenticate users at all without a tunnel
B) The tunnel is required for DHCP to function
C) MSCHAPv2 only works over IPv6
D) MSCHAPv2 has known cryptographic weaknesses that the protected tunnel helps mitigate

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

definition: An MSP is a third-party company that remotely manages a customer's IT infrastructure and systems, such as networks or help desk support, typically under a service-level agreement. MSPs can introduce supply-chain risk since they often require privileged access to client environments.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes an MSP, which manages general IT, from an MSSP, which manages security specifically; know third-party MSP access is a notable supply-chain and vendor risk concern.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's company outsources day-to-day network management to an MSP that requires remote administrative access to every internal router and switch. During a vendor risk review, she discovers the MSP's own credentials were never rotated in two years and requires them to enforce MFA and periodic password rotation as a condition of the contract.
detail.quizQuestion: A vendor risk review finds that a third-party IT management firm has held unrotated, privileged remote access to internal network devices for two years. What risk category does this best illustrate?
quizOptions: A) Supply-chain and third-party vendor risk
C) Insider threat from an employee

definition: An MSSP is a third-party provider that specifically delivers outsourced security monitoring and management, such as SOC-as-a-service, SIEM monitoring, or vulnerability management. Organizations without in-house security staff often rely on an MSSP for 24/7 threat monitoring.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know an MSSP focuses specifically on security services like monitoring, SIEM, and incident response support, distinguishing it from a general-purpose MSP.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's small company cannot afford a 24/7 in-house SOC, so it contracts an MSSP to monitor its SIEM alerts around the clock and escalate confirmed incidents. When a late-night ransomware alert fires, the MSSP's analysts contain the threat and notify Sam's team before most employees have even woken up.
detail.quizQuestion: A small company without an internal security operations team wants round-the-clock SIEM monitoring and incident escalation. Which type of provider specifically offers this service?
quizOptions: D) A CSP offering only storage

definition: MTBF is a reliability metric representing the average expected time between failures of a repairable system, used to estimate hardware dependability and plan maintenance. A higher MTBF indicates a more reliable component.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs MTBF with MTTR; know MTBF measures reliability or uptime expectation, while MTTR measures how quickly a failure is fixed once it occurs.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan compares two server models during procurement and selects the one with a significantly higher MTBF rating, expecting fewer unplanned outages over its lifespan. A year later, the chosen model has indeed required far less emergency maintenance than the cheaper alternative would have.
detail.quizQuestion: A procurement team compares the reliability of two server models before purchasing new hardware for a critical system. Which metric indicates the average expected time before a failure occurs?

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

definition: MTTF is a reliability metric representing the average expected time until a non-repairable component or system fails completely and must be replaced, as opposed to being repaired. It differs from MTBF, which applies to repairable systems and measures the average time between failures.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish MTTF (non-repairable items, replaced after failure) from MTBF (repairable items, fixed and returned to service) and MTTR (how long a repair takes), as these resilience metrics are frequently tested together.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan reviews vendor reliability data showing a batch of SSDs has a stated MTTF of 1.5 million hours, meaning the drives are expected to be replaced rather than repaired once they fail. He uses this figure to plan a proactive replacement cycle for the storage array before failures start impacting production.
detail.quizQuestion: A hardware vendor publishes a reliability figure for a non-repairable storage component, representing the average expected time before the component fails and must be replaced outright rather than fixed. Which metric is this?

definition: MTTR is the average time required to diagnose, fix, and restore a failed system or component to normal operation. Organizations aim to minimize MTTR to reduce downtime's impact on availability.
examContext: SY0-701 tests MTTR as a measure of recovery speed, often discussed alongside MTBF, the frequency of failures, and RTO, the target recovery time objective.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team tracks that their average MTTR for critical server failures has crept up to six hours, well beyond their two-hour target. She invests in better runbooks and spare hardware on standby, cutting the average repair time back down to ninety minutes.
detail.quizQuestion: A team wants to measure and reduce how long it takes, on average, to restore a failed system once an outage has already begun. Which metric should they track?
