definition: A security technology that uses behavioral analytics and machine learning on network traffic to detect anomalous or malicious activity, such as lateral movement or command-and-control traffic, and supports automated or analyst-driven response.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference NDR alongside EDR and XDR as part of the broader detection-and-response product family; remember NDR specifically analyzes network traffic patterns, rather than endpoint telemetry, to catch threats that evade signature-based tools.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's SOC keeps missing attackers who move laterally between servers using legitimate administrative protocols that do not trigger signature-based alerts. Jordan deploys an NDR solution that baselines normal traffic behavior and flags a workstation suddenly making unusual internal connections consistent with lateral movement, well before data exfiltration occurs.
detail.quizQuestion: A SOC wants to detect an attacker moving laterally between internal servers using legitimate administrative protocols that evade signature-based detection. Which technology analyzes network traffic behavior to catch this activity?

definition: A network protocol developed by Cisco for collecting and monitoring metadata about IP traffic flows, such as source and destination addresses, ports, and byte counts, without capturing full packet payloads, enabling traffic analysis and anomaly detection at scale.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know NetFlow data provides flow-level visibility, meaning who talked to whom and how much, useful for detecting anomalous traffic patterns and feeding SIEM or NDR tools, without the storage overhead of full packet capture.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya wants to detect unusual data transfer patterns across the network without the storage cost of capturing every packet. Priya enables NetFlow export on the core routers and feeds the flow data into a monitoring tool that flags a server sending an abnormally large volume of traffic to an unfamiliar external IP address.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants visibility into which hosts are communicating, over which ports, and how much data is being transferred, without the storage overhead of capturing full packet payloads. Which technology provides this?

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

definition: NFC is a short-range wireless technology that enables data exchange between devices in very close proximity, commonly used for contactless payments and access badges. Its very short range limits, but does not eliminate, interception or relay attack risks.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference NFC in the context of contactless payment security or physical access control badges, noting its short range as a partial, not absolute, security benefit.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company issues NFC-based badges for building entry, relying on the technology's short range to prevent someone from reading a badge from across the room. A penetration test later demonstrates a relay attack using an antenna, prompting Priya to add a PIN as a second factor at sensitive doors.
detail.quizQuestion: A company uses short-range contactless badges for building access, assuming the short range alone makes them impossible to intercept. A penetration test later proves this assumption wrong using specialized equipment. What is the best additional control?
quizOptions: A) Add a PIN or biometric as a second factor alongside the badge
B) Increase the badge's transmission range
C) Remove all physical access controls
D) Disable logging of badge reads

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: An NGFW extends traditional port-and-protocol firewall filtering with deeper capabilities such as application-aware inspection, integrated intrusion prevention, and identity-based rules, allowing it to block threats based on application behavior rather than just IP addresses and ports. It effectively combines several security functions, like a basic firewall, IPS, and application control, into one appliance.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know an NGFW goes beyond simple packet filtering by adding application-layer visibility and integrated IPS functionality, often cited as the modern replacement for a traditional stateful firewall alone.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria replaces the company's aging stateful firewall with an NGFW that can identify and block a specific unauthorized file-sharing application by its traffic behavior, even though it uses a common port that a traditional firewall would have allowed. This application-aware blocking stops data exfiltration attempts that the old firewall never would have caught.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's traditional firewall allows traffic on a commonly used port, but an unauthorized file-sharing application is using that same port to exfiltrate data. Which type of firewall could identify and block this specific application regardless of the port it uses?
quizOptions: B) A static ACL on a router
D) A next-generation firewall with application awareness

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

definition: The hardware component, either a physical card or integrated chip, that connects a computer to a network, providing the physical and data link layer functions needed to transmit and receive data, each identified by a unique MAC address.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize the NIC as the hardware layer where MAC addresses live and where technologies like port security and 802.1X network access control are enforced at the point a device connects to the network.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam is implementing port security on office network switches to prevent unauthorized devices from connecting. Sam configures each switch port to recognize only the specific NIC's MAC address of the authorized device plugged into it, automatically disabling the port if a different device's NIC is detected.
detail.quizQuestion: A switch port is configured to recognize only one specific hardware address and automatically shut down if a different device connects. Which component's unique address is this control based on?

definition: A NIDS monitors traffic across an entire network segment, analyzing copies of traffic for signs of malicious activity and generating alerts without blocking it directly. It's typically deployed at a strategic network chokepoint, such as a span port or network tap.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes NIDS, which is network-wide and passive, from a host-based IDS monitoring a single system; know NIDS sees traffic patterns across many hosts at once.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex installs a NIDS sensor on a network tap positioned at the core switch, giving it visibility into traffic flowing between every department's subnet. When a worm begins scanning for open ports across multiple subnets simultaneously, the NIDS correlates the pattern and raises a single high-priority alert.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants visibility into malicious traffic patterns across every subnet in the organization, not just a single host, without the device sitting inline and risking a bottleneck. Which solution fits best?
quizOptions: D) A NIDS deployed on a network tap

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

definition: A NIPS monitors network traffic in real time and automatically blocks malicious traffic inline, rather than merely alerting as a NIDS would. Because it sits directly in the traffic path, a NIPS can stop an attack before it reaches its target, but a misconfiguration can also disrupt legitimate traffic.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the NIDS/NIPS distinction: NIDS passively monitors a copy of traffic (often via a tap or mirrored port) and only alerts, while NIPS sits inline and can actively drop malicious packets in real time.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen deploys a NIPS inline between the internet edge and the internal network so that detected exploit traffic targeting a known vulnerability is dropped automatically before it ever reaches the vulnerable server. During a worm outbreak targeting that exact vulnerability, the NIPS blocks every exploit attempt in real time without an analyst needing to intervene.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants a network security device that sits directly in the traffic path and automatically blocks malicious packets in real time, rather than only generating alerts for analysts to act on afterward. Which solution fits this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A network-based intrusion detection system
C) A network-based intrusion prevention system

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

expansion: National Institute of Standards and Technology
definition: NIST is a U.S. government agency that publishes widely adopted cybersecurity frameworks, guidelines, and standards, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and the SP 800 series. Many compliance programs and best practices referenced on the exam point back to NIST publications as an authoritative source.
examContext: SY0-701 references NIST frameworks, like the Risk Management Framework and Cybersecurity Framework, as foundational guidance for risk management and security controls.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's federal contracting client requires his company to implement controls aligned with a specific NIST Special Publication before systems can be authorized to operate. He maps every existing control to the NIST framework's requirements and documents gaps that still need remediation.
detail.quizQuestion: A company working with a U.S. federal agency is required to align its security controls with a specific government-published framework before its system can be authorized to operate. Which organization publishes this framework?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A NOC is a centralized location where IT staff monitor and manage network infrastructure performance and availability around the clock. While a SOC focuses on security events, a NOC focuses primarily on network performance and uptime, though the two often collaborate.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes the NOC, which focuses on network performance and availability, from the SOC, which focuses on security monitoring; know they frequently share tools and escalate issues to each other.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's NOC team notices a sudden spike in latency across a core router and begins troubleshooting it as a performance issue. When they discover the latency is actually caused by a DDoS attack rather than a hardware fault, they escalate the incident to the SOC for security-focused response.
detail.quizQuestion: A team monitoring network latency and uptime discovers that a performance issue is actually caused by a malicious attack and escalates it to the security team. Which team originally detected the issue?

definition: NTFS is the default file system used by modern Windows systems, supporting fine-grained file and folder permissions, encryption (via EFS), and detailed audit logging, unlike older file systems such as FAT32 which lack these security features. Choosing NTFS over a legacy file system is itself a basic but important access-control decision.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference NTFS permissions as the mechanism Windows uses to enforce discretionary access control on files and folders, and may contrast it with FAT32's lack of any native permission or encryption support.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya finds a shared drive still formatted as FAT32, meaning no file-level permissions can be enforced on it at all, so anyone with network access can read or modify any file. She reformats the drive as NTFS and applies granular folder permissions so only the HR team can access payroll files.
detail.quizQuestion: A shared network drive is formatted with a legacy file system that cannot enforce any file-level permissions, meaning every user with network access can read or modify every file on it. Converting the drive to which file system would allow granular, per-folder access control to be applied?

definition: NTLM is a legacy Microsoft authentication protocol that uses a challenge-response mechanism to verify user identity, largely superseded by Kerberos in modern Active Directory environments. Its weaknesses make it vulnerable to relay and pass-the-hash attacks, so security guidance recommends disabling it where possible.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference NTLM relay attacks and pass-the-hash as reasons to migrate to Kerberos-based authentication in Windows environments.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's penetration test captures NTLM authentication hashes from network traffic and successfully relays them to authenticate to another server without ever cracking the actual password. He recommends the client disable NTLM in favor of Kerberos wherever legacy application compatibility allows it.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester captures authentication hashes from network traffic and successfully relays them to log into another server without cracking the original password. Which legacy protocol's weakness does this exploit?

definition: NTP synchronizes clocks across computers and network devices over a network, keeping system times accurate and consistent. Accurate, synchronized time is critical for security because log correlation, certificate validity checks, and authentication protocols with time-limited tickets all depend on closely matched clocks across systems.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know that without NTP synchronization, log timestamps from different systems can't be reliably correlated during an incident investigation, and that ticket-based authentication can fail outright if clock drift between systems exceeds its allowed tolerance.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is investigating an incident and finds that log timestamps from the firewall, the domain controller, and the web server are all slightly different, making it hard to build an accurate attack timeline. He discovers the NTP service had silently failed on two of the servers weeks earlier and restores proper time synchronization across the environment.
detail.quizQuestion: During an incident investigation, an analyst struggles to correlate events because timestamps across the firewall, server, and domain controller logs don't line up consistently. What underlying service issue most likely caused this problem?
quizOptions: D) A failed NTP synchronization service

definition: The NVD is a U.S. government repository that provides additional analysis, severity scoring, and metadata for publicly disclosed CVE entries. Security teams use it to research vulnerability details and prioritize patching based on CVSS scores.
examContext: SY0-701 ties NVD to CVE and CVSS as the database that hosts enriched vulnerability data, including CVSS scores and affected product lists, for each CVE identifier.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's vulnerability management process automatically cross-references every CVE identified by the internal scanner against the NVD to pull in its official CVSS score and affected software versions. This enrichment lets his team prioritize patching without having to manually research every disclosed vulnerability.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability management program wants to automatically enrich internal scan results with official severity scores and affected version details for each identified vulnerability. Which government-run resource provides this data?

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: An open-standard authorization framework that lets a user grant a third-party application limited access to their resources on another service without sharing their password. It underlies most modern delegated-login and API-access scenarios.
examContext: SY0-701 lists OAuth as an authorization (not authentication) framework used alongside SAML/OpenID Connect for federated access; remember OAuth grants access tokens for resource access, it does not by itself verify identity.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures her company's mobile app to let employees sign in with their Google account using OAuth, issuing a scoped access token instead of storing Google passwords. This reduces the app's credential-handling liability and limits what the app can access in the employee's Google account.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer wants a third-party app to read a user's calendar without ever seeing the user's password. Which framework should be used?

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: A protocol clients use to check in real time whether a digital certificate has been revoked, instead of downloading an entire certificate revocation list. It speeds up and streamlines certificate validation during TLS handshakes.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts OCSP with CRLs: OCSP gives a real-time revocation check for a single certificate, while a CRL is a full downloaded list; OCSP stapling lets the web server provide the signed response itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam enables OCSP stapling on the company's web servers so browsers get a timestamped, signed revocation status directly from the server instead of querying the CA separately. This reduces handshake latency and avoids exposing client browsing patterns to the CA.
detail.quizQuestion: A security engineer wants browsers to verify certificate validity without a separate round trip to the certificate authority on every connection. What should be enabled?

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: A globally unique, hierarchical string of numbers used to formally name an object, policy, or attribute type, most commonly seen identifying certificate extensions and policies inside X.509 certificates. It lets systems unambiguously reference a specific standard or field.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference OIDs in the context of certificate fields and extensions (such as certificate policies) inside a PKI; know that an OID is just a unique numeric identifier, not an encryption algorithm.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya is auditing a batch of issued certificates and uses the certificate policy OID embedded in each one to confirm which issuance policy (standard validation versus extended validation) the CA applied. This lets her programmatically distinguish certificate classes across thousands of certificates.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst needs to programmatically determine which issuance policy a CA applied to a certificate. Which certificate field should be inspected?

definition: An identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework that allows a client application to verify a user's identity and obtain basic profile information through an identity provider, commonly used for single sign-on web logins.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish OIDC, which handles authentication (who you are), from OAuth, which handles authorization (what you can access); OIDC adds an ID token to OAuth's access token to let applications verify user identity.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam is integrating a third-party application that needs to let users log in with their existing corporate Google account rather than creating a new password. Sam implements OIDC so the application receives a signed ID token confirming the user's identity from Google, without ever handling the user's actual credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application wants to let users log in using their existing Google account and needs to receive verified proof of the user's identity, not just an access token for an API. Which protocol should it use?

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: The OS is the foundational software that manages a computer's hardware resources and provides the platform on which all other applications run, such as Windows, Linux, or macOS. Because the OS controls nearly everything on a device, keeping it patched and properly hardened is one of the most fundamental security responsibilities for any endpoint or server.
examContext: SY0-701 references the OS constantly as the layer where patch management, hardening, EOL/EOS risk, and privilege management all take place; an outdated or end-of-life OS is a recurring exam theme for unmitigated vulnerability risk.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam discovers several servers are still running an operating system version that reached end-of-life two years ago and no longer receives security patches from the vendor. He prioritizes an OS upgrade project for those servers, since no amount of other hardening can fully compensate for unpatched, unsupported OS-level vulnerabilities.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan reveals several production servers are running an operating system version that the vendor stopped releasing security patches for two years ago. What is the most appropriate long-term remediation?
quizOptions: A) Upgrade the servers to a currently supported OS version
B) Add more firewall rules around the servers and leave the OS as-is indefinitely
C) Disconnect the servers from the network permanently
D) Increase the frequency of vulnerability scans only

definition: A conceptual seven-layer model, including Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application layers, that describes how network communication functions are organized, used as a common reference for understanding where specific protocols and attacks operate.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to map security devices and attacks to OSI layers; for example, switches and VLANs operate at Layer 2, routers and IP at Layer 3, firewalls commonly at Layers 3 through 4, and web application attacks at Layer 7.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is training junior analysts to understand where different attacks occur in the network stack. Maria explains that ARP spoofing happens at Layer 2 of the OSI model, IP spoofing at Layer 3, and cross-site scripting at Layer 7, helping the team choose the right layer-appropriate defenses for each threat.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst is explaining that a switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses while a router forwards packets based on IP addresses, using a common reference for describing these different functions. Which model is being used?

definition: Information gathered from publicly available sources, such as social media, websites, and public records, to support security assessments or attacks. Both penetration testers and threat actors use OSINT during the reconnaissance phase.
examContext: SY0-701 places OSINT under reconnaissance techniques used in the attack lifecycle and during authorized penetration testing engagements; know it involves no direct interaction with the target systems themselves.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan, a penetration tester, spends the first day of an engagement mining LinkedIn profiles, DNS records, and job postings to map the target company's technology stack and employee names before any active scanning begins. The resulting OSINT report informs a realistic phishing pretext for the next test phase.
detail.quizQuestion: During the reconnaissance phase of an authorized penetration test, a tester collects employee names and technologies from public job listings and social media without touching the target's network. What is this activity called?

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

definition: A link-state interior gateway routing protocol that determines the most efficient path for data across a network by calculating shortest paths between routers, widely used within large enterprise and service-provider networks.
examContext: SY0-701 expects baseline recognition of OSPF as a dynamic interior routing protocol; security considerations include enabling route authentication to prevent route injection or spoofing attacks that could redirect traffic through a malicious router.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria notices that routers on the internal network are accepting route updates from any device on the segment, creating a risk of a rogue device injecting false routes. Maria enables OSPF route authentication so routers only accept link-state updates from trusted, authenticated neighbors, preventing route injection attacks.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer wants to prevent a rogue device from injecting false routes into the internal dynamic routing protocol used between enterprise routers. What should be enabled on this link-state protocol?

definition: Hardware and software that monitors and controls physical devices and industrial processes, such as SCADA systems and manufacturing equipment. OT environments often prioritize availability and safety over confidentiality, requiring different security approaches than traditional IT.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes OT/ICS environments from IT, noting OT often runs legacy, unpatched systems where availability and safety are paramount, so security controls like network segmentation and monitoring are preferred over disruptive patching.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen segments the water treatment plant's OT network from the corporate IT network using a dedicated firewall and data diode, preventing an IT-side ransomware infection from ever reaching the programmable logic controllers. Production continues uninterrupted even after the corporate network is compromised.
detail.quizQuestion: A manufacturing plant cannot patch its industrial control systems without halting production for weeks. Which strategy best reduces risk in this operational technology environment?
quizOptions: A) Force immediate patching regardless of downtime
B) Move the OT systems directly onto the public internet
C) Disable all monitoring to reduce overhead
D) Network segmentation and compensating controls

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: OTA refers to the wireless delivery of software, firmware, or configuration updates directly to a device without a physical cable connection, common for smartphones, IoT devices, and connected vehicles. OTA update mechanisms must be secured with code signing and encrypted delivery, since an insecure OTA channel could let an attacker push malicious firmware to thousands of devices at once.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference OTA updates in the context of mobile device and IoT firmware security, where verifying the authenticity and integrity of an OTA update package (e.g., via digital signatures) prevents attackers from distributing malicious firmware through the update channel itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's team reviews the OTA update process for the company's fleet of IoT sensors and confirms that every firmware package is digitally signed and verified by the device before installation. This prevents an attacker who intercepts the OTA channel from pushing unsigned, malicious firmware onto thousands of deployed sensors at once.
detail.quizQuestion: A manufacturer wants to ensure that its IoT devices cannot be tricked into installing malicious firmware if an attacker intercepts or spoofs the wireless update channel. Which control on the over-the-air update process would best prevent this?
quizOptions: A) Sending updates over an unencrypted channel for speed
B) Requiring digitally signed firmware that the device verifies before installing
C) Disabling all future updates after the first one
D) Allowing any file with a matching filename to install

definition: A standardized XML-based language for describing system configuration information, vulnerabilities, and compliance checks so automated tools can consistently assess machine state. It is one of the component standards that make up SCAP.
examContext: SY0-701 groups OVAL under SCAP as a standard for expressing vulnerability and configuration checks in a machine-readable format; remember it is about describing checks, not performing the scan itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex writes an OVAL definition describing the exact registry key and patch level that indicates a vulnerable Windows service, then feeds it into the organization's SCAP-compliant scanner so every endpoint is checked the same way. Audit results become consistent and automatically comparable across thousands of machines.
detail.quizQuestion: A compliance team wants vulnerability checks expressed in a standardized, machine-readable format so multiple scanning tools interpret them identically. Which component of SCAP enables this?

definition: A nonprofit community that produces freely available resources on web application security, most notably the OWASP Top 10, a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks.
examContext: SY0-701 commonly references the OWASP Top 10 in the context of web application vulnerabilities like injection and broken access control; know that OWASP is the authoritative source for web app risk categories, testing guides, and secure coding standards.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's team is launching a new customer-facing web application and wants to validate its security posture before launch. Jordan runs the application through tests aligned with the OWASP Top 10 and finds a broken access control flaw that would have let any logged-in user view other customers' order histories.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants a widely recognized, regularly updated reference list of the most critical web application security risks to guide their secure coding review. Which resource should they consult?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A P12 (or PFX) file is a password-protected archive format that bundles a private key together with its corresponding public key certificate (and any chain certificates) into a single portable file. It's commonly used to import or export a certificate and its private key together, such as when installing a certificate on a new server.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference P12/PFX files in the context of certificate management and PKI; know that because a P12 file contains the private key itself, it must be protected with a strong password and handled far more carefully than a public-only certificate file like a .cer or .pem containing no private key.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen needs to migrate a web server's TLS certificate to a new load balancer and exports it as a password-protected P12 file containing both the certificate and its private key. He transfers the file over an encrypted channel and immediately deletes the local copy afterward, since anyone who obtains that P12 file could impersonate the server.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator needs to move a TLS certificate and its private key together to a new server as a single file. Which file format is designed to bundle both a certificate and its private key into one password-protected archive?
quizOptions: A) A .pem file containing only the public certificate
C) A plain .txt export of the public key

definition: P2P is a network architecture in which devices communicate and share resources directly with each other rather than through a centralized server, commonly seen in file-sharing applications and some blockchain/cryptocurrency networks. P2P traffic is a common vector for malware distribution and can also expose sensitive files if an employee misconfigures sharing software on a corporate machine.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference P2P applications as a security risk needing policy restriction (e.g., via an AUP or application whitelisting), since P2P software run on a corporate endpoint can both leak sensitive files and serve as a malware entry point.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's DLP alerts show a corporate laptop running a P2P file-sharing application that has inadvertently shared the entire "Documents" folder, including confidential contracts, with anyone on that P2P network. She has the software removed and updates the acceptable use policy to explicitly prohibit P2P applications on company devices.
detail.quizQuestion: A DLP alert reveals that an employee's laptop is running file-sharing software that has made an entire local folder, including confidential company documents, available to unknown users on the internet. What type of application is most likely responsible for this exposure?
quizOptions: B) A cloud storage sync client

definition: A cloud service model that provides a managed runtime environment, including operating system, middleware, and development tools, so developers can build and deploy applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish PaaS from IaaS and SaaS on the shared responsibility model: in PaaS, the provider manages the OS and runtime while the customer is responsible for the application code and data.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's development team wants to deploy a web application without managing servers, patching operating systems, or configuring runtime environments. Maria selects a PaaS offering so developers can push code directly, while the cloud provider handles the underlying OS, patching, and infrastructure scaling.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants to focus solely on writing application code without managing servers, operating systems, or runtime patching. Which cloud service model best fits this need?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: A PAC file is a small script that tells a web browser which proxy server to use for a given URL, allowing automatic and centralized control of how web traffic is routed. Organizations use PAC files to force browsers through inspection proxies or content filters without manual configuration on each device.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference PAC files as a mechanism for transparently directing client web traffic to a secure web gateway or proxy for content filtering and monitoring; know it is distributed automatically rather than configured by hand on each machine.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya pushes a PAC file to every managed laptop through group policy so that all web requests are automatically routed through the company's secure web gateway, even when employees work from home, ensuring content filtering and malware scanning apply consistently.
detail.quizQuestion: A security administrator wants every corporate laptop's browser to automatically route web traffic through a content-filtering proxy without requiring users to manually enter proxy settings. Which mechanism accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) A PAC file distributed via group policy
C) A new DNS A record
D) A local hosts file edit

definition: A set of tools and policies for controlling, monitoring, and auditing accounts with elevated permissions, such as administrator or root accounts. PAM reduces the attack surface created by standing privileged access through techniques like credential vaulting and just-in-time elevation. (Note: PAM can also stand for Pluggable Authentication Modules — a Linux authentication framework — distinct from Privileged Access Management, which this card focuses on.)
examContext: SY0-701 covers PAM under privileged account management, including concepts like just-in-time access, password vaulting, and session recording; know PAM minimizes the time and scope of elevated privileges rather than eliminating them.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria deploys a PAM solution that vaults all domain administrator passwords and requires approval plus automatic password rotation after each checkout. When an admin account is checked out for a single maintenance task, its credentials are automatically rotated afterward so no standing privileged session remains.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants administrators to request temporary elevated access that is automatically revoked and rotated after use, rather than holding permanent admin rights. Which solution addresses this?

items.name: Privileged Access Management
items.detail: Controls, vaults, rotates and audits the credentials of administrator and other powerful accounts: password vaulting, just-in-time elevation, session recording and ephemeral credentials.

items.name: Pluggable Authentication Modules
items.detail: A Linux/Unix framework (configured in /etc/pam.d) that lets administrators plug different authentication methods (passwords, MFA, LDAP, smart cards) into services without changing the applications.

items.name: Just-in-time permissions
items.detail: Privilege is granted only when needed and removed automatically afterwards, so no one holds standing admin rights.

items.name: Password vaulting
items.detail: Privileged credentials are stored encrypted in a vault, checked out by approved users, and rotated after use.

items.name: Ephemeral credentials
items.detail: Short-lived credentials or tokens created on demand for a single task or session, so there is nothing long-lived to steal.

items.name: Session recording
items.detail: Privileged sessions are monitored and recorded for audit and forensics.

items.name: Least privilege / separation of duties
items.detail: Give only the access needed, and split sensitive tasks across people so no single person can complete fraud alone.

definition: A legacy authentication protocol that transmits usernames and passwords in plaintext over a point-to-point link, offering no encryption or protection against eavesdropping. It has largely been replaced by stronger protocols like CHAP and EAP.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize PAP as an insecure, cleartext authentication method often mentioned alongside CHAP as the secure alternative; if a scenario mentions passwords sent unencrypted during PPP authentication, think PAP.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam discovers during a network assessment that an old dial-up VPN concentrator is still configured to accept PAP authentication, exposing user passwords in cleartext on the wire. He reconfigures the device to require CHAP or a modern EAP method instead, eliminating the plaintext exposure.
detail.quizQuestion: A packet capture reveals that a legacy remote-access link transmits user credentials completely unencrypted during authentication. Which protocol is most likely in use?

definition: A form of network address translation that maps many internal private IP addresses to a single public IP address by distinguishing connections using different port numbers. It conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides internal network topology.
examContext: SY0-701 may test PAT as a variant of NAT where one public address is shared among many internal hosts via port mapping; distinguish it from static NAT (DNAT), which maps one-to-one.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures the branch office firewall to use PAT so that all 200 internal workstations share the single public IP address assigned by the ISP, with the firewall tracking each session by source port. This conserves the limited public IPv4 allocation while still letting every workstation reach the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A small office has only one public IP address but needs dozens of internal devices to access the internet simultaneously. Which technology makes this possible?

items.name: Static NAT
items.detail: One-to-one fixed mapping between a private and a public address. Used to publish an internal server.

items.name: Dynamic NAT
items.detail: Private addresses are mapped to a pool of public addresses on demand.

items.name: PAT (NAT overload)
items.detail: Many private hosts share ONE public IP, distinguished by port numbers. What home routers do.

items.name: DNAT / port forwarding
items.detail: Destination NAT: rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so an outside client can reach an internal service.

items.name: Security note
items.detail: NAT hides internal addressing but is NOT a firewall; it provides no real protection by itself.

definition: PBKDF2 is a key derivation function that repeatedly hashes a password together with a random salt thousands or millions of times to produce a cryptographic key, deliberately slowing down the process to resist brute-force and rainbow table attacks. It is widely used for securely storing password hashes and deriving encryption keys from passphrases.
examContext: Exam questions test recognition of PBKDF2 as a key-stretching algorithm alongside bcrypt and Argon2; remember it combines salting with a configurable iteration count to increase computational cost for attackers.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen updates the user authentication service to store password hashes using PBKDF2 with a unique salt per account and 600,000 iterations, so that even if the password database is stolen, attackers cannot feasibly brute-force the original passwords.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer wants to store user passwords in a way that resists brute-force cracking even if the database is stolen, by making each guess computationally expensive. Which technique should be used?
quizOptions: B) PBKDF2 with a unique salt and high iteration count
C) A single unsalted MD5 hash
D) Symmetric encryption with a shared key

definition: A PBX is a private telephone switching system that routes calls within an organization and connects internal extensions to outside phone lines. Unsecured or misconfigured PBX systems can be exploited for toll fraud, eavesdropping, or as a pivot point into the corporate network.
examContext: SY0-701 covers PBX under physical and communications security; know that default credentials and remote administration features on a PBX are common attack vectors for toll fraud and voicemail hacking.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan audits the company's PBX and finds the remote administration portal still using the factory default password, which could let an outsider reroute calls or rack up charges through expensive international lines; he changes the credentials and disables remote access from the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's monthly phone bill shows thousands of dollars in international calls that no employee placed. Which system was most likely compromised to enable this toll fraud?

definition: A file format and method for recording the full contents of network traffic as it crosses an interface, capturing complete packet data, including headers and payloads, for detailed forensic analysis and troubleshooting.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know PCAP files preserve full packet content, unlike NetFlow which only captures metadata, making them essential for deep forensic investigation but costly to store at scale; tools like Wireshark read and analyze PCAP files.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is investigating a suspected data exfiltration incident and needs to see the exact contents of the suspicious traffic, not just summary statistics. Maria pulls the PCAP captured by a network tap at the time of the incident and opens it in Wireshark, confirming that sensitive customer data was sent unencrypted to an external IP address.
detail.quizQuestion: A forensic investigator needs to examine the exact payload contents of suspicious traffic captured during an incident, not just summary flow statistics like source, destination, and byte counts. What should the investigator analyze?

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

definition: Refers to the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a set of security requirements that organizations handling credit card data must follow to protect cardholder information. Non-compliance can result in fines, increased transaction fees, or loss of card processing privileges.
examContext: SY0-701 treats PCI DSS as a key example of an industry-specific regulatory framework (as opposed to a government law); remember it applies to any organization that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, regardless of size.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's e-commerce company undergoes an annual PCI DSS assessment, which requires her to segment the cardholder data environment onto its own VLAN and encrypt stored card numbers. Passing the assessment keeps the company's merchant account with its payment processor in good standing.
detail.quizQuestion: An online retailer that stores customer credit card numbers must comply with which standard to maintain its ability to process card payments?

expansion: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
definition: PCI DSS is a contractual security standard created by major card brands that defines requirements for protecting cardholder data, including network segmentation, encryption, access control, and regular testing. Any organization that stores, processes, or transmits credit card data must comply, regardless of size or industry.
examContext: Know PCI DSS as an industry-mandated contractual standard rather than a government law, and that it specifically targets payment card data; expect it in scenario questions about e-commerce or retail environments handling card transactions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's online retail company fails its annual PCI DSS assessment because customer card numbers are stored unencrypted on an internal reporting server; the team segments that server off the main network and encrypts the stored data before the next audit cycle.
detail.quizQuestion: An e-commerce company that accepts credit card payments must follow a specific industry security standard covering encryption, access control, and network segmentation for cardholder data. Which standard applies?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: A PDU is a device that distributes electrical power from a single source to multiple pieces of equipment in a server rack or data center, often with remote monitoring and outlet-level switching. PDUs are a key part of availability planning alongside UPS systems and backup generators.
examContext: Exam scenarios about resiliency and redundancy may reference dual PDUs fed from separate circuits as a control against a single power failure taking down an entire rack.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam installs two PDUs in each server rack, each fed from a different electrical circuit, so that servers with redundant power supplies stay online automatically if one circuit or PDU fails during maintenance.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center wants to ensure that a single electrical circuit failure does not take down an entire server rack. What should be implemented alongside dual power supplies in each server?
quizOptions: D) Dual PDUs fed from separate circuits

definition: A version of EAP that wraps the authentication exchange in an encrypted TLS tunnel before credentials are transmitted, commonly used to secure wireless network authentication in WPA2 and WPA3 Enterprise deployments.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know PEAP protects user credentials during 802.1X wireless authentication by establishing a TLS tunnel first, similar to how HTTPS protects HTTP, preventing credentials from being exposed in plaintext over the air.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is configuring enterprise Wi-Fi authentication and wants to ensure employee usernames and passwords are never exposed in plaintext over the air. Chen configures PEAP so the authentication server establishes an encrypted TLS tunnel before the client's credentials are ever transmitted across the wireless network.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator configuring WPA2-Enterprise wireless authentication wants to ensure user credentials are never sent over the air without encryption. Which EAP method wraps credentials inside a TLS tunnel before transmission?

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

definition: A PED is any personally owned portable device, such as a smartphone, tablet, or smartwatch, that an employee or visitor might bring into a secure facility. Unrestricted PEDs create risks of unauthorized photography, audio recording, data exfiltration, and introduction of malware through unmanaged devices.
examContext: SY0-701 may test PED restrictions as a physical security control in sensitive areas like data centers or SCIFs, often alongside clean desk and visitor logging policies.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's organization requires visitors and even employees to leave personal phones and tablets in lockers before entering the data center floor, reducing the risk that a PED could be used to photograph sensitive rack labeling or cabling diagrams.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to prevent visitors from photographing sensitive equipment inside its data center. Which policy addresses this risk?
quizOptions: B) Restricting personal electronic devices from the secure area
C) Enabling full disk encryption on servers
D) Rotating service account passwords monthly

definition: A Base64 ASCII text format for encoding and storing X.509 certificates, private keys, and certificate chains, delimited by header and footer lines such as '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----'. It is the most common certificate container format used across web servers and PKI tooling.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to recognize PEM as a Base64-encoded certificate file format (readable as plain text) as opposed to binary formats like DER or PKCS#12; know that a .pem file can contain a certificate, a private key, or both.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex exports a web server's certificate and private key into a single PEM file so the Nginx configuration can reference one plain-text file for TLS termination. Because PEM is Base64 text, Alex can also open the file in a text editor to confirm the certificate boundaries before deployment.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator needs to copy a certificate and private key between systems in a human-readable, Base64-encoded text format. Which file format should be used?

definition: PFS is a property of certain key exchange methods ensuring that each session uses a unique, temporary key that is not derived from a long-term private key. This means that even if an attacker later steals the server's private key, previously captured encrypted sessions cannot be decrypted.
examContext: Exam questions link PFS to ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (DHE or ECDHE) in TLS cipher suites, and may ask why these are preferred over static RSA key exchange for protecting past traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya reconfigures the organization's web servers to prioritize ECDHE-based cipher suites instead of static RSA key exchange, enabling perfect forward secrecy so that a future compromise of the server's private key cannot be used to decrypt previously recorded HTTPS sessions.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to ensure that if a web server's private key is ever stolen in the future, previously captured encrypted traffic cannot be decrypted. Which property should the TLS configuration provide?

definition: An encryption application that provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for emails and files using a combination of symmetric and asymmetric cryptography and a decentralized web-of-trust model. It is a common alternative to S/MIME for securing email content.
examContext: SY0-701 may contrast PGP's web-of-trust key validation model with S/MIME's hierarchical CA-based trust model; both provide email encryption and digital signatures but manage trust differently.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria encrypts a sensitive contract using the recipient's PGP public key before emailing it, and digitally signs the message with her own private key so the recipient can verify both confidentiality and authenticity. Neither party needs to trust a centralized certificate authority because they exchanged public keys directly.
detail.quizQuestion: Two business partners want to encrypt and sign emails without purchasing certificates from a certificate authority, instead directly exchanging and verifying each other's public keys. Which approach fits this model?
quizOptions: A) S/MIME with an enterprise CA

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: Any individually identifiable health information, such as medical records, diagnoses, or treatment history, that is created, received, or maintained by a healthcare provider and protected under regulations like HIPAA. Breaches of PHI carry specific legal reporting and penalty requirements.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize PHI as a regulated data type under HIPAA, distinct from PII; a scenario describing a hospital or clinic data breach usually signals PHI-specific compliance obligations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's hospital encrypts all patient records containing PHI both at rest in the database and in transit to the billing vendor, and logs every access to satisfy HIPAA's audit requirements. When a laptop containing unencrypted PHI is later reported stolen, the breach must be reported within the regulation's required timeframe.
detail.quizQuestion: A healthcare clinic's database stores patient diagnosis codes and treatment histories. Under which classification must this data be protected?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

items.name: Public
items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: Any data that can be used on its own or combined with other information to identify a specific individual, such as a name, Social Security number, or email address. Protecting PII is a core driver of data classification, privacy law, and data loss prevention programs.
examContext: SY0-701 treats PII as a foundational data classification category tested alongside PHI and data privacy concepts; expect scenario questions about labeling, handling, or a breach involving customer PII.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's DLP solution to automatically detect and block emails containing unmasked Social Security numbers and credit card numbers from leaving the network. This prevents accidental PII exposure when employees mistakenly attach the wrong spreadsheet to an external email.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to automatically prevent employees from emailing unmasked customer Social Security numbers outside the organization. Which control best achieves this?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: A PIV card is a government-issued smart card that cryptographically proves an employee's or contractor's identity for both physical building access and logical access to computer systems. It typically combines a certificate-holding chip with a PIN, providing multifactor authentication in a single credential.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs PIV with CAC (Common Access Card) as examples of smart-card-based authentication; remember it combines something you have (the card) with something you know (the PIN) to satisfy MFA.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's federal agency issues PIV cards containing an embedded certificate, requiring employees to insert the card into a reader and enter a PIN before they can log into any workstation, satisfying multifactor authentication with a single physical credential.
detail.quizQuestion: A federal agency wants employees to use a single physical credential that satisfies multifactor authentication for both building entry and computer login. Which solution fits this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A PIV card with an embedded certificate and PIN
B) A printed list of one-time codes
C) A username and password stored in a browser
D) A shared RFID badge with no PIN

definition: A set of numbered specifications (PKCS#1 through PKCS#15) published by RSA Security that define standard formats and procedures for implementing public-key cryptography, such as PKCS#12 for bundling a certificate with its private key. They promote interoperability between cryptographic software and hardware.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference PKCS#12 specifically as a password-protected file format (.p12/.pfx) used to export a certificate and its private key together; know it differs from the plain-text PEM format.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen exports a code-signing certificate along with its private key into a password-protected PKCS#12 file so the build server can sign application releases without storing the key in plain text. The .p12 file is then stored in a hardware security module rather than on the build server's disk.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer needs to export a certificate and its private key together into a single password-protected file for safe transport to another server. Which standard format should be used?
