definition: The complete framework of policies, roles, hardware, and software used to create, manage, distribute, store, and revoke digital certificates and public keys. It underpins trust for TLS, email encryption, code signing, and more.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests PKI components, including certificate authorities, registration authorities, CRLs, OCSP, and certificate chains of trust; expect scenario questions about certificate issuance, revocation, and trust validation.
relatedAcronyms: CA, CRL, OCSP, RSA, PEM, PKCS

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan builds out a two-tier PKI with an offline root CA and an online issuing CA, so the organization can issue, renew, and revoke employee and server certificates without ever exposing the root key to the network. If the issuing CA is ever compromised, the offline root remains safe and can issue a replacement.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to minimize the risk of its root signing key being compromised while still issuing certificates regularly. What architecture should be used?
quizOptions: A) A single online root CA
B) A two-tier CA hierarchy with an offline root
C) Self-signed certificates for all servers
D) Shared private keys across all departments

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: An email retrieval protocol (commonly POP3) that downloads messages from a mail server to a single client, typically deleting them from the server afterward. It lacks native encryption, so it is normally run over an encrypted tunnel or replaced with IMAP.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to identify POP3's default port (110, or 995 for POP3S) and recognize it as an email retrieval protocol that, unlike IMAP, does not keep mail synchronized across multiple devices.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex notices that sales staff using POP3 on their laptops lose access to old emails once they're downloaded and removed from the server, causing confusion when switching between a phone and a laptop. He migrates the team to IMAP so messages stay synchronized across every device.
detail.quizQuestion: Users complain that emails downloaded on one device no longer appear on their phone. Which legacy protocol configuration is the most likely cause?
quizOptions: D) POP3 configured to delete mail from the server

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: POTS refers to the traditional analog landline telephone network, which carries voice calls without the encryption, authentication, or modern signaling features found in digital or VoIP systems. Legacy POTS lines left in place for fax machines or alarm systems can become an overlooked and unmonitored path into a facility's communications.
examContext: Exam scenarios may reference a forgotten POTS line, such as one used for a fax machine or alarm dialer, as a legacy communication path that bypasses network security monitoring entirely.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen discovers an old POTS line still active for a fax machine in the finance department that bypasses the corporate firewall and network monitoring entirely; he has it disconnected since it could serve as an unmonitored channel for data exfiltration.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit finds an active analog phone line connected to a fax machine that never appears in any network monitoring logs. What risk does this legacy POTS line represent?
quizOptions: A) It provides an unmonitored communication path outside normal network security controls
C) It consumes excessive network bandwidth
D) It requires a firmware update

definition: PPP is a data link layer protocol that establishes a direct connection between two network nodes, commonly used for dial-up, DSL, and some WAN links. It supports authentication methods such as PAP and CHAP to verify the identity of the connecting party before allowing traffic.
examContext: Exam may ask you to distinguish PPP, a general point-to-point link protocol, from PPTP, which tunnels PPP traffic over an IP network for VPN use; know PAP sends credentials in clear text while CHAP uses a challenge-response.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex configures a legacy WAN link between two branch offices to use PPP with challenge-response authentication instead of the older plain-text method, preventing credentials from being captured by anyone monitoring the link.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer is configuring authentication for a point-to-point WAN link and wants to avoid sending credentials in clear text. Which authentication method used with PPP achieves this?

definition: PPTP is an early VPN tunneling protocol that wraps PPP packets for transmission across an IP network to create a private tunnel. It is now considered insecure because of weaknesses in its MS-CHAPv2 authentication and encryption, and modern VPNs use stronger alternatives.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to identify PPTP as a deprecated, insecure VPN protocol and choose a stronger replacement such as an IPSec-based VPN when asked to remediate a weak remote access solution.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria discovers that a remote branch office still connects to headquarters using a PPTP VPN tunnel; she migrates the connection to an IPSec-based VPN after learning that PPTP's authentication can be cracked, exposing the tunnel's traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: During a security review, an analyst finds a site-to-site VPN still using PPTP. What is the most appropriate remediation?
quizOptions: A) Increase the PPTP encryption key length
B) Disable logging on the VPN concentrator
C) Switch from MS-CHAPv2 to PAP
D) Migrate the tunnel to a modern protocol such as IPSec

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: A PSK is a secret value shared in advance between two parties and used to authenticate or derive encryption keys for their communication, commonly seen in WPA2/WPA3-Personal Wi-Fi and some site-to-site VPN configurations. Because everyone uses the same key, PSKs scale poorly and are hard to revoke for a single user in a large organization.
examContext: Exam distinguishes WPA2-PSK (Personal mode, a single shared passphrase) from WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X with individual RADIUS credentials); know that PSK cannot selectively revoke access for one user without changing the key for everyone.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya sets up a small branch office Wi-Fi network with WPA2-PSK and a strong shared passphrase since only five employees use it, but she recommends headquarters move to 802.1X enterprise authentication so each of its two hundred employees can have individually revocable credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: A company with hundreds of employees wants the ability to instantly revoke a single terminated employee's Wi-Fi access without changing credentials for everyone else. Why is a pre-shared key configuration unsuitable for this?
quizOptions: A) PSK only works with 2.4GHz networks
B) Every device shares the same key, so revoking one user requires changing it for everyone
C) PSK requires a certificate authority
D) PSK cannot be used with WPA3

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: PTZ describes a security camera that can be remotely panned, tilted, and zoomed to actively track activity across a wide area, rather than only covering a single fixed field of view. PTZ cameras let a smaller security staff monitor larger areas as a detective physical security control.
examContext: SY0-701 covers PTZ cameras under physical security and surveillance controls; know they are a detective control and are often combined with motion detection to automatically track movement.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security team installs a PTZ camera above the loading dock so a single guard can remotely follow a delivery vehicle and zoom in to verify a driver's badge, replacing four fixed cameras that previously left blind spots between their fields of view.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants one camera to actively follow personnel movement across a large loading dock and zoom in on identification badges instead of installing several fixed cameras. Which camera type should they deploy?
quizOptions: C) A fisheye lens static camera
D) A thermal imaging sensor only

definition: A PUP is software bundled with a legitimate application installer that gets installed with minimal or deceptive user consent. While not always outright malicious, PUPs commonly display intrusive ads, change browser settings, or track user activity, and can weaken overall system security.
examContext: Exam questions may ask you to classify an unwanted toolbar or bundled adware as a PUP rather than a virus or trojan, since it typically arrives through a legitimate-looking installation rather than direct exploitation.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's help desk receives a complaint about a new toolbar and a changed default search engine after a user installed a free file-conversion tool; endpoint protection flags the bundled software as a PUP, and Alex removes it before it can collect more browsing data.
detail.quizQuestion: After installing a free utility downloaded from the internet, a user's browser now has an unfamiliar toolbar and a different default search engine, though no overtly malicious activity is detected. How should this software be classified?

definition: RA can refer to either a Recovery Agent, a trusted role or entity holding special keys or credentials that can recover encrypted data if the original key is lost, forgotten, or unavailable, or a Registration Authority, the PKI component that verifies a requester's identity before a Certificate Authority issues a certificate. Context determines which meaning applies.
examContext: SY0-701 most often tests the Recovery Agent meaning in key-escrow scenarios, where a designated role can decrypt data such as EFS-protected files using an escrowed key when the original user's key is lost; separately, remember a Registration Authority offloads identity verification from the CA in a PKI hierarchy.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization designates a Recovery Agent role holding an escrowed key for EFS-encrypted files; when an employee departs unexpectedly without decrypting files needed for a legal hold, the recovery agent uses the escrowed key to restore access without ever needing the former employee's password.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee who encrypted sensitive files with EFS leaves the company abruptly, and legal needs the files decrypted for a hold. Which role can recover the data using an escrowed key?

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

items.name: Recovery Agent
items.detail: A designated person or role allowed to recover encrypted data when a user's own key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example EFS or BitLocker recovery).

items.name: Registration Authority
items.detail: A PKI component that verifies a requester's identity on the certificate authority's behalf before the CA issues a certificate. It does not sign certificates.

expansion: Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe
definition: RACE was a European research program that funded advanced communications and cryptography research, including the work that led to the RIPEMD family of hash functions. On the exam, it appears mainly as background explaining where RIPEMD originated.
examContext: You are unlikely to be tested on RACE in isolation; its exam relevance is almost entirely as the origin of RIPEMD, so remember the link between the two rather than details of the program itself.

detail.practicalScenario: While reviewing cryptographic hash history, Alex learns that RACE was the European research initiative that sponsored the work leading to the RIPEMD hash function, explaining why RIPEMD's name traces back to a European research effort.
detail.quizQuestion: The RIPEMD family of cryptographic hash functions originated from research funded by which European program?

definition: RAD is a software development methodology that emphasizes quick iterative prototyping and continuous user feedback over extensive upfront planning, allowing functional software to be delivered faster than traditional waterfall approaches. Security teams must adapt their review and testing processes to keep pace with RAD's fast release cycles.
examContext: Exam questions may contrast RAD's rapid, prototype-driven cycles with the more rigid phases of a traditional SDLC, and ask how security testing (such as automated scanning in CI/CD) should be integrated to keep up.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's development team adopts RAD to deliver a customer-facing feature in weekly prototype cycles, so she integrates automated security scanning directly into their CI/CD pipeline rather than relying on a single lengthy review at the end, keeping pace with the accelerated release schedule.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants to deliver working prototypes to users every week instead of following a lengthy multi-month planning phase. Which development methodology are they using, and what must security testing do to keep up?
quizOptions: A) RAD; integrate automated security testing into each rapid iteration
B) Waterfall; perform one final review before launch
C) Spiral; skip testing until the final spiral
D) Agile; eliminate all security reviews

definition: A centralized client/server protocol that provides authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) for users connecting to a network, such as through VPN or 802.1X-secured Wi-Fi. It encrypts only the password field within an otherwise unencrypted packet, using a shared secret between the client and server.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know RADIUS is a widely used AAA protocol for network access control (e.g., tying into 802.1X), and that it uses UDP and encrypts only the password, unlike protocols that encrypt the entire payload.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the corporate wireless controllers to authenticate every Wi-Fi connection against a central RADIUS server tied to Active Directory, so employees use their domain credentials instead of a shared pre-shared key. This also lets her instantly revoke a single terminated employee's network access without changing the Wi-Fi password for everyone else.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants centralized authentication for VPN and Wi-Fi access so a single disabled account immediately loses access to both. Which service should be deployed?

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: A storage technology that combines multiple physical disks into a single logical unit to improve performance, provide fault tolerance, or both, depending on the RAID level chosen. It supports the availability leg of the CIA triad by letting a system survive one or more disk failures without data loss.
examContext: SY0-701 ties RAID to availability and fault tolerance planning; know common levels conceptually (RAID 1 mirroring, RAID 5/6 striping with parity) and that RAID is not a backup substitute since it doesn't protect against accidental deletion or ransomware.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures the file server's storage array as RAID 6 so that up to two simultaneous disk failures can occur without any data loss or downtime, while a hot-spare drive rebuilds automatically. He still maintains separate offsite backups, since he knows RAID does not protect against accidental file deletion.
detail.quizQuestion: A server's storage must continue operating even if two drives fail simultaneously, without needing to restore from backup. Which solution addresses this requirement?

items.name: RAID 0 · striping
items.detail: Min 2 disks. Data is split (striped) across the disks so reads and writes are fast, but there is NO redundancy: one failed disk destroys the whole array. 100% of capacity is usable. Exam cue: "performance only / not fault tolerant."

items.name: RAID 1 · mirroring
items.detail: Min 2 disks. Every write is duplicated onto a second disk, so the array survives one disk failure. Usable capacity is 50%. Fast reads, simple recovery; a common choice for OS/boot volumes.

items.name: RAID 5 · striping + parity
items.detail: Min 3 disks. Data and parity are striped across all disks; survives ONE disk failure. Usable capacity is (n − 1) disks. Good read speed but slower writes (parity math), and a second failure during a rebuild loses the array.

items.name: RAID 6 · striping + dual parity
items.detail: Min 4 disks. Two independent parity blocks per stripe, so it survives TWO simultaneous disk failures. Usable capacity is (n − 2) disks. Safer than RAID 5 for large arrays; writes are slower still.

items.name: RAID 10 (1+0) · mirrored stripes
items.detail: Min 4 disks. Disks are mirrored in pairs, then the pairs are striped: high performance AND redundancy. It survives one failure per mirrored pair (not just any two), and only 50% of capacity is usable. Costly; popular for busy databases.

items.name: Parity
items.detail: Calculated check data (XOR math) stored alongside the data so the array can rebuild the contents of a failed disk from the surviving ones. RAID 5 and 6 use parity; RAID 0, 1 and 10 do not.

items.name: Hot spare
items.detail: An idle drive already installed in the array. When a disk fails, the controller automatically rebuilds onto the spare, shortening the window of reduced redundancy.

items.name: RAID is not a backup
items.detail: RAID protects against disk hardware failure only. It does NOT protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, corruption, or a site disaster, because the damage is mirrored or striped instantly. You still need backups.

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: A server or service that provides remote users with a secure entry point into an organization's internal network, historically over dial-up and now typically via VPN. It centralizes authentication and policy enforcement for remote connections.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference RAS in the context of legacy or VPN-based remote connectivity; recognize it as the general concept of a gateway that authenticates and grants remote users access to internal resources.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya deploys a RAS appliance that requires remote employees to authenticate with MFA and a corporate certificate before granting access to the internal file shares over an encrypted tunnel. Contractors who fail the device health check are redirected to a restricted guest network instead of the full internal network.
detail.quizQuestion: Remote employees need a single, centrally managed entry point into the corporate network that enforces authentication before granting access. What provides this function?

definition: A type of malware that gives an attacker covert remote control over an infected system, often enabling keylogging, file exfiltration, and webcam or microphone access. It typically arrives disguised as legitimate software or through phishing attachments.
examContext: SY0-701 classifies RATs as a malware type under remote-control malicious tooling; distinguish a RAT (attacker-controlled backdoor) from legitimate remote access software by its covert, unauthorized nature.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's EDR platform flags an unusual process establishing an encrypted outbound connection to an unfamiliar IP address every few minutes, which turns out to be a RAT installed via a malicious email attachment opened by an employee. Isolating the host and tracing the command-and-control traffic stops the attacker from exfiltrating further data.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst discovers a hidden process on an employee's workstation that gives an external IP address full control of the keyboard, mouse, and webcam. What type of malware is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: An access control model that grants permissions based on a user's assigned role within an organization rather than to each individual user directly. It simplifies permission management at scale because adding or removing a role automatically adjusts access. (Note: RBAC can also stand for Rule-based Access Control — access decisions driven by administrator-defined if-then rules — distinct from Role-Based Access Control, which this card focuses on.)
examContext: SY0-701 commonly contrasts RBAC with DAC and MAC; know that RBAC ties permissions to job function or role, making onboarding, offboarding, and audits more consistent and scalable.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen defines a 'Helpdesk Technician' role in the identity management system that bundles exactly the permissions needed to reset passwords and view, but not modify, user accounts. When new helpdesk staff are hired, Chen simply assigns them to the role instead of manually configuring dozens of individual permissions.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants new employees in the same job function to automatically receive an identical, pre-approved set of permissions without manual configuration for each person. Which access control model fits best?

items.name: Role-based access control
items.detail: Permissions are attached to ROLES (job functions) and users inherit them by holding the role. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties. This is the usual meaning.

items.name: Rule-based access control
items.detail: Access is decided by fixed RULES that apply to everyone regardless of identity or role, such as firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," or time-of-day restrictions.

items.name: How to tell which
items.detail: Job titles, groups and roles point to role-based. Conditions, schedules and ACL-style rules point to rule-based.

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: A fast symmetric stream cipher that was once widely used in protocols like WEP and early SSL/TLS, but is now considered cryptographically broken due to biases in its keystream output. It has been deprecated in favor of stronger algorithms like AES.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize RC4 as a deprecated, insecure stream cipher associated with WEP and legacy SSL; if a scenario describes a weak or outdated cipher being replaced, RC4 is a common answer.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex audits an old point-of-sale system and finds it still negotiates RC4 for its SSL connections, a cipher known to leak patterns in encrypted data over time. He disables RC4 in the server's cipher suite configuration, forcing all connections to use AES-based ciphers instead.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit finds a legacy system still supports a stream cipher known for statistical biases that can reveal plaintext patterns over many sessions. Which cipher is most likely being flagged?

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

definition: A structured problem-solving process used after an incident to identify the underlying cause of a failure or security event, rather than just its symptoms, so corrective actions can prevent recurrence.
examContext: SY0-701 ties RCA to the lessons-learned phase of incident response; expect it in the context of post-incident activity where teams determine not just what happened, but why it happened, to drive process or control improvements.

detail.practicalScenario: After containing a malware outbreak, Alex's incident response team conducts an RCA and discovers the actual root cause was not the malware itself but a missing patch management process that left a known vulnerability unaddressed for months. Alex uses this finding to justify funding for an automated patch management system.
detail.quizQuestion: After containing a malware outbreak, an incident response team investigates not just what happened but why the vulnerability existed in the first place, in order to prevent recurrence. What is this process called?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: A vulnerability class that allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code on a target system from a remote location, typically representing the most severe type of software flaw since it can lead to complete system compromise.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize RCE as the highest-severity vulnerability outcome, often scored critical in CVSS, frequently resulting from unpatched software, deserialization flaws, or buffer overflows that let attackers run their own code on the victim machine.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen reviews a vulnerability scan and finds a critical CVSS 9.8 finding on an internet-facing server describing an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in outdated web server software. Chen immediately isolates the server from the network and applies the emergency patch before attackers can exploit it to gain a foothold.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan flags an unauthenticated finding on an internet-facing server with a CVSS score of 9.8, noting that an attacker could run arbitrary commands on the host without any local access. What type of vulnerability is this?

definition: A Microsoft protocol that lets a user remotely view and control the full graphical desktop of another Windows computer over a network. It is a frequent target for attackers via brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks when exposed directly to the internet.
examContext: SY0-701 commonly cites exposed RDP (port 3389) as a high-risk attack surface for ransomware intrusion; the expected mitigation is placing RDP behind a VPN or RAS gateway and enforcing MFA and account lockout rather than exposing it directly to the internet.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria finds that a branch office server has port 3389 open directly to the internet for RDP, which internal logs show is being hit by thousands of brute-force login attempts daily. She closes the direct exposure and requires employees to connect through the VPN with MFA before reaching RDP internally.
detail.quizQuestion: A ransomware investigation reveals the initial access point was a Windows server with its remote desktop port exposed directly to the internet. Which control would have best prevented this?
quizOptions: C) Enabling IPv6 on the server
D) Requiring RDP access only through a VPN with MFA

definition: The electromagnetic spectrum range used for wireless communication, including Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and RFID. Security concerns involve signal jamming, eavesdropping, and unauthorized signal injection within this spectrum.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference RF in the context of wireless attacks such as jamming or RF signal analysis during a wireless site survey; know that RF interference can be a denial-of-service style attack on wireless availability.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam investigates recurring Wi-Fi dropouts in the warehouse and uses an RF spectrum analyzer to discover a malfunctioning forklift radio is jamming the 2.4 GHz band. Relocating the access points to the 5 GHz band and shielding the forklift radio resolves the connectivity loss.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees in one area of a warehouse report constant wireless disconnections. An RF spectrum analyzer shows heavy interference on the 2.4 GHz band. What is the most likely cause?
quizOptions: D) RF interference from another device

definition: A formal document published by the IETF that defines internet standards, protocols, and best practices, such as the documents defining IP or RADIUS. RFCs provide the authoritative technical specification that vendors implement against for interoperability.
examContext: SY0-701 may mention RFCs as the source of formal protocol definitions; you don't need to memorize specific RFC numbers, but should recognize RFC as the standards-document mechanism behind internet protocols.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team references the relevant RFC while implementing a custom RADIUS attribute, ensuring their vendor's implementation stays interoperable with other vendors' AAA servers. Following the published standard avoids compatibility issues during a later network merger with an acquired company.
detail.quizQuestion: Two vendors' networking equipment must interoperate using the same version of a protocol. Which type of document defines the authoritative technical standard both vendors implement?

definition: RFID is a wireless technology that uses radio waves to identify and track tags attached to objects, badges, or inventory without requiring direct line of sight or contact. In security contexts, RFID badges are commonly used for building access control, but unencrypted or poorly secured tags can be cloned or skimmed.
examContext: SY0-701 may test RFID in physical security scenarios involving badge cloning attacks; know that an attacker with a cheap reader can sometimes copy an unencrypted RFID badge's credentials from a short distance.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's penetration test team uses a concealed RFID reader to clone an employee's unencrypted access badge while standing near them in an elevator, then uses the cloned badge to walk into a restricted server room, demonstrating why the company needs encrypted, mutual-authentication badges.
detail.quizQuestion: During an authorized physical penetration test, testers use a hidden reader near employees to copy badge credentials and later gain building access with the clones. What weakness does this demonstrate?
quizOptions: C) Unencrypted RFID badges vulnerable to cloning

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

expansion: RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest
definition: RIPEMD is a family of cryptographic hash functions, with RIPEMD-160 being the most widely used variant, designed as an alternative to MD5 and SHA for producing a fixed-length digest of data to verify integrity. It is less commonly deployed today than the SHA-2 family but still appears in some cryptocurrency and legacy systems.
examContext: Exam may list RIPEMD among hashing algorithms alongside MD5 and SHA; know it is a hash function used for integrity verification, not an encryption algorithm, and that it originated from the RACE research program.

detail.practicalScenario: While documenting the cryptographic algorithms used by a legacy application, Sam notes that it relies on RIPEMD-160 for file integrity checks, and recommends evaluating a migration to SHA-256 since RIPEMD is far less commonly supported in modern toolchains.
detail.quizQuestion: A legacy application computes a fixed-length digest of each file to verify it has not been altered, using an algorithm that originated from European cryptographic research rather than NIST. Which algorithm is being used?

items.name: MD5
items.detail: 128-bit digest. Broken: practical collision attacks exist, so never use it where security matters. Still seen for quick, non-security file checks.

items.name: SHA-1
items.detail: 160-bit digest. Deprecated: collisions were demonstrated in 2017. Browsers and CAs no longer accept SHA-1 certificates.

items.name: SHA-2 (SHA-256 / SHA-512)
items.detail: The current workhorse family (224/256/384/512-bit digests). SHA-256 is the most common choice for file integrity, certificates and signatures.

items.name: SHA-3
items.detail: Standardized in 2015 using a different internal design (Keccak) from SHA-2. Not a replacement forced by SHA-2 weakness; it is a structurally different fallback.

items.name: RIPEMD
items.detail: Open-design 160-bit hash (RIPEMD-160), an alternative to the SHA family; best known for use in Bitcoin address generation.

items.name: bcrypt / PBKDF2 / Argon2
items.detail: NOT general-purpose hashes: these are deliberately slow password-hashing / key-stretching functions with built-in salting. Use them to store passwords, never plain SHA or MD5.

definition: A structured, NIST-defined process (categorize, select, implement, assess, authorize, monitor) for integrating security and risk management into an information system's lifecycle. It is widely mandated for U.S. federal information systems.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference RMF alongside NIST frameworks as a structured approach to managing organizational risk through continuous monitoring and authorization; know its cyclical, ongoing nature rather than a one-time checklist.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's federal agency follows the NIST RMF, categorizing a new system's data sensitivity, selecting applicable security controls, and obtaining a formal authorization to operate before the system goes live. Continuous monitoring afterward ensures the system's risk posture is reassessed rather than evaluated just once at launch.
detail.quizQuestion: A federal agency must formally categorize a system, select and implement controls, and obtain authorization before deployment, followed by ongoing monitoring. Which process describes this lifecycle?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: ROI is a financial metric that compares the benefit gained from an investment to its cost, expressed as a ratio or percentage. In security, ROI (or the related ROSI) helps justify spending on controls by weighing the cost of a safeguard against the reduction in expected loss it provides.
examContext: Exam scenarios may ask you to use ROI alongside ALE and ARO to justify whether a proposed security control is cost-effective, comparing its price to the amount of expected annual loss it would prevent.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria calculates the ROI of a proposed $50,000 intrusion prevention system by comparing its cost against the $200,000 annual loss expectancy it would eliminate, giving management a clear financial justification to approve the purchase.
detail.quizQuestion: A CISO must justify the cost of a new security control to executive leadership by comparing its price against the reduction in expected annual loss it provides. Which financial metric is being calculated?

definition: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time, that an organization can tolerate following a disruption, essentially how far back in time backups must reach. It directly drives how frequently backups must be taken.
examContext: SY0-701 frequently pairs RPO with RTO in business continuity and disaster recovery scenarios; remember RPO deals with data loss tolerance (backup frequency) while RTO deals with downtime tolerance (restoration speed).

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's organization sets an RPO of 15 minutes for its order database, which means backups and transaction log shipping must occur at least every 15 minutes to meet that target. After a server failure, the database is restored and replayed to within 15 minutes of the last transaction, satisfying the defined RPO.
detail.quizQuestion: A business impact analysis states the order database can lose no more than 15 minutes of transactions in a disaster. Which metric does this describe?

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

definition: A widely used asymmetric encryption algorithm based on the mathematical difficulty of factoring large prime numbers, used for secure key exchange, digital signatures, and certificate encryption. It underpins much of PKI and TLS key exchange, though it is gradually being supplemented by elliptic-curve alternatives for performance.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize RSA as a foundational asymmetric algorithm used in certificates and key exchange; compare it against ECC as a faster, smaller-key alternative providing equivalent security.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex generates a 2048-bit RSA key pair for the company's new web server certificate, balancing strong security against reasonable handshake performance. For a resource-constrained IoT deployment, he instead chooses ECC keys, which provide comparable security with much smaller key sizes.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator needs to choose an asymmetric algorithm for a new TLS certificate and wants broad compatibility with older clients. Which algorithm is the most common traditional choice?

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: RTBH is a network defense technique that uses BGP routing to redirect traffic to or from a targeted IP address into a null route, effectively dropping it at the network edge before it can consume bandwidth or reach its destination. It is commonly used by ISPs and large networks to mitigate volumetric DDoS attacks.
examContext: Exam may reference RTBH as a DDoS mitigation technique; know that it works at the routing layer by discarding traffic matched to a black-holed destination or source address, often coordinated with an upstream ISP.

detail.practicalScenario: During a large volumetric DDoS attack, Jordan works with the company's ISP to trigger an RTBH route that drops all traffic destined for the targeted server's IP address at the ISP's edge routers, preventing the flood from ever reaching the company's own network link.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's internet link is being saturated by a volumetric DDoS attack targeting one server's public IP. Which BGP-based technique can the ISP use to drop the malicious traffic before it consumes the customer's bandwidth?
quizOptions: A) Remotely Triggered Black Hole routing
C) Increasing the server's TTL value
D) Disabling NAT on the edge router

items.name: DoS vs DDoS
items.detail: DoS comes from a single source; DDoS is distributed across many compromised devices (a botnet), so it cannot be stopped by blocking one IP.

items.name: Volumetric
items.detail: Saturates bandwidth (UDP or ICMP floods).

items.name: Protocol
items.detail: Exhausts connection-state resources, such as a SYN flood against a firewall or server's state table.

items.name: Application layer
items.detail: Low bandwidth but expensive requests (HTTP floods, Slowloris) that tie up the web application.

items.name: Amplification
items.detail: A small spoofed request makes a third-party server (open DNS, NTP or memcached) send a much larger reply to the victim.

items.name: Reflection
items.detail: The attacker spoofs the VICTIM's IP as the source so that innocent servers send their responses to the victim, hiding the real attacker.

items.name: Defenses
items.detail: Rate limiting, CDN or scrubbing services, SYN cookies, WAF, RTBH (remotely triggered black hole) routing, and over-provisioned capacity.

definition: The maximum acceptable length of time a system or business process can remain down after a disruption before causing unacceptable harm to the organization. It drives the design and cost of disaster recovery solutions needed to meet that deadline.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs RTO with RPO; remember RTO answers how long the organization can be down, while RPO answers how much data can be lost. A shorter RTO typically requires more expensive high-availability solutions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's e-commerce company sets a 1-hour RTO for its checkout service, so she architects an active-standby cluster in a second data center that can take over automatically within minutes of an outage. Meeting this aggressive RTO required a higher infrastructure budget than a 24-hour RTO would have needed.
detail.quizQuestion: A business impact analysis determines that the online checkout system must be restored within one hour of an outage to avoid unacceptable revenue loss. Which metric does this one-hour figure represent?

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

definition: An operating system designed to process inputs and execute tasks within a guaranteed, strict time constraint, commonly used in embedded systems, industrial controllers, and IoT devices where predictable timing is critical to safety and function.
examContext: SY0-701 ties RTOS to embedded systems and ICS or OT security discussions; know that these systems often cannot be patched like general-purpose operating systems without risking timing-critical failures, making compensating controls like network segmentation essential.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is assessing security for an industrial robotic arm controller running an RTOS that cannot accept a general-purpose antivirus agent without risking missed real-time deadlines. Jordan instead isolates the controller on a segmented OT network with strict access controls, compensating for the RTOS's inability to run traditional endpoint security software.
detail.quizQuestion: A security assessor finds that an industrial controller's operating system cannot run traditional antivirus software without risking missed timing deadlines critical to the physical process it controls. What type of operating system is this?

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: RTP is a network protocol used to deliver audio and video over IP networks in real time, forming the media transport layer underneath many VoIP and video conferencing systems. RTP itself provides no encryption, so it is commonly paired with SRTP to protect call content from eavesdropping.
examContext: Exam questions may ask you to recognize RTP as the unencrypted media transport used by VoIP and VTC systems, and to choose SRTP when confidentiality of voice or video traffic is required.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen discovers that the company's VoIP system transmits call audio using plain RTP across the office network, making it possible for anyone with network access to capture and replay conversations; he reconfigures the system to use SRTP so call content is encrypted in transit.
detail.quizQuestion: A security assessment finds that a VoIP system's call audio can be captured and replayed by anyone with access to the local network segment. Which protocol substitution would best address this?
quizOptions: A) Replace RTP with SRTP to encrypt the media stream
C) Disable DHCP on the VoIP VLAN

definition: A standard for public-key encryption and digital signing of email, relying on certificates issued by a trusted CA to confirm sender identity and encrypt message content. It is commonly built into enterprise email clients like Outlook.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts S/MIME's CA-based trust model with PGP's web of trust; both provide email confidentiality and integrity, but S/MIME relies on a certificate hierarchy, which fits better in centrally managed enterprise environments.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam issues S/MIME certificates to every executive through the company's internal CA so that signed emails automatically show a verified sender badge in Outlook. When an executive's account is later phished, employees notice that spoofed emails lack the expected S/MIME signature and report them.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants its email client to automatically verify sender authenticity using certificates issued by its internal certificate authority. Which technology should be deployed?

items.name: Self-signed
items.detail: Signed by its own private key, so no third party vouches for it. Free and fine for labs or internal dev, but browsers warn users and it cannot be revoked by a public CA.

items.name: Public CA-issued
items.detail: Signed by a CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Required for public-facing sites.

items.name: Wildcard
items.detail: One certificate for *.example.com, covering every first-level subdomain. Convenient, but one stolen key exposes all of them.

items.name: SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
items.detail: One certificate that lists several specific hostnames or domains. Not to be confused with a SAN as a Storage Area Network; the exam uses both meanings.

items.name: DV / OV / EV
items.detail: Domain Validation proves only control of the domain; Organization Validation vets the company; Extended Validation is the strictest vetting.

items.name: Code signing
items.detail: Proves who published software and that it has not been altered since signing.

items.name: Machine / user / email
items.detail: Certificates that authenticate a device or a person, or sign and encrypt email (S/MIME).

items.name: Root certificate
items.detail: Self-signed certificate at the top of a chain, pre-installed in the OS/browser trust store.

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: A cloud computing model in which a provider hosts and manages a fully functional application that customers access over the internet, typically via subscription, without installing or maintaining the underlying infrastructure. Security responsibility is shared, with the provider securing the infrastructure and platform while the customer manages data and access configuration.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and their shared responsibility boundaries; for SaaS, remember the customer's main responsibilities are typically identity and access management and data classification, not patching servers.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company adopts a SaaS CRM platform and focuses its security efforts on enforcing SSO with MFA and configuring data-sharing permissions, since the vendor handles patching and infrastructure security. When evaluating a new SaaS vendor, she reviews their compliance report rather than their server hardening practices, which are outside the customer's visibility.
detail.quizQuestion: A company adopts a cloud-hosted CRM where the vendor manages the entire application and underlying infrastructure. Which responsibility most likely remains with the customer?
quizOptions: A) Patching the application server operating system
B) Managing user access and data permissions
C) Maintaining the physical data center

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: SAE is the secure key-establishment handshake used by WPA3 to replace WPA2's vulnerable four-way handshake, protecting Wi-Fi networks against offline dictionary attacks even when a weak passphrase is used. It is based on a technique sometimes called the Dragonfly handshake.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to associate SAE specifically with WPA3-Personal as the replacement for WPA2's PSK handshake, and to know it resists offline password-guessing attacks that worked against WPA2.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya upgrades the office Wi-Fi access points to WPA3, which uses the SAE handshake instead of WPA2's four-way handshake, protecting the network passphrase from the offline dictionary attacks that previously could have targeted captured WPA2 handshake traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator upgrades wireless access points from WPA2 to WPA3 specifically to prevent offline dictionary attacks against captured handshake traffic. Which handshake mechanism provides this protection in WPA3?

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: An XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an identity provider and a service provider, enabling single sign-on across different domains. It is widely used to let employees log into multiple web applications with one corporate identity.
examContext: SY0-701 ties SAML to federated identity and SSO scenarios; know that SAML assertions are issued by an identity provider and consumed by a service provider to grant access without re-entering credentials.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures SAML federation between the company's Active Directory and a third-party expense-reporting SaaS application, letting employees log in with their existing domain credentials through a single sign-on portal. When an employee is terminated, disabling their AD account immediately revokes access to every federated SAML application at once.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants employees to authenticate once internally and automatically gain access to several external web applications without separate logins. Which standard enables this federated single sign-on?

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: SAN most often refers to a Subject Alternative Name, a certificate extension field that lists additional identities, such as multiple domain names or IP addresses, that a single certificate is valid for. SAN can also mean a Storage Area Network, a dedicated high-speed network that provides block-level access to consolidated data storage, separate from the certificate meaning.
examContext: SY0-701 most commonly tests the Subject Alternative Name meaning, where a single certificate secures multiple domains or subdomains; remember that modern browsers require a matching SAN entry and increasingly ignore the older Common Name field alone. The Storage Area Network meaning appears separately in infrastructure and availability discussions.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam requests a single TLS certificate with several SAN entries covering www.example.com, mail.example.com, and app.example.com, letting one certificate secure all three subdomains instead of purchasing and managing a separate certificate for each.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants one TLS certificate to be valid for three different subdomains instead of issuing three separate certificates. Which certificate field makes this possible?
quizOptions: C) The Subject Alternative Name field

items.name: Self-signed
items.detail: Signed by its own private key, so no third party vouches for it. Free and fine for labs or internal dev, but browsers warn users and it cannot be revoked by a public CA.

items.name: Public CA-issued
items.detail: Signed by a CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Required for public-facing sites.

items.name: Wildcard
items.detail: One certificate for *.example.com, covering every first-level subdomain. Convenient, but one stolen key exposes all of them.

items.name: SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
items.detail: One certificate that lists several specific hostnames or domains. Not to be confused with a SAN as a Storage Area Network; the exam uses both meanings.

items.name: DV / OV / EV
items.detail: Domain Validation proves only control of the domain; Organization Validation vets the company; Extended Validation is the strictest vetting.

items.name: Code signing
items.detail: Proves who published software and that it has not been altered since signing.

items.name: Machine / user / email
items.detail: Certificates that authenticate a device or a person, or sign and encrypt email (S/MIME).

items.name: Root certificate
items.detail: Self-signed certificate at the top of a chain, pre-installed in the OS/browser trust store.

items.name: Storage Area Network
items.detail: A dedicated high-speed network that gives servers block-level access to shared storage arrays (Fibre Channel or iSCSI). Relevant to availability, replication and segmentation of storage traffic.

items.name: Subject Alternative Name
items.detail: A certificate field that lists additional hostnames, domains or IP addresses the certificate is valid for, so one certificate can cover several names. Modern browsers rely on SAN rather than the old Common Name.

definition: A cloud-delivered architecture that converges wide-area networking with network security functions like CASB, secure web gateway, and ZTNA into a single service, enabling secure access for remote and distributed users without routing traffic back through a central data center.
examContext: SY0-701 ties SASE to the shift toward cloud-delivered, identity-aware network security for remote and hybrid workforces; know that it combines networking (SD-WAN) and security (ZTNA, CASB) into one cloud-native service edge.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company has shifted to a fully remote workforce and needs secure, low-latency access to cloud applications without backhauling all traffic through an aging corporate data center. Jordan adopts a SASE architecture that combines SD-WAN connectivity with cloud-delivered zero trust access, letting remote employees connect securely and directly to cloud resources.
detail.quizQuestion: A company with a largely remote workforce wants to replace its traditional hub-and-spoke VPN with a cloud-delivered architecture that combines networking and security functions like ZTNA and CASB in one service. What should it adopt?

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: A system architecture used to monitor and control industrial processes across large geographic areas, commonly found in utilities, water treatment, and manufacturing, combining remote terminal units, sensors, and a central control system.
examContext: SY0-701 groups SCADA under ICS and OT security; expect questions about SCADA systems having legacy protocols, limited patching windows, and requiring network segmentation since availability often outweighs confidentiality in these environments.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is securing a water treatment facility's control network and discovers the SCADA system runs on decades-old software that cannot be patched without vendor support. Jordan implements strict network segmentation and a unidirectional data diode so the SCADA network can send monitoring data outward without allowing any inbound connections that could compromise the control system.
