detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst is asked to protect a water treatment plant's industrial control system that cannot tolerate downtime for patching. What type of system is this analyst protecting?

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: A NIST-developed suite of standards, including OVAL and CVE, that enables automated vulnerability management, measurement, and policy compliance evaluation across systems. It lets organizations run standardized, repeatable security checks with compatible tools.
examContext: SY0-701 groups SCAP with its component standards like CVE and OVAL as the automated framework for checking configuration and vulnerability compliance; expect it tied to vulnerability scanning and compliance automation questions.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's team adopts an SCAP-validated scanner to automatically check every server against the organization's STIG baseline, producing a standardized compliance report instead of a manual checklist. This lets auditors verify configuration compliance across thousands of servers in hours rather than weeks.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization needs an automated, standardized way to check thousands of servers against a security configuration baseline. Which framework enables this?

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: SCEP is a protocol that automates the process of requesting and issuing digital certificates to large numbers of devices, commonly used by MDM and UEM platforms to enroll mobile devices with certificates without manual intervention. It simplifies certificate lifecycle management at scale.
examContext: Exam may reference SCEP in the context of mobile device management, where it allows automatic certificate enrollment for devices connecting to corporate Wi-Fi or VPN; know it reduces manual PKI administration overhead for large device fleets.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures the organization's UEM platform to use SCEP so that every newly enrolled corporate smartphone automatically receives a certificate for Wi-Fi and VPN authentication without an administrator manually issuing and installing one on each device.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization needs to automatically issue authentication certificates to thousands of mobile devices as they enroll in the MDM platform, without manual administrator intervention per device. Which protocol enables this automated enrollment?

definition: A set of standards for physically connecting and transferring data between computers and peripheral devices such as hard drives and tape drives. While mostly a legacy hardware and storage interface, exposed or misconfigured SCSI/iSCSI storage targets can become a data exposure risk on a network.
examContext: SY0-701 touches on SCSI mainly in the context of storage and legacy hardware interfaces; know it as a storage connectivity standard rather than a security protocol itself, and that iSCSI (SCSI over IP) needs network-level protections like authentication and segmentation.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex discovers an iSCSI storage target on the network with no authentication configured, allowing any host on the VLAN to mount the raw disk volumes. He enables CHAP authentication on the iSCSI target and segments the storage network from general user traffic to close the exposure.
detail.quizQuestion: A network scan reveals an iSCSI storage target that any device on the VLAN can mount without credentials. What should be configured to remediate this?
quizOptions: A) Disable RAID on the array
B) Convert the array to SCSI from iSCSI
C) Enable CHAP authentication and segment the storage network
D) Increase the disk's rotational speed

definition: A virtualized approach to managing wide-area network connections across multiple sites that intelligently routes traffic over the best available path based on application needs and centrally applies security and routing policy.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SD-WAN improves branch office connectivity and is a key building block of SASE architectures, replacing expensive dedicated MPLS links with centrally managed, policy-driven routing over multiple transport types.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company has 50 branch offices relying on expensive MPLS circuits and wants to reduce costs while maintaining reliable connectivity to cloud applications. Alex deploys SD-WAN to intelligently route latency-sensitive traffic over the best available link, whether broadband or LTE, while centrally enforcing consistent security policy across all branches.
detail.quizQuestion: A company with many branch offices wants to replace costly dedicated circuits with a centrally managed solution that intelligently selects the best path for traffic across broadband, LTE, and MPLS links. What should it deploy?

definition: A collection of software tools, libraries, documentation, and code samples that developers use to build applications for a specific platform or service. A vulnerable or malicious SDK embedded in an app can introduce security flaws across every application that includes it.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference SDKs in the context of supply chain risk, since a compromised third-party SDK can propagate vulnerabilities into many downstream applications; also relevant to secure coding and application development practices.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security team discovers that a popular analytics SDK embedded in the company's mobile app silently exfiltrates more user data than disclosed in the privacy policy. They replace the SDK with a vetted alternative and add SDK review to the application security checklist before future dependencies are approved.
detail.quizQuestion: An investigation finds that a third-party analytics library bundled into a mobile app is secretly collecting excessive user data. What supply chain risk does this best illustrate?
quizOptions: C) A vulnerable or malicious SDK dependency

definition: The structured process of planning, designing, building, testing, deploying, and maintaining software, ideally with security integrated at every phase, a practice often called DevSecOps or shifting left. Embedding security early reduces the cost and impact of fixing vulnerabilities found late in development.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the concept of integrating security throughout the SDLC rather than only at the end (shift-left/DevSecOps); expect questions about where to insert code review, static or dynamic testing, and threat modeling within the lifecycle.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization adds automated static application security testing into the build pipeline early in the SDLC, catching an SQL injection flaw in a pull request before it ever reaches a test environment. Fixing the flaw during code review costs a fraction of what remediation after production release would have cost.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to catch vulnerabilities as early as possible rather than after deployment. At which phase should security testing first be introduced into the software development life cycle?
quizOptions: B) Only during user acceptance testing
C) During design and coding, before release
D) Only during the retirement phase

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: SDLM refers to the overarching methodology an organization chooses for structuring its software development lifecycle, such as waterfall, agile, spiral, or RAD, including where security activities like threat modeling and code review are embedded in the process. Choosing and enforcing a consistent SDLM helps ensure security is built in rather than bolted on after release.
examContext: Exam questions may ask you to identify where security controls, such as secure code review or static analysis, should be inserted within a chosen SDLM; know that a documented methodology is a governance control supporting a secure SDLC.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization formally adopts an agile SDLM and mandates that a static code analysis gate run automatically at the end of every sprint, ensuring security review happens continuously rather than only once at the end of a long release cycle.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to ensure security reviews happen consistently throughout software development rather than only at the very end of a project. What should it formally define and enforce?
quizOptions: A) A single end-of-project penetration test
B) A one-time employee security awareness class
C) An unstructured ad hoc coding process
D) A documented software development lifecycle methodology with embedded security checkpoints

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: A network architecture that separates the control plane, which makes forwarding decisions, from the data plane, which forwards traffic, allowing centralized, programmable management of network behavior through software rather than manual configuration of individual devices.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to understand SDN's control-plane and data-plane separation enables centralized security policy enforcement and rapid network reconfiguration, useful for microsegmentation and automated response to threats across the network.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's data center team wants to dynamically reroute traffic and apply security policies across hundreds of switches without manually touching each device. Chen implements an SDN controller that centrally programs forwarding and segmentation rules, allowing the security team to quarantine a compromised host by pushing a single policy change network-wide.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center wants to centrally program network forwarding behavior and security policy across hundreds of switches from a single controller, rather than configuring each device manually. Which architecture enables this?

definition: SE Linux is a Linux kernel security module that enforces mandatory access control policies, restricting what actions processes and users can perform regardless of standard file permissions. Even if an application is compromised, SE Linux policies can confine it to a limited set of allowed actions, reducing the impact of an exploit.
examContext: SY0-701 ties SE Linux directly to Mandatory Access Control (MAC) as a real-world implementation; know it enforces security labels and policies independently of the discretionary permissions a file owner sets.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables SE Linux in enforcing mode on a public-facing web server, so that even after an attacker exploits a vulnerability in the web application, the compromised process is confined by policy and cannot read sensitive files outside its designated web directory.
detail.quizQuestion: After a web application on a Linux server is exploited, the attacker's process is unable to access files outside the web directory even though the compromised account technically has broader file permissions. What security mechanism is enforcing this restriction?
quizOptions: C) SE Linux mandatory access control policy

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: A storage drive with encryption hardware built directly into its controller, automatically encrypting all data written to it using a key that never leaves the drive. It provides full-disk encryption with minimal performance overhead and no reliance on host-based software.
examContext: SY0-701 may mention SEDs as a hardware-based alternative to software full-disk encryption; know that a SED protects data at rest even if the drive is physically removed, as long as it's properly locked and the key is managed securely.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company standardizes on laptops with self-encrypting drives so that data at rest is automatically encrypted at the hardware level with no noticeable performance impact for users. When a laptop is later stolen from an employee's car, the SED ensures the data remains unreadable without the unlock credential.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants full-disk encryption on all laptops with minimal performance impact and no reliance on host software. Which solution best fits?

items.name: Full-disk
items.detail: Everything on the drive, including the OS (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS). Protects a lost or stolen device; data is exposed once the system is unlocked and running.

items.name: Partition / volume
items.detail: One partition or logical volume is encrypted while others stay in the clear.

items.name: File / folder
items.detail: Individual files (EFS, GPG, 7-Zip AES). Protects specific data even from other users of the same machine.

items.name: Database
items.detail: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files; column- or record-level encryption protects individual fields such as SSNs.

items.name: Transport / communication
items.detail: Protects data in motion: TLS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3. The data is not necessarily encrypted at the other end.

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: SEH is a Windows mechanism that manages how a program responds to runtime errors and exceptions. Attackers have historically exploited SEH by overwriting its handler records during a buffer overflow, redirecting program execution to attacker-controlled code when the corrupted exception handler is triggered.
examContext: Exam may mention SEH overwrite attacks as a specific buffer overflow exploitation technique on Windows; know that modern mitigations like SEHOP and ASLR were developed specifically to defend against this class of attack.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's security team finds that a legacy Windows application is vulnerable to an SEH overwrite attack, where a crafted overly long input corrupts the exception handler chain; she enables SEHOP and recommends the application be rebuilt with modern compiler protections.
detail.quizQuestion: A legacy Windows application crashes when fed an overly long crafted input, and analysis shows the exception handler chain was overwritten to redirect execution to attacker-controlled code. What type of exploitation technique does this describe?
quizOptions: B) A DNS cache poisoning attack

definition: A secure file transfer protocol that runs over an encrypted SSH connection, providing confidentiality and integrity for uploaded and downloaded files as well as strong authentication. It is the encrypted replacement for plaintext FTP.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize SFTP as the secure alternative to FTP, running over SSH (port 22) rather than FTP's cleartext channels; don't confuse it with FTPS, which instead wraps FTP in TLS.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan migrates the finance team's nightly file transfers from plaintext FTP to SFTP, ensuring that vendor payment files are encrypted in transit and that the server authenticates connections with SSH key pairs. A later packet capture confirms no payment file content is visible on the wire.
detail.quizQuestion: A finance team transfers sensitive payment files to a vendor every night and needs the transfer encrypted and authenticated with key-based credentials. Which protocol should replace their legacy plaintext FTP?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: A family of cryptographic hash functions, such as SHA-256, that produce a fixed-length digest from input data, used to verify data integrity and support digital signatures and password storage. Modern implementations like SHA-256 or SHA-3 are preferred over the broken SHA-1 and MD5.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize SHA-256 as a secure, currently recommended hashing algorithm, while SHA-1 and MD5 are considered cryptographically broken and should be flagged as findings in a security assessment.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's file integrity monitoring tool calculates a SHA-256 hash of every critical system file at a known-good baseline, then recalculates and compares hashes nightly to detect unauthorized modification. When a configuration file's hash unexpectedly changes overnight, the tool immediately alerts the security team to investigate.
detail.quizQuestion: A security tool needs to verify that a downloaded software installer has not been tampered with since the vendor published it. Which type of function is used to generate a comparable fixed-length value for this check?
quizOptions: C) A cryptographic hash function such as SHA-256

items.name: MD5
items.detail: 128-bit digest. Broken: practical collision attacks exist, so never use it where security matters. Still seen for quick, non-security file checks.

items.name: SHA-1
items.detail: 160-bit digest. Deprecated: collisions were demonstrated in 2017. Browsers and CAs no longer accept SHA-1 certificates.

items.name: SHA-2 (SHA-256 / SHA-512)
items.detail: The current workhorse family (224/256/384/512-bit digests). SHA-256 is the most common choice for file integrity, certificates and signatures.

items.name: SHA-3
items.detail: Standardized in 2015 using a different internal design (Keccak) from SHA-2. Not a replacement forced by SHA-2 weakness; it is a structurally different fallback.

items.name: RIPEMD
items.detail: Open-design 160-bit hash (RIPEMD-160), an alternative to the SHA family; best known for use in Bitcoin address generation.

items.name: bcrypt / PBKDF2 / Argon2
items.detail: NOT general-purpose hashes: these are deliberately slow password-hashing / key-stretching functions with built-in salting. Use them to store passwords, never plain SHA or MD5.

definition: S-HTTP was an early protocol designed to secure individual HTTP messages through encryption and digital signatures, developed as an alternative approach to what became HTTPS. It saw little real-world adoption and was superseded entirely by HTTPS, which secures the underlying transport connection using TLS/SSL instead of individual messages.
examContext: Exam may test whether you can distinguish the historical S-HTTP from the now-ubiquitous HTTPS; remember that HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) became the industry standard while S-HTTP did not, and the exam wants you to recognize this is a legacy/rarely-used protocol, not the one actually securing the modern web.

detail.practicalScenario: While researching legacy web security protocols for a history-of-cryptography presentation, Alex explains to junior analysts that S-HTTP was an early competing approach to securing web traffic that never gained adoption, while HTTPS using TLS became the standard every modern browser relies on today.
detail.quizQuestion: Which statement correctly distinguishes S-HTTP from HTTPS?
quizOptions: A) They are two names for the exact same protocol
B) S-HTTP became the modern web standard while HTTPS was abandoned
C) S-HTTP secured individual messages and saw little adoption, while HTTPS secures the transport connection using TLS and is the modern standard
D) S-HTTP is used only for email, not web traffic

definition: A platform that aggregates, correlates, and analyzes log and event data from across an organization's systems in real time to detect security incidents and support investigations. It centralizes visibility that would otherwise be scattered across dozens of individual device logs.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests SIEM as the central tool for log aggregation, correlation rules, and alerting; expect scenarios about detecting an incident through correlated log data from multiple sources feeding into a SIEM.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex builds a correlation rule in the SIEM that triggers an alert whenever a single user account fails login on five systems within one minute, a pattern indicative of password spraying. The SIEM's centralized view lets the SOC analyst spot the attack immediately instead of it being buried across five separate device logs.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to detect a password-spraying attack that generates failed logins across multiple separate systems within a short time window. Which tool is best suited to correlate these scattered events?
quizOptions: C) A single router's local log file

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Many failed logins from one account or source suggest brute force or spraying.

items.name: Concurrent session usage
items.detail: The same account logged in from several places or devices at once.

items.name: Impossible travel
items.detail: Logins from locations too far apart for the elapsed time, suggesting stolen credentials.

items.name: Blocked content
items.detail: Spikes of blocked connections or filtered downloads, which can reveal malware phoning home or users hitting malicious sites.

items.name: Resource consumption
items.detail: Unexplained CPU, memory, disk or bandwidth use, such as cryptojacking or data exfiltration.

items.name: Resource inaccessibility
items.detail: Services, files or systems suddenly unavailable: DoS, ransomware or a wiper.

items.name: Out-of-cycle logging
items.detail: Log entries or activity at unusual times, such as a batch job or admin login at 3 a.m.

items.name: Missing logs
items.detail: Gaps or deleted logs, a sign that an attacker is covering their tracks.

items.name: Published / documented
items.detail: Known IoCs and attack patterns from threat intelligence, such as a documented IP, hash or domain.

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

items.name: Log aggregation
items.detail: Collect logs from many sources into one place for correlation and search.

items.name: Alerting
items.detail: Notify people or systems when events match a rule or threshold.

items.name: Alert tuning
items.detail: Adjust thresholds and rules to cut false positives without missing real attacks.

items.name: Scanning and reporting
items.detail: Regular scans and reports show trends and compliance.

items.name: Archiving
items.detail: Keep logs for the retention period required for investigations and regulations.

items.name: Quarantine
items.detail: Isolate a suspicious file, system or message until it can be investigated.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agents give deep visibility and work off-network. Agentless is easier to deploy but shallower.

definition: A small smart card inserted into a mobile device that securely stores the subscriber's identity, authentication keys, and network credentials used to connect to a cellular carrier. SIM swapping, where an attacker tricks a carrier into porting a victim's number to a new SIM, is a common attack used to intercept SMS-based MFA codes.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference SIM swapping as a real-world attack against SMS-based multi-factor authentication; know that this is a major reason security guidance favors app-based or hardware-token MFA over SMS codes.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's bank account is compromised after an attacker convinces her mobile carrier to transfer her phone number to a new SIM card, allowing the attacker to intercept her SMS-based MFA codes. After the incident, she switches to an authenticator app for MFA, which is not tied to her phone number at all.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker convinces a victim's mobile carrier to port their phone number to a new SIM card in order to intercept one-time passcodes. What is the best mitigation against this attack?
quizOptions: A) Spam filtering on the email gateway
B) App-based MFA instead of SMS codes
C) Disabling Bluetooth on the device
D) DNS filtering on the corporate network

definition: A formal contract between a service provider and customer that defines measurable performance commitments, such as uptime percentage, response times, and remediation timelines. It gives the customer a contractual basis for holding a vendor accountable for service quality and security response times.
examContext: SY0-701 lists SLA among third-party and vendor agreement types; know that an SLA specifically defines measurable performance and support expectations, often including security incident response timeframes.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam negotiates an SLA with the company's cloud hosting provider that guarantees 99.9% uptime and a four-hour response time for critical security incidents, with financial penalties if the provider misses either target. When the provider suffers an outage exceeding the agreed terms, Sam's contract entitles the company to a service credit.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants a contractual guarantee specifying its cloud provider's uptime percentage and incident response time, with penalties for missed targets. Which document should be used?

items.name: SLA
items.detail: Service Level Agreement: measurable performance commitments (uptime, response time) between provider and customer, usually with penalties.

items.name: MOU
items.detail: Memorandum of Understanding: a general, usually NON-binding statement of shared intent.

items.name: MOA
items.detail: Memorandum of Agreement: more formal than an MOU, with specific responsibilities and commitments.

items.name: MSA
items.detail: Master Service Agreement: the umbrella contract with general terms; later SOWs and work orders fall under it.

items.name: SOW
items.detail: Statement of Work: the specifics of one project (deliverables, schedule, cost).

items.name: WO
items.detail: Work Order: authorization for a specific task, often under an MSA.

items.name: NDA
items.detail: Non-Disclosure Agreement: legally binds the parties to keep information confidential.

items.name: BPA
items.detail: Business Partners Agreement: how partner firms share responsibilities, profits and losses.

definition: A risk calculation representing the monetary loss expected from a single occurrence of a specific risk event, calculated by multiplying asset value by the exposure factor. It is a core building block for quantitative risk assessment.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the formula SLE equals Asset Value multiplied by Exposure Factor, and that SLE feeds into the ALE calculation (ALE = SLE x ARO) used to prioritize risk treatment decisions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is building a quantitative risk register for a data center housing a $500,000 server cluster. She estimates that a fire would destroy 80% of the cluster's value, giving a single loss expectancy of $400,000, which she then uses to justify the cost of a fire-suppression system.
detail.quizQuestion: A critical database server valued at $200,000 would lose an estimated 25% of its value if compromised by a specific ransomware strain. What is the SLE for this risk?

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: A network file-sharing protocol that allows applications and users to read and write files and request services from server programs, most commonly used for Windows file and printer sharing. Older SMB versions, like SMBv1, have well-known vulnerabilities, including the one exploited by the WannaCry ransomware worm.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference SMBv1 vulnerabilities as a reason to disable legacy SMB versions; know that SMB is the underlying protocol for Windows file shares and that it should be restricted to internal networks, never exposed to the internet.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's vulnerability scan flags several internal servers still running SMBv1, the same protocol version exploited by the WannaCry worm. She disables SMBv1 domain-wide and enforces SMBv3 with encryption, closing off a major lateral-movement vector for ransomware.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan identifies several servers running an outdated file-sharing protocol version associated with a major ransomware worm. Which protocol version should be disabled?

definition: SMS is the text messaging service used on cellular networks to send short messages between phones. In security contexts, SMS is commonly used to deliver one-time passcodes for multifactor authentication, but it is also vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, making it one of the weaker MFA delivery methods.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize SMS-based MFA as a weaker option compared to authenticator apps or hardware tokens, due to risks like SIM swapping attacks and SMS interception.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's bank client moves away from SMS-based one-time codes for customer account logins after several customers fall victim to SIM-swapping attacks, switching instead to an authenticator app that generates TOTP codes directly on the device.
detail.quizQuestion: A bank experiences several account takeovers where attackers convinced carriers to transfer victims' phone numbers to new SIM cards and intercepted login codes. Which MFA delivery method was most likely compromised, and what is a stronger alternative?
quizOptions: A) SMS codes; switch to an authenticator app generating TOTP codes
B) Email codes; switch to security questions
C) Push notifications; switch to SMS
D) Hardware tokens; switch to SMS

definition: The standard protocol used to send and relay email between mail servers across the internet. By default it transmits in plaintext and has no built-in sender verification, which is why additional controls like SPF are layered on top.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SMTP (port 25) is used for sending and relaying mail and lacks built-in authentication of the sender's domain, which is why anti-spoofing records like SPF are necessary; SMTPS adds encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan notices the company's mail server is configured as an open relay, letting anyone on the internet send SMTP mail through it to spoof the organization's domain. He reconfigures the server to require authentication for relaying and restricts it to internal senders only.
detail.quizQuestion: A mail server is found to allow any external sender to relay outbound email through it without authentication, enabling spam and spoofing. What should be configured to fix this?
quizOptions: B) Restrict SMTP relay to authenticated internal senders
D) Switch from IMAP to POP3

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: SMTP transmitted over an encrypted TLS/SSL connection, protecting email content and credentials in transit between mail servers or between a client and server. It prevents attackers from passively intercepting email traffic on the wire.
examContext: SY0-701 may distinguish SMTPS, encrypted submission typically on port 465/587 with STARTTLS, from plain SMTP on port 25, often unencrypted; recognize the pattern that appending an S to a protocol name generally signals a TLS-wrapped version.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables STARTTLS and enforces SMTPS on the mail relay so that email content and authentication credentials are encrypted between the client and the server rather than sent in cleartext. A subsequent network capture confirms email traffic is no longer readable by anyone monitoring the link.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator wants email submitted from client devices to be encrypted in transit rather than sent in cleartext over the traditional mail port. What should be configured?
quizOptions: B) Plain SMTP on port 25 only
C) Disabling all mail submission ports

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: A protocol used to monitor and manage network devices such as routers, switches, and servers, collecting status information and allowing configuration changes. Older versions send community strings in plaintext, making SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption the recommended version.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know that SNMPv1/v2c use weak, cleartext community strings as a shared secret and should be upgraded to SNMPv3, which adds authentication and encryption for device management traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex discovers the network monitoring system still uses SNMPv2c with the default 'public' community string across every switch in the building, letting anyone on the network query device configurations. He migrates all devices to SNMPv3 with unique credentials and encryption, closing the information disclosure risk.
detail.quizQuestion: A network scan reveals every switch responds to SNMP queries using the default 'public' community string. What is the best remediation?
quizOptions: B) Upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption
C) Change the switches' IP addresses

items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: An XML-based messaging protocol used for exchanging structured information between web services, typically over HTTP. It is more rigid and verbose than REST/JSON-based APIs but supports built-in standards for message security and transactional reliability.
examContext: SY0-701 may mention SOAP as an older, XML-based web services protocol contrasted with lighter-weight REST APIs; know it's associated with formal API contracts and enterprise integrations.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's integration team builds a SOAP-based web service for a banking partner that requires a strict XML schema contract and message-level signing for every transaction. The rigid schema validation catches malformed requests before they ever reach the backend transaction processor.
detail.quizQuestion: A financial integration project requires a strictly defined, XML-based message contract with built-in support for message-level security and transactional reliability. Which protocol fits this requirement?

definition: A security technology that integrates multiple security tools, automates repetitive investigation and response tasks through playbooks, and orchestrates workflows across a security operations center to reduce manual effort and speed up incident response.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SOAR platforms use predefined playbooks to automate routine response actions, such as isolating a host or blocking an IP, and typically integrate with a SIEM, reducing analyst workload and mean time to respond.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's SOC analysts are overwhelmed manually investigating hundreds of repetitive phishing alerts every day. Sam deploys a SOAR platform with a playbook that automatically extracts indicators from reported emails, checks them against threat intelligence feeds, and quarantines confirmed malicious messages without analyst intervention.
detail.quizQuestion: A SOC is overwhelmed by hundreds of repetitive phishing alerts daily and wants to automatically execute a predefined playbook that investigates and remediates confirmed threats without manual analyst steps. Which technology should it deploy?

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

variants.title: Automation and orchestration: benefits and drawbacks

items.name: Efficiency / time saving
items.detail: Routine work is done faster and with less manual effort.

items.name: Enforcing baselines
items.detail: Every system is configured the same way, every time.

items.name: Standard infrastructure configurations
items.detail: Consistent builds reduce errors and drift.

items.name: Scaling securely
items.detail: Security grows automatically with the environment.

items.name: Employee retention
items.detail: Staff spend less time on repetitive tasks.

items.name: Reaction time
items.detail: Machines respond to incidents in seconds.

items.name: Workforce multiplier
items.detail: A small team can do the work of a much larger one.

items.name: Drawbacks
items.detail: Complexity, cost, a single point of failure (a broken script breaks everything), technical debt, and ongoing supportability.

items.name: Log aggregation
items.detail: Collect logs from many sources into one place for correlation and search.

items.name: Alerting
items.detail: Notify people or systems when events match a rule or threshold.

items.name: Alert tuning
items.detail: Adjust thresholds and rules to cut false positives without missing real attacks.

items.name: Scanning and reporting
items.detail: Regular scans and reports show trends and compliance.

items.name: Archiving
items.detail: Keep logs for the retention period required for investigations and regulations.

items.name: Quarantine
items.detail: Isolate a suspicious file, system or message until it can be investigated.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agents give deep visibility and work off-network. Agentless is easier to deploy but shallower.

definition: A centralized team and facility responsible for continuously monitoring, detecting, analyzing, and responding to security incidents across an organization's systems and networks. It is typically staffed around the clock and relies heavily on SIEM and EDR tooling.
examContext: SY0-701 places the SOC at the center of security operations, tying together alerting from SIEM, EDR, and threat intelligence feeds into a 24/7 monitoring and incident response function; expect questions about analyst escalation tiers and workflows.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization stands up a 24/7 SOC where tier-1 analysts triage SIEM alerts, escalating anything suspicious to tier-2 analysts for deeper investigation and containment. When a tier-1 analyst spots unusual after-hours data transfers, the SOC's escalation process gets a senior analyst involved within minutes instead of the next business day.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants continuous, around-the-clock monitoring and triage of security alerts generated across its environment. What should it establish?

definition: A SoC is a single integrated circuit that combines a processor, memory, and other components such as graphics or networking controllers onto one chip, commonly found in smartphones, IoT devices, and embedded systems. Because all components are tightly integrated, a SoC can be harder to patch or modify individually, and a flaw in one integrated component can affect the whole device.
examContext: Do not confuse this SoC (System on Chip, a hardware term) with SOC (Security Operations Center, a team and facility) elsewhere in the exam objectives; the exam may test embedded and IoT device security where SoC design limits patching options.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen evaluates a new line of IoT security cameras and notes that because the camera's SoC bundles the processor, memory, and Wi-Fi radio onto a single chip with vendor-locked firmware, the manufacturer may struggle to patch a discovered vulnerability without replacing the whole device fleet.
detail.quizQuestion: A security researcher finds a firmware vulnerability in an IoT device and learns that the processor, memory, and wireless radio are all integrated onto a single chip with vendor-locked firmware, limiting patching options. What term describes this integrated chip design?

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: A formal document that defines the specific scope, deliverables, timeline, and responsibilities for a project or engagement, such as a penetration test. In a security context, the SOW is critical because it sets the legal boundaries of what testers are authorized to do.
examContext: SY0-701 ties SOW directly to penetration testing engagements and vendor contracts; remember that a SOW defines the authorized scope of activities, and performing actions outside it, even if well-intentioned, can expose the tester to legal liability.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan signs a SOW with a penetration testing vendor that explicitly excludes the production payment-processing servers from testing scope. When the testers accidentally discover an open port on an excluded server, they stop and report it rather than testing it, since doing so would violate the agreed SOW.
detail.quizQuestion: During an authorized penetration test, the testing team discovers a vulnerability on a server explicitly excluded from the engagement's documented scope. What should the team do?
quizOptions: A) Report it without testing further, since it falls outside the statement of work
B) Exploit it anyway since it improves the report
C) Ignore it completely and never mention it

items.name: SLA
items.detail: Service Level Agreement: measurable performance commitments (uptime, response time) between provider and customer, usually with penalties.

items.name: MOU
items.detail: Memorandum of Understanding: a general, usually NON-binding statement of shared intent.

items.name: MOA
items.detail: Memorandum of Agreement: more formal than an MOU, with specific responsibilities and commitments.

items.name: MSA
items.detail: Master Service Agreement: the umbrella contract with general terms; later SOWs and work orders fall under it.

items.name: SOW
items.detail: Statement of Work: the specifics of one project (deliverables, schedule, cost).

items.name: WO
items.detail: Work Order: authorization for a specific task, often under an MSA.

items.name: NDA
items.detail: Non-Disclosure Agreement: legally binds the parties to keep information confidential.

items.name: BPA
items.detail: Business Partners Agreement: how partner firms share responsibilities, profits and losses.

definition: A US federal law enacted after major corporate accounting scandals that requires publicly traded companies to maintain accurate financial records and implement internal controls over financial reporting, with IT controls playing a key role in ensuring data integrity.
examContext: SY0-701 ties SOX to financial reporting integrity and internal controls for publicly traded companies; expect questions distinguishing it from healthcare (HIPAA) or privacy (GDPR) regulations by its focus on financial data accuracy and executive accountability.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan works in IT for a publicly traded company and must ensure that changes to the financial reporting system go through documented approval and testing before deployment. Jordan implements change management controls and segregation of duties so no single employee can both modify financial data and approve the change, satisfying SOX's internal control requirements.
detail.quizQuestion: An auditor is reviewing a publicly traded company's IT change management process to verify that financial reporting systems have proper internal controls. Which regulation is driving this audit?

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: An email authentication standard that lets a domain owner publish a DNS record listing which mail servers are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf. Receiving mail servers check this record to help detect spoofed sender addresses.
examContext: SY0-701 groups SPF with other email anti-spoofing controls; know that SPF specifically works through a DNS TXT record listing authorized sending IP addresses or hosts.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen publishes an SPF TXT record for the company's domain listing only the IP addresses of its approved mail servers and cloud email provider. When an attacker later tries to spoof an invoice email from the company's domain, the recipient's mail server detects the sending IP isn't authorized and flags the message as likely spoofed.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants receiving mail servers to verify that email claiming to be from its domain was actually sent by an authorized server. Which DNS-based control should be published?

items.name: A / AAAA
items.detail: Map a hostname to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

items.name: CNAME
items.detail: An alias that points one name at another name.

items.name: MX
items.detail: Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.

items.name: NS
items.detail: Names the authoritative name servers for the zone.

items.name: PTR
items.detail: Reverse lookup: IP address to hostname.

items.name: TXT
items.detail: Free-form text. Used for domain verification and for email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).

items.name: SOA
items.detail: Start of authority: zone metadata such as the serial number and refresh timers.

items.name: SRV
items.detail: Locates a service, giving host and port.

items.name: DNSSEC
items.detail: Signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity (defeats cache poisoning). It does NOT encrypt queries.

items.name: DoH / DoT
items.detail: DNS over HTTPS / TLS: encrypt DNS queries for privacy.

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: SPIM is unsolicited spam sent through instant messaging platforms rather than email, often used to deliver phishing links or malware. Because users tend to trust messages arriving in chat apps more than email, SPIM can be an effective social engineering delivery method.
examContext: Exam may list SPIM alongside spam and phishing as a social engineering delivery vector; know it specifically refers to instant messaging platforms rather than email or SMS.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security awareness team warns employees after several receive unsolicited instant messages containing links to a fake login page through the company's internal chat tool; she classifies the campaign as SPIM and configures the messaging platform to block links from external accounts.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees report receiving unsolicited instant messages containing suspicious links through the company's chat application rather than email. What is this type of unwanted messaging called?

definition: A standardized language used to query, insert, update, and manage data in relational databases. When user input is improperly sanitized, attackers can inject malicious SQL statements, known as SQL injection, to read, modify, or delete data they shouldn't have access to.
examContext: SY0-701 most commonly tests SQL in the context of SQL injection as an application attack rooted in improper input validation; recognize parameterized queries and prepared statements as the standard mitigation.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's code review finds a login form that concatenates user input directly into a SQL query string, making it vulnerable to SQL injection. She refactors the code to use parameterized queries, which treat user input strictly as data rather than executable query logic.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application builds database queries by directly concatenating unsanitized user input into SQL statements. Which attack is this application most vulnerable to?

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: SQLi is an attack that inserts malicious SQL code into input fields that are improperly validated, tricking a database into executing unintended commands. It can allow an attacker to read, modify, or delete data, or bypass authentication entirely.
examContext: Exam scenarios commonly show unsanitized input leading to unauthorized data access; know that parameterized queries (prepared statements) and input validation are the primary defenses against SQLi.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya finds that a login form's username field is vulnerable to SQLi after testing an input of a single quote followed by SQL logic that returns true for any password; she works with developers to replace dynamic string concatenation with parameterized queries, eliminating the vulnerability.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester enters a crafted string containing SQL syntax into a website's login field and successfully bypasses authentication without knowing a valid password. Which remediation best addresses this vulnerability?
quizOptions: B) Enabling HTTPS on the login page
C) Using parameterized queries instead of dynamic SQL string concatenation
D) Adding a CAPTCHA to the login form

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: SRTP is an extension of RTP that adds encryption, message authentication, and replay protection to real-time audio and video streams, commonly used to secure VoIP and video conferencing traffic. It protects call content from eavesdropping while preserving the low-latency delivery RTP provides.
examContext: Exam pairs SRTP with RTP, expecting you to know SRTP is the encrypted version used when confidentiality of voice or video calls is required, similar to how HTTPS relates to HTTP.

detail.practicalScenario: After discovering that call audio could be captured in clear text on the network, Chen reconfigures the organization's VoIP platform to use SRTP instead of plain RTP, encrypting all call media so that anyone capturing network traffic cannot reconstruct the conversations.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to prevent eavesdroppers on its internal network from reconstructing VoIP call audio captured in transit. Which protocol should replace plain RTP to provide encryption for the media stream?

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: An SSD is a storage device that uses flash memory instead of spinning magnetic platters to store data, offering faster performance but presenting different secure-erasure challenges than traditional hard drives. Because SSDs use wear-leveling, standard overwrite-based wiping methods may not reliably erase all copies of data, making full-disk encryption and vendor-specific secure erase commands important.
examContext: Exam may test that traditional degaussing and simple overwrite wiping, effective on HDDs, are unreliable on SSDs due to wear-leveling, and that full-disk encryption or the drive's built-in secure erase command should be used instead.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization retires a batch of laptops and learns that the standard disk-wiping tool used for old HDDs does not reliably erase data on the new SSDs due to wear-leveling; the team switches to each drive's built-in ATA secure erase command and verifies that full-disk encryption had been enabled from day one as a backup safeguard.
detail.quizQuestion: An IT team decommissions old laptops and runs their usual multi-pass overwrite wiping tool on the drives, but later learns this method may not fully erase data on the newer solid-state drives. Why is this standard wiping method unreliable on SSDs?
quizOptions: A) SSDs are too fast for wiping software to read
B) SSDs cannot be erased under any circumstances
C) Wear-leveling moves data across physical cells, so standard overwrites may not reach every copy
D) SSDs automatically encrypt all data at the factory

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: An encrypted network protocol used to securely access and manage remote systems via command line, replacing insecure legacy protocols like Telnet. It supports both password and public-key authentication and also tunnels other protocols like SFTP.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SSH (port 22) as the secure, encrypted replacement for Telnet for remote administration, and that key-based authentication is generally preferred over passwords for SSH access.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam disables Telnet on every network switch and requires SSH with public-key authentication for all administrative access instead. A subsequent audit confirms no administrative credentials are ever transmitted in cleartext across the management VLAN.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator wants to replace a legacy remote administration protocol that transmits credentials in cleartext with an encrypted alternative. Which protocol should be used?
quizOptions: A) Telnet with a stronger password

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: The human-readable name broadcast by a wireless access point to identify a Wi-Fi network, used by devices to locate and connect to it. Hiding an SSID provides little real security since it can still be discovered through passive wireless monitoring, and attackers can also set up rogue APs that spoof a legitimate SSID.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know that SSID hiding or disabling broadcast is a weak security-through-obscurity control, not a real protection; also recognize evil twin attacks where a rogue AP broadcasts a legitimate-looking SSID to lure victims.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's wireless security assessment finds an evil twin access point broadcasting the same SSID as the corporate Wi-Fi network in the parking lot, attempting to capture employee credentials. The deployed WIDS detects the duplicate SSID with a mismatched hardware address and alerts the security team to the rogue device.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless intrusion detection system alerts on an access point broadcasting the same network name as the corporate Wi-Fi but with a different hardware address. What does this most likely indicate?
quizOptions: A) A legitimate access point firmware update
C) An evil twin rogue access point

items.name: Evil twin
items.detail: A rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it and can be eavesdropped on or phished.

items.name: Rogue access point
items.detail: ANY unauthorized AP plugged into your network, often by an employee, which creates a back door around your perimeter.

items.name: Deauthentication
items.detail: Forged deauth frames knock clients off the Wi-Fi (denial of service, or to force a reconnect so a handshake can be captured). Defeated by 802.11w protected management frames (mandatory in WPA3).

items.name: Jamming
items.detail: Transmitting noise on the same frequency to block wireless communication. A radio-frequency denial of service.

items.name: Bluejacking
items.detail: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices. An annoyance rather than data theft.

items.name: Bluesnarfing
items.detail: Stealing data (contacts, email) from a Bluetooth device without permission. Far more serious than bluejacking.

items.name: War driving
items.detail: Driving around with a laptop or phone mapping and probing Wi-Fi networks. War chalking (marking them) is the older sibling.

items.name: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.detail: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so disable WPS.

definition: The predecessor encryption protocol to TLS for securing network communications, now considered obsolete and insecure due to multiple known vulnerabilities such as POODLE. The term SSL is still used colloquially even though modern deployments actually use TLS.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SSL is deprecated and broken and should be disabled in favor of TLS 1.2 or 1.3; a scenario describing a server still accepting SSL connections is a finding that should be remediated.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's vulnerability scan flags a legacy application server that still accepts SSL 3.0 connections, exposing it to the POODLE downgrade attack. She disables SSL entirely on the server and enforces TLS 1.2 as the minimum supported protocol version.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan flags a web server for still supporting an obsolete encryption protocol vulnerable to a known downgrade attack. Which protocol should be disabled in favor of TLS?

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

definition: An authentication capability that lets a user log in once and gain access to multiple independent applications or systems without re-entering credentials for each one. It improves user convenience and centralizes authentication, though a compromised SSO credential can grant access to everything downstream.
examContext: SY0-701 tests SSO as both a convenience and a risk concentration point; expect scenarios about using SAML or OAuth to implement SSO, as well as the mitigation of pairing SSO with strong MFA since a single compromised credential now unlocks multiple systems.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan rolls out SSO across the organization's cloud applications so employees authenticate once each morning instead of managing a dozen separate passwords. Recognizing that SSO concentrates risk into a single credential, Jordan also mandates MFA on the SSO portal itself to offset that risk.
detail.quizQuestion: A company implements single sign-on across all of its cloud applications. Which additional control most directly addresses the increased impact of a single compromised SSO credential?
quizOptions: B) Sharing one SSO account across the team
D) Requiring multi-factor authentication on the SSO portal

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: A configuration standard published by the U.S. Defense Information Systems Agency that provides detailed, prescriptive hardening instructions for specific operating systems, applications, and network devices. Organizations use STIGs as an authoritative baseline for secure configuration, especially in government and defense environments.
