examContext: SY0-701 pairs STIG with SCAP-based compliance scanning as a prescriptive hardening baseline commonly used for government systems; know it provides specific, actionable configuration settings rather than general policy guidance.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex hardens a new batch of government-issued laptops by applying the relevant STIG for the operating system, disabling unnecessary services and enforcing the prescribed password and audit settings. An SCAP-compliant scan afterward confirms each laptop meets the STIG baseline before deployment.
detail.quizQuestion: A government contractor must harden Windows servers to a prescriptive, publicly published configuration baseline before deployment. Which document provides these detailed settings?

definition: A standardized language and format for representing and sharing cyber threat intelligence, including indicators, threat actors, and attack patterns, in a structured, machine-readable way so organizations can exchange threat data consistently.
examContext: SY0-701 commonly pairs STIX with TAXII; remember STIX defines the structured format and language for describing threat intelligence, while TAXII defines the transport protocol used to share STIX data between organizations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's threat intelligence team wants to share indicators of a new phishing campaign with an industry information-sharing group in a format every member's tools can automatically parse. Sam structures the threat data using STIX, ensuring threat actors, indicators, and attack patterns are described consistently across all participating organizations.
detail.quizQuestion: A threat intelligence team wants to describe a newly discovered threat actor's indicators and attack patterns in a standardized, machine-readable format that any partner organization's tools can automatically ingest. Which standard should they use?

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

definition: A SWG is a security appliance or cloud service that sits between users and the internet to enforce acceptable use policy, filter malicious or inappropriate content, and inspect web traffic for threats such as malware downloads. It gives organizations centralized visibility and control over outbound web browsing regardless of where users connect from.
examContext: SY0-701 may group SWG with CASB and SASE as modern approaches to inspecting and controlling user traffic to the internet and cloud services; know its core function is web traffic filtering and threat inspection.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya deploys a cloud-based SWG so that remote employees' web traffic is filtered and inspected for malware the same way it would be if they were sitting in the office, even though they now connect from home networks outside the corporate perimeter.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants all employees' outbound web traffic, whether they work in the office or remotely, to be filtered for malicious content and policy violations through a single consistent control point. Which solution fits this need?
quizOptions: B) A local hosts file block list

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

expansion: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
definition: A Cisco-developed AAA protocol that encrypts the entire authentication packet and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct processes, giving administrators granular control over which commands a user can run on network devices.
examContext: SY0-701 candidates should know TACACS+ uses TCP port 49 and encrypts the full packet (unlike RADIUS, which only encrypts the password), and that it is commonly used for device administration AAA on routers and switches.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex manages a fleet of core routers and switches and needs per-command authorization so junior technicians can run show commands but not configuration changes. Alex deploys TACACS+ on the network devices, pointing them at a centralized AAA server, so every command a technician types is individually authorized and logged for audit purposes.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator needs to log every single command entered on a router by each technician and restrict which configuration commands junior staff can execute. Which protocol best meets this requirement?

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

expansion: Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information
definition: An application protocol used to transport cyber threat intelligence, typically formatted in STIX, between organizations and security platforms in a standardized, automated way. It lets threat intel feeds be shared and consumed programmatically rather than manually.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs TAXII with STIX as the mechanism for transporting standardized threat intelligence data between organizations and tools; know TAXII as the transport/protocol layer, not the data format itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's threat intelligence platform automatically pulls indicator feeds from an information-sharing community over TAXII every hour, ingesting new malicious IP addresses and file hashes without any manual download. This automated feed lets her firewall block newly reported command-and-control servers within minutes of public disclosure.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to automatically receive and ingest standardized threat intelligence indicators from an industry sharing community on a recurring basis. Which protocol enables this automated exchange?

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

definition: A connection-oriented transport layer protocol that establishes a reliable session through a three-way handshake and guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery of data between applications, forming the basis for protocols like HTTP and SSH.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know TCP's three-way handshake, consisting of SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK, as the basis for understanding SYN flood attacks, and to contrast TCP's reliable, connection-oriented delivery with UDP's connectionless, best-effort delivery.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam notices a server becoming unresponsive and traffic captures show thousands of incomplete connection attempts stuck after the initial SYN packet. Sam recognizes this as a SYN flood attack exploiting the TCP three-way handshake, and enables SYN cookies on the server to mitigate the resource exhaustion.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker sends thousands of initial connection requests but never completes the handshake, exhausting the server's connection table. Which protocol's handshake process is being exploited in this attack?

definition: TCP/IP is the foundational suite of protocols that governs how data is addressed, transmitted, routed, and received across the internet and most modern networks. Understanding TCP/IP's layered structure is essential for troubleshooting connectivity and recognizing where different security controls, such as firewalls and IDS/IPS, operate.
examContext: Exam expects general familiarity with TCP/IP as the underlying model for network communication, including how it maps loosely to the OSI model's layers, and recognition of common protocols (HTTP, DNS, FTP) that run on top of it.

detail.practicalScenario: When troubleshooting why a new server cannot reach the internet, Jordan walks through the TCP/IP stack layer by layer, confirming the IP address and subnet mask first, then checking routing, before finally discovering a misconfigured firewall rule blocking the specific port.
detail.quizQuestion: When troubleshooting a connectivity issue, a technician checks IP addressing and routing before examining application-level firewall rules. This systematic approach reflects an understanding of which concept?
quizOptions: B) The OSI model only, since TCP/IP is unrelated
C) The layered structure of the TCP/IP protocol suite
D) The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis

definition: A TGT is a credential issued by the Key Distribution Center in Kerberos after a user successfully authenticates, allowing the user to request access tickets for specific services without re-entering their password each time. It is time-limited and reduces how often credentials must be transmitted across the network.
examContext: Exam ties TGT directly to the Kerberos authentication flow: the KDC's Authentication Service issues the TGT, which is then presented to the Ticket Granting Service to obtain service tickets for individual resources; know this sequence for scenario questions about Kerberos.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria explains to a new hire that after logging into the domain in the morning, their workstation receives a TGT from the KDC, which is then used throughout the day to silently request individual service tickets for file shares and applications without prompting for a password again.
detail.quizQuestion: In a Kerberos environment, after a user successfully authenticates once at login, what does the Key Distribution Center issue that allows the user to request access to individual services without re-entering credentials all day?

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: An encryption protocol introduced to fix WEP's weaknesses by generating a unique per-packet key, used as part of the original WPA. TKIP is itself now considered deprecated and insecure, having been replaced by the stronger CCMP/AES encryption used in WPA2 and WPA3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize TKIP as the encryption method used in original WPA, an interim fix for WEP, now deprecated in favor of AES-CCMP in WPA2/WPA3; a scenario describing a network still allowing TKIP is a finding to remediate.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's wireless audit finds several access points still configured to allow legacy WPA/TKIP connections for compatibility with old devices. He disables TKIP entirely and requires WPA2/WPA3 with AES-CCMP, retiring the last of the incompatible legacy hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless audit finds access points still permitting an older per-packet-keyed encryption method associated with original WPA. What should replace it?

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: The modern cryptographic protocol that secures network communications in transit, providing confidentiality, integrity, and server (and optionally client) authentication. It is the successor to SSL and underlies HTTPS, secure email, and countless other encrypted connections.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the currently recommended versions, that TLS replaced SSL, and that the TLS handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to establish a shared symmetric session key.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's web servers to support only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, disabling all older protocol versions and weak cipher suites. A follow-up scan confirms every client connection now negotiates a strong, modern cipher suite.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator wants to ensure all web traffic is encrypted using only modern, currently recommended protocol versions. Which configuration should be enforced?
quizOptions: A) Allow SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 for compatibility
C) Disable encryption for internal traffic
D) Use RC4 for faster handshakes

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

definition: TOC refers to the moment a program checks a condition, such as verifying a file's permissions or state, before acting on it. TOC is the first half of the TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) race condition, where an attacker exploits the gap between the check and the later use of that resource.
examContext: Exam pairs TOC with TOU as a classic race condition vulnerability; know that the risk comes from an attacker changing the resource's state in the gap between the check and the subsequent use.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam reviews a script that checks whether a file is a safe, non-symbolic regular file and then opens it moments later; because an attacker could swap the file for a symlink to a sensitive file in that gap, Sam rewrites the code to perform the check and the open as a single atomic operation.
detail.quizQuestion: A script verifies that a file is safe to process, then opens and processes that same file a moment later using its file path. What class of vulnerability does this pattern create?
quizOptions: D) A time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition

definition: An algorithm that generates a temporary numeric passcode derived from a shared secret and the current time, typically valid for only 30-60 seconds, commonly used as a second authentication factor via an authenticator app. Because the code depends on time synchronization rather than a server-issued counter, it works even without network connectivity to the authentication server.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts TOTP with HOTP: TOTP codes are time-based and expire quickly, while HOTP codes are counter-based and remain valid until used; both are common 'something you have' MFA factor implementations via an authenticator app.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan requires all employees to pair an authenticator app generating TOTP codes with their account password, so logging in requires both the password and a code that changes every 30 seconds. Even if an attacker steals a password in a data breach, the stolen credential alone is useless without the synchronized TOTP code.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants a second authentication factor that changes automatically on a short interval and does not require network connectivity to validate against the server. Which mechanism fits this requirement?

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: TOU refers to the moment a program actually uses or acts on a resource after previously checking it. Paired with TOC, it forms the TOCTOU race condition, where an attacker swaps or modifies the resource during the window between the check and the use, causing the program to act on something different than what it validated.
examContext: Exam expects you to recognize TOU as the second half of a TOCTOU race condition; the fix is typically to eliminate the time gap by making the check-and-use sequence atomic or by using file handles instead of re-resolving paths.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan discovers that a privileged helper program checks a temporary file's ownership and then, moments later, uses that same file path to write sensitive output; an attacker could replace the file with a symlink in between, so Jordan changes the program to retain the original file handle from the check through the use step.
detail.quizQuestion: A privileged process validates a temporary file's ownership, and shortly afterward performs a write operation using the same file path. An attacker who can swap the file in that brief interval could redirect the write to an unintended location. What vulnerability class does this describe?
quizOptions: A) A time-of-check to time-of-use race condition

definition: A dedicated hardware chip embedded in a device's motherboard that securely generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys, and can attest to the integrity of the boot process. It underpins features like full-disk encryption key storage and measured or secure boot.
examContext: SY0-701 ties TPM to hardware-based key storage and secure/measured boot alongside UEFI Secure Boot; know that full-disk encryption can store its key sealed inside a TPM so the key is unavailable if the boot process is tampered with.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables full-disk encryption on all company laptops, storing the encryption key sealed inside each laptop's TPM chip rather than in software. If an attacker tries to boot the stolen laptop's drive in a different machine, the TPM refuses to release the key because the boot environment doesn't match.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants its full-disk encryption key to be released only when the device's own untampered boot environment is verified. What hardware component enables this capability?

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: TSIG is a mechanism that uses a shared secret key and HMAC to cryptographically authenticate DNS messages, most commonly used to secure dynamic DNS updates and zone transfers between servers. It ensures that only a server possessing the correct shared key can submit changes to a DNS zone.
examContext: Exam may pair TSIG with DNSSEC; know the distinction that DNSSEC authenticates DNS responses to clients using public-key signatures, while TSIG authenticates server-to-server transactions like zone transfers and dynamic updates using a shared secret.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures TSIG with a shared secret key between the primary and secondary DNS servers so that zone transfer requests are cryptographically authenticated, preventing an attacker from impersonating a secondary server and pulling a full copy of the internal DNS zone.
detail.quizQuestion: A DNS administrator wants to ensure that only an authorized secondary server can request a zone transfer from the primary DNS server, using a shared secret to authenticate the transaction. Which mechanism should be configured?

items.name: A / AAAA
items.detail: Map a hostname to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

items.name: CNAME
items.detail: An alias that points one name at another name.

items.name: MX
items.detail: Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.

items.name: NS
items.detail: Names the authoritative name servers for the zone.

items.name: PTR
items.detail: Reverse lookup: IP address to hostname.

items.name: TXT
items.detail: Free-form text. Used for domain verification and for email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).

items.name: SOA
items.detail: Start of authority: zone metadata such as the serial number and refresh timers.

items.name: SRV
items.detail: Locates a service, giving host and port.

items.name: DNSSEC
items.detail: Signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity (defeats cache poisoning). It does NOT encrypt queries.

items.name: DoH / DoT
items.detail: DNS over HTTPS / TLS: encrypt DNS queries for privacy.

definition: TTP describes the behavior patterns of a threat actor, including their high-level strategies (tactics), the specific methods used to execute them (techniques), and the detailed step-by-step actions taken (procedures). Security teams use TTP analysis, often mapped to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK, to profile adversaries and anticipate their next moves.
examContext: Exam expects you to recognize TTP as the framework for describing adversary behavior, commonly referenced alongside threat intelligence and the MITRE ATT&CK framework; know the three terms build from general strategy down to specific implementation detail.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's threat intelligence team documents the TTPs of a ransomware group targeting their industry, mapping each phishing lure, lateral movement technique, and data staging procedure to MITRE ATT&CK, which helps the SOC build detections tuned to that specific group's known behavior.
detail.quizQuestion: A threat intelligence analyst documents that a specific adversary group's attacks always begin with a particular phishing lure (strategy), followed by a credential-dumping tool (method), executed in a documented step-by-step sequence (detailed actions). This complete behavioral profile is best described as which of the following?
quizOptions: C) The group's tactics, techniques, and procedures

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: A framework for describing the behavior of threat actors: the overall strategies (tactics), the specific methods (techniques), and the detailed implementation steps (procedures) they use during an attack. Security teams use TTPs, often mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, to profile adversaries and build targeted detections.
examContext: SY0-701 ties TTPs directly to threat intelligence and the MITRE ATT&CK framework; know that TTPs describe adversary behavior patterns used for attribution and detection engineering, rather than a single indicator like an IP address.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's threat intel team maps a recent intrusion's observed behaviors to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, documenting the attacker's TTPs from initial phishing access through lateral movement and data exfiltration. Comparing these TTPs to previous incidents lets the team attribute the intrusion to a known APT group with similar historical behavior.
detail.quizQuestion: A threat intelligence analyst documents an attacker's overall strategy, specific methods, and step-by-step execution details observed during an intrusion, then maps them to a known framework. What is this collectively known as?

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: The final phase of software testing where actual end users validate that an application meets business requirements and works correctly in realistic scenarios, performed before production release. Security issues can still surface during UAT, so it should include realistic data handling and permission scenarios rather than only functional checks.
examContext: SY0-701 places UAT at the end of the SDLC and change management process, just before production deployment; know it's where business stakeholders validate behavior, and skipping it is a cited root cause for post-deployment incidents.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's team conducts UAT on a new expense-reporting feature using a sanitized copy of real workflows, and a finance user discovers during testing that a report inadvertently exposes other employees' salary data. Catching this during UAT prevents the sensitive data exposure from ever reaching the production release.
detail.quizQuestion: Before releasing a new application feature to production, business users test it against realistic workflows to confirm it meets requirements and doesn't introduce unexpected issues. What is this testing phase called?

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: A UAV, or drone, is a remotely piloted or autonomous aircraft that can be used for legitimate purposes like facility inspection and perimeter surveillance, but also poses a security risk when used by attackers for unauthorized surveillance, signal jamming, or even physically delivering a rogue wireless access point near a target building.
examContext: SY0-701 covers UAVs under physical security threats; know that drones can be used offensively to capture images of badge codes or screens, or to place a rogue access point within range of a target's Wi-Fi network from outside normal perimeter security.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's physical security assessment flags that a UAV could hover near the building's upper floors and photograph whiteboards or badge entry codes through windows, bypassing fences and guards entirely; he recommends window film and policies restricting drone flight over the property.
detail.quizQuestion: A physical security assessment finds that an attacker could use a small aircraft to hover near upper-floor windows and photograph sensitive whiteboard content, completely bypassing the building's fences and guard checkpoints. Which threat vector does this describe?
quizOptions: A) A UAV (drone) used for aerial surveillance

definition: A connectionless transport layer protocol that sends data without establishing a session or guaranteeing delivery, order, or error correction, trading reliability for speed and lower overhead; used by applications like DNS, DHCP, and streaming media.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know UDP's lack of a handshake makes it the protocol of choice for amplification and reflection DDoS attacks, such as DNS or NTP amplification, since the source IP can be spoofed with no connection verification.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's organization experiences a massive volume of unsolicited DNS responses flooding its network from servers it never queried. Priya identifies this as a UDP-based amplification DDoS attack, where attackers spoofed the victim's IP address in DNS queries sent to open resolvers, since UDP requires no connection setup to verify the source.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's network is flooded with a massive volume of DNS responses from servers it never queried, after attackers spoofed its IP address in requests to open resolvers. Which protocol's lack of connection verification enabled this attack?

definition: A security technology that uses machine learning and statistical analysis to establish a baseline of normal user and device behavior, then flags anomalies that may indicate compromised credentials or insider threats. It can detect subtle attacks that signature-based tools miss, such as a legitimate account suddenly accessing unusual resources.
examContext: SY0-701 ties UEBA to behavioral and anomaly-based detection as opposed to signature-based detection, often integrated with or feeding into a SIEM; know it's particularly effective for detecting insider threats and compromised account misuse.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's UEBA platform flags an accountant's user account for suddenly downloading gigabytes of files from the HR system at 3 a.m., a sharp deviation from that user's established behavioral baseline. Investigation reveals the account's credentials were stolen and are being used by an attacker rather than the legitimate employee.
detail.quizQuestion: A security tool establishes a baseline of each employee's normal file access patterns and alerts when a user account suddenly behaves far outside that baseline. What type of technology is this?
quizOptions: C) User and entity behavior analytics

definition: The modern firmware interface that replaces the legacy BIOS, responsible for initializing hardware and loading the operating system, with support for Secure Boot, larger drives, and a richer pre-boot environment. Secure Boot within UEFI cryptographically verifies that only trusted, signed bootloaders and OS components run during startup.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts UEFI's Secure Boot capability with legacy BIOS, which has no such protection; know that Secure Boot helps prevent bootkits and rootkits from loading unsigned code before the operating system starts.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam enables UEFI Secure Boot on all new company laptops, which cryptographically verifies every bootloader component against a trusted signature list before allowing startup to proceed. When malware later attempts to install a bootkit on a test machine, Secure Boot refuses to load the unsigned, tampered bootloader.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to prevent unsigned, tampered bootloader code from executing during system startup. Which firmware feature should be enabled?
quizOptions: C) A master boot record partition

definition: UEM is a management platform that combines mobile device management, application management, and traditional desktop and laptop management into a single console, allowing administrators to enforce consistent security policies across every type of endpoint an organization supports. It consolidates what were once separate MDM and EMM tools into one unified approach.
examContext: Exam may present UEM as the evolution of MDM/EMM, covering phones, tablets, laptops, and desktops from one console; know it is used to push patches, enforce encryption, and remotely wipe lost or stolen devices across all device types.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's IT team replaces separate mobile device and desktop management tools with a single UEM platform, letting them push the same encryption and patch compliance policies to every laptop, tablet, and phone in the company from one console instead of juggling multiple systems.
detail.quizQuestion: An IT department currently uses one tool to manage mobile phones and a completely separate tool to manage laptops, making it hard to enforce consistent security policy across all devices. Which type of platform consolidates this into a single console?

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: A battery-backed device that provides short-term emergency power to connected equipment during a utility power outage, giving systems time to gracefully shut down or switch to a generator. It supports the availability objective of the CIA triad by protecting against abrupt power loss.
examContext: SY0-701 lists UPS among physical and environmental security and resiliency controls alongside generators and HVAC, supporting availability during short power disruptions; know a UPS is a short-term bridge, not a replacement for a generator during extended outages.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's data center installs UPS units on every server rack so that a brief utility power flicker doesn't cause an abrupt, disk-corrupting shutdown. When a storm later causes a sustained outage, the UPS bridges power long enough for the backup generator to start and take over seamlessly.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center wants to prevent abrupt server shutdowns during brief power flickers while a backup generator starts. Which device provides this short-term bridge power?

definition: A URI is a string of characters that uniquely identifies a resource, such as a web page, file, or API endpoint; a URL is the most common type of URI that also specifies how to access the resource's location. Attackers sometimes manipulate URIs to perform directory traversal or injection attacks by embedding malicious characters or encoded sequences.
examContext: Exam may test that a URL is a specific type of URI that includes a retrieval method (like https://), while a URI can also simply name a resource without specifying how to fetch it; watch for questions about malicious or encoded characters hidden in a URI during input validation scenarios.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex reviews a web application's logs and notices a URI containing encoded directory traversal sequences attempting to escape the web root and read a system password file; the web application firewall blocks the request and Alex tightens input validation on all URI parameters.
detail.quizQuestion: A web server log shows an incoming request where the URI contains repeated encoded ../ sequences attempting to escape the intended web directory. What type of attack does this most likely represent?

definition: The text address used to locate a specific resource on the internet, such as a web page, specifying the protocol, domain, and path. Attackers frequently manipulate or disguise URLs, through typosquatting, shorteners, and homograph characters, to trick victims into visiting malicious sites during phishing campaigns.
examContext: SY0-701 ties URLs to phishing indicators such as typosquatting, URL shorteners hiding a malicious destination, and homograph attacks using look-alike characters; expect scenario questions about identifying a suspicious URL in an email or message.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan trains employees to hover over hyperlinks before clicking, after a phishing simulation shows that a URL displaying a trusted brand name in the link text actually points to a lookalike domain with a swapped character. The training reduces the click-through rate on the next simulated phishing test significantly.
detail.quizQuestion: An email displays a link whose visible text reads as a trusted bank's name, but hovering over it reveals a different, suspicious destination domain. What technique is being used against the recipient?
quizOptions: B) A legitimate redirect from a CDN

definition: A standard interface for connecting peripherals and storage devices to a computer. USB ports and removable drives are a common vector for both data exfiltration and malware introduction, such as via an infected flash drive, which is why many organizations restrict or disable USB storage through endpoint policy.
examContext: SY0-701 ties USB to removable media risks, including data exfiltration and malware delivery such as a dropped malicious USB drive in a parking lot, and the mitigation of disabling USB mass storage or using DLP/endpoint controls to restrict it.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security team disables USB mass storage on all workstations through group policy after an employee plugged in an unknown flash drive found in the parking lot, which turned out to be loaded with malware. Endpoint DLP logs now also flag any attempt to copy sensitive files to removable media.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee plugs an unknown flash drive found in the parking lot into their work computer, leading to a malware infection. Which control would have best prevented this?
quizOptions: C) Disabling USB mass storage via endpoint policy
D) Extending the password expiration period

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: USB OTG is a specification that allows a mobile device, such as a smartphone, to act as a USB host and directly connect to peripherals like flash drives, keyboards, or other phones without needing a computer in between. This capability can be exploited to exfiltrate data directly from a managed mobile device to removable media, bypassing cloud-based data loss prevention controls.
examContext: Exam may test USB OTG as a data exfiltration risk on mobile devices, since it lets a phone read or write directly to a USB flash drive, which some MDM/UEM policies specifically disable to enforce data loss prevention.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's UEM policy review finds that corporate phones can still use USB OTG adapters to copy files directly to a USB flash drive, completely bypassing the cloud-based DLP controls monitoring email and app data; she pushes a policy disabling USB OTG peripheral access on managed devices.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's data loss prevention controls monitor cloud storage and email attachments on managed smartphones, but an employee is still able to copy sensitive files directly onto a USB flash drive plugged into their phone. Which capability allowed this bypass?

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: A single security appliance or platform that consolidates multiple protective functions, such as firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, content filtering, and VPN, into one integrated solution. It simplifies management for smaller organizations compared to deploying and maintaining separate point solutions.
examContext: SY0-701 presents UTM as an all-in-one network security appliance combining several functions such as firewall, IPS, antimalware, and content filtering; know the trade-off is a single point of failure/bottleneck versus the simplicity of consolidated management.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's small business deploys a single UTM appliance at the network edge that handles firewalling, intrusion prevention, web content filtering, and the site-to-site VPN, replacing five separate devices the company previously struggled to manage. The consolidated dashboard lets Sam's small IT team monitor every security function from one interface.
detail.quizQuestion: A small business wants to consolidate firewall, intrusion prevention, content filtering, and VPN functions into a single manageable appliance rather than maintaining separate devices. What type of solution fits this need?
quizOptions: B) A unified threat management appliance

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

definition: UTP is a common type of copper network cabling, such as Cat5e or Cat6, that twists pairs of wires together to reduce electromagnetic interference without an additional shielding layer. It is inexpensive and widely used for standard Ethernet connections, but is more susceptible to eavesdropping and interference than shielded or fiber alternatives in high-interference or high-security environments.
examContext: Exam may contrast UTP with shielded twisted pair (STP) or fiber optic cabling when discussing susceptibility to electromagnetic interference and ease of physical tapping in a wiring closet.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's facilities team runs new network drops through an area near heavy manufacturing equipment and chooses shielded cabling instead of standard UTP specifically to reduce electromagnetic interference from the nearby machinery, after noticing intermittent packet loss on the existing UTP runs.
detail.quizQuestion: A network segment running near heavy industrial equipment experiences intermittent packet loss that disappears when a laptop is moved further from the machinery. Which cabling characteristic most likely explains this issue?
quizOptions: A) Fiber optic cable's susceptibility to electromagnetic interference
B) Unshielded twisted pair's susceptibility to electromagnetic interference compared to shielded alternatives

definition: A scripting language built into Microsoft Office applications that automates tasks through macros. Attackers frequently abuse VBA macros embedded in Word or Excel documents to execute malicious code when a victim opens the file and enables macros.
examContext: SY0-701 ties VBA macros to a common malware delivery vector in phishing attachments; know that disabling macros by default, or allowing only signed macros, is the standard mitigation for this attack vector.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's organization blocks all VBA macros from running in documents downloaded from the internet, after a phishing campaign tried to deliver ransomware through a malicious invoice spreadsheet with an embedded macro. Employees who need legitimate macros must have them digitally signed and explicitly approved by IT.
detail.quizQuestion: A phishing email delivers an Excel attachment that, once opened, prompts the user to enable content before downloading additional malware. What underlying feature is being abused to execute the malicious code?

definition: A VDE is the individual virtual desktop session a user interacts with, running on a server and streamed to the user's endpoint device, as opposed to the backend infrastructure that hosts it. Centralizing the actual desktop environment on a server lets administrators keep sensitive data off endpoint devices and apply consistent security controls to every session.
examContext: Exam may use VDE alongside VDI, where VDI is the overall infrastructure and a VDE is the individual desktop session a specific user experiences; know that data stays on the server rather than the local endpoint in both cases.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex provisions a standardized VDE for each contractor so that regardless of what personal laptop they connect from, they see the same locked-down desktop with no ability to copy files to their local machine, keeping sensitive project data entirely on company servers.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants contractors using their own personal laptops to access company applications without any sensitive data ever being stored on those personal devices. Which approach addresses this?
quizOptions: A) Providing each contractor a virtual desktop environment hosted on company servers
B) Requiring contractors to install full disk encryption on their personal laptop
C) Emailing files directly to contractors as needed
D) Issuing contractors a company VPN client only

definition: VDI is the backend infrastructure that hosts and manages virtual desktops on centralized servers, delivering a consistent desktop experience to users on a wide variety of endpoint devices, including thin clients, personal laptops, or tablets. Because the actual computing and data storage happen in the data center, VDI can reduce the impact of a lost or stolen endpoint device, since little or no sensitive data is stored locally on it.
examContext: Exam expects you to know VDI centralizes desktop computing and data storage in the data center rather than on the endpoint, making it a strong control for BYOD scenarios where endpoint devices are not fully trusted or managed.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's company deploys VDI for all remote call-center staff using personal computers at home, so that even if an employee's home PC is compromised or stolen, no customer data was ever actually stored on that device, since every session runs on servers back at the data center.
detail.quizQuestion: A call center wants remote employees to use their own home computers while ensuring that no customer data is ever stored on those uncontrolled endpoint devices. Which technology best achieves this?
quizOptions: A) A local full-disk encryption policy

definition: A logical segmentation of a physical network into multiple separate broadcast domains, allowing administrators to isolate groups of devices for security or organizational purposes without requiring separate physical switches or cabling.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know VLANs provide network segmentation, a key defense-in-depth control, and that inter-VLAN traffic must pass through a router or Layer 3 device; also be aware of VLAN hopping attacks that exploit misconfigured trunk ports.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan wants to isolate IoT devices on the corporate network from sensitive finance workstations without installing new physical switches. Jordan creates separate VLANs for IoT devices and finance systems, configuring the switch to prevent any direct Layer 2 communication between them.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator wants to logically separate IoT devices from finance workstations on the same physical switches without running new cabling. Which technology should be used?

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: VLSM is a technique for subnetting a network into subnets of different sizes, rather than dividing it into equally sized blocks, allowing more efficient use of available IP address space. Proper VLSM design supports network segmentation, which is itself a key security control for isolating systems with different trust levels.
examContext: Exam may test VLSM as the method enabling efficient, differently-sized subnets in support of network segmentation; know that it reduces wasted IP addresses compared to fixed-size classful subnetting.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam redesigns the company's IP addressing scheme using VLSM so that a small subnet of eight addresses is allocated for the point-to-point link between routers, while a larger subnet of 500 addresses is allocated for the main office network, avoiding the massive address waste a fixed-size subnetting scheme would have caused.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer needs to allocate a tiny subnet for a two-router point-to-point link and a much larger subnet for an office of hundreds of hosts, without wasting large blocks of unused IP addresses. Which technique allows subnets of different sizes to be created efficiently?

definition: A VM is a software-based emulation of a physical computer, running its own operating system on top of a hypervisor that shares the underlying hardware with other VMs. Virtualization enables workload isolation and rapid provisioning, but a vulnerability in the hypervisor could potentially allow an attacker to escape one VM and access others on the same host.
examContext: Exam may reference VM escape as a key virtualization risk, where an attacker breaks out of a guest VM's isolation to access the hypervisor or other VMs on the same physical host; know that keeping hypervisors patched is the primary defense.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's cloud security review flags an outdated hypervisor version known to be vulnerable to a VM escape exploit, where a compromised VM on the shared host could potentially break out and access other customers' virtual machines running on the same physical server; she schedules immediate patching.
detail.quizQuestion: A security researcher demonstrates that a vulnerability in a hypervisor could allow an attacker who compromises one virtual machine to break out and access other virtual machines running on the same physical host. What is this type of attack called?

definition: VoIP is technology that transmits voice calls as digital data over IP networks rather than traditional analog phone lines, typically using RTP for media transport and SIP or similar protocols for call signaling. Because it runs over the same network as other data, VoIP traffic needs its own security considerations like VLAN segmentation and encrypted media to prevent eavesdropping or toll fraud.
examContext: Exam may ask you to recommend placing VoIP phones on a separate VLAN from general data traffic and using SRTP for encryption; know that VoIP traffic shares infrastructure with other IP traffic unless segmented.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen segments the office's VoIP phones onto their own dedicated VLAN separate from employee workstations, so that a compromised computer on the data VLAN cannot easily eavesdrop on or disrupt voice traffic traveling across the phone VLAN.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to prevent a compromised employee workstation from being able to eavesdrop on or disrupt voice call traffic traveling across the same physical network. What is the most effective control?
quizOptions: A) Using a longer DHCP lease time
B) Increasing the Wi-Fi password length
D) Placing VoIP phones on a separate VLAN from data traffic

definition: An isolated, logically segmented section of a public cloud provider's infrastructure where an organization can deploy resources with its own private IP addressing, subnets, and network controls. It lets a cloud tenant apply network segmentation and security controls similar to a traditional private data center network.
examContext: SY0-701 ties VPC to cloud network segmentation and isolation; know that a VPC lets an organization control subnetting, routing, and security groups or ACLs within a cloud provider's shared infrastructure, isolating their resources from other tenants.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex designs the company's cloud environment with a VPC split into public and private subnets, placing database servers in the private subnet with no direct internet route and only the web tier in the public subnet. This segmentation ensures that even if the web tier is compromised, the database servers aren't directly reachable from the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud architect wants to isolate database servers from direct internet access while still allowing a web tier to be publicly reachable, all within the same cloud account. What should be configured?
quizOptions: A) A VPC with separate public and private subnets
B) A single flat public subnet for everything
C) Disabling all cloud networking features
D) A shared tenancy with no segmentation

definition: A technology that creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet, allowing remote users or sites to securely access private network resources as if directly connected. It protects data confidentiality and integrity in transit and can mask the user's originating IP address and location.
examContext: SY0-701 tests VPN in both remote-access and site-to-site forms, often alongside IPsec and TLS as the underlying encryption protocols; also know split-tunnel versus full-tunnel VPN configurations as exam-relevant distinctions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures a full-tunnel VPN for remote employees so that all of their internet traffic, not just traffic destined for the corporate network, routes through and is inspected by the company's security stack. This prevents remote workers from bypassing content filtering and DLP controls by browsing directly out to the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants all remote employee internet traffic, not just traffic to internal resources, to pass through its security monitoring stack. Which VPN configuration should be used?
quizOptions: C) No VPN, direct internet access
D) A VPN limited to DNS traffic only

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

items.name: AH
items.detail: Authentication Header: integrity and authentication of the whole packet but NO encryption. IP protocol 51, and it breaks when NAT rewrites the header.

items.name: ESP
items.detail: Encapsulating Security Payload: encryption plus (optional) integrity and authentication. IP protocol 50. This is what provides confidentiality.

items.name: Transport mode
items.detail: Encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header; typically host-to-host.

items.name: Tunnel mode
items.detail: Encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header; typically gateway-to-gateway (site-to-site VPN).

items.name: IKE
items.detail: Internet Key Exchange: negotiates the security associations and keys (UDP 500; UDP 4500 for NAT traversal).

definition: VTC refers to systems and services that allow participants in different locations to communicate using real-time video and audio. Unsecured VTC sessions can be joined by unauthorized participants (sometimes called meeting bombing) or intercepted if the stream is not properly encrypted, risking exposure of sensitive discussions.
examContext: Exam may reference VTC alongside VoIP as collaboration technology that needs strong access controls, such as meeting passwords and waiting rooms, and encryption to prevent eavesdropping or unauthorized participants.

detail.practicalScenario: After an uninvited participant joins a confidential executive VTC meeting by guessing a predictable meeting link, Sam enables mandatory meeting passwords and a waiting room feature requiring host approval before anyone can join future video conferences.
detail.quizQuestion: An uninvited attendee joins a confidential video conference by simply guessing a predictable meeting URL, overhearing sensitive business discussions before being removed. Which control would most directly have prevented this?
quizOptions: A) Enabling a firewall on the host's laptop
B) Requiring a meeting password and host-approved waiting room
C) Rotating the company's email passwords
D) Upgrading the office Wi-Fi router

definition: A security appliance or service that filters, monitors, and blocks malicious HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from a web application, defending against attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It operates at the application layer, inspecting request content rather than just IP addresses and ports like a traditional network firewall.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes a WAF's application-layer content inspection from a traditional network firewall's lower-layer filtering; expect scenarios where a WAF blocks a specific attack pattern, like a SQL injection payload, targeting a public web application.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen deploys a WAF in front of the company's public-facing e-commerce site, configuring rules that block requests containing common SQL injection and XSS payload patterns. When an automated scanner later probes the site with injection attempts, the WAF blocks every malicious request before it reaches the application server.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to block malicious HTTP requests containing SQL injection and cross-site scripting payloads before they reach its public web application. Which control should be deployed?

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

definition: A WAP is a networking device that allows wireless client devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi. Misconfigured or rogue WAPs, including ones secretly connected by an employee or physically placed by an attacker, can bypass perimeter security controls entirely and provide a direct wireless path into the internal network.
examContext: Exam may test rogue access point scenarios, where an unauthorized WAP plugged into a network jack creates a backdoor; know that wireless intrusion prevention systems (WIPS) and port security help detect and prevent this.

detail.practicalScenario: During a routine sweep, Maria's WIPS detects a cheap consumer-grade WAP that an employee quietly plugged into a conference room network jack to get better Wi-Fi reception for personal devices, completely bypassing the corporate wireless security policies; she removes it and reports the incident.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless intrusion prevention system alerts on an unauthorized access point broadcasting from inside a conference room, created when an employee plugged in a personal router for better reception. What risk does this rogue device introduce?
quizOptions: A) It reduces the office's electricity costs
B) It improves the company's official Wi-Fi coverage with no downside
C) It automatically patches nearby devices
D) It creates an unmonitored wireless path into the internal network that bypasses corporate security controls

definition: An early, now completely broken Wi-Fi encryption standard that used a static, weak implementation of the RC4 cipher, making it crackable within minutes using widely available tools. It has been entirely superseded by WPA2 and WPA3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to immediately recognize WEP as deprecated and insecure and never an acceptable answer for securing a wireless network; it's a classic wrong-answer option alongside correct choices like WPA2/WPA3.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam discovers a forgotten guest wireless network in a warehouse still configured with WEP encryption from over a decade ago. He immediately reconfigures the access point to WPA2, or WPA3 if supported, since WEP can be cracked in minutes with freely available tools.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit discovers a wireless access point still configured with an encryption standard that can be cracked within minutes using publicly available tools. Which standard is this?

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: A system that monitors radio-frequency spectrum and wireless traffic to detect unauthorized access points, rogue devices, and wireless attack patterns such as deauthentication floods or evil twin APs. Unlike a wireless intrusion prevention system, a WIDS only alerts on suspicious activity rather than automatically blocking it.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts a detection-only WIDS with a prevention-capable WIPS; know both monitor wireless-specific threats like rogue APs and deauth attacks that a wired IDS/IPS wouldn't see.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's WIDS sensors detect a rogue access point broadcasting from an unrecognized device in the building's parking lot, alerting the SOC before any employee connects to it. Because the system is a WIDS rather than a WIPS, security staff must manually locate and remove the rogue device rather than having it automatically blocked.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless monitoring system alerts the SOC about a rogue access point but does not automatically take any action against it. What type of system is this?
quizOptions: A) A wireless intrusion prevention system

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

items.name: Evil twin
items.detail: A rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it and can be eavesdropped on or phished.

items.name: Rogue access point
items.detail: ANY unauthorized AP plugged into your network, often by an employee, which creates a back door around your perimeter.

items.name: Deauthentication
items.detail: Forged deauth frames knock clients off the Wi-Fi (denial of service, or to force a reconnect so a handshake can be captured). Defeated by 802.11w protected management frames (mandatory in WPA3).

items.name: Jamming
items.detail: Transmitting noise on the same frequency to block wireless communication. A radio-frequency denial of service.

items.name: Bluejacking
