items.detail: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices. An annoyance rather than data theft.

items.name: Bluesnarfing
items.detail: Stealing data (contacts, email) from a Bluetooth device without permission. Far more serious than bluejacking.

items.name: War driving
items.detail: Driving around with a laptop or phone mapping and probing Wi-Fi networks. War chalking (marking them) is the older sibling.

items.name: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.detail: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so disable WPS.

definition: A WIPS monitors the wireless spectrum to detect and automatically respond to threats such as rogue access points, evil twin networks, and wireless denial-of-service attacks. Unlike a standard WIDS, which only detects and alerts, a WIPS can take active measures, such as disconnecting unauthorized devices from the network.
examContext: Exam may distinguish WIPS from WIDS the same way IPS is distinguished from IDS: WIPS can actively block or disconnect a detected wireless threat, while a detection-only system simply generates an alert.

detail.practicalScenario: When an evil twin access point mimicking the corporate SSID appears near the building, Jordan's WIPS automatically sends deauthentication frames to disconnect any clients that attempt to associate with the rogue network, without requiring a security analyst to manually intervene.
detail.quizQuestion: An evil twin access point broadcasting the same SSID as the corporate network appears nearby, and the security system automatically disconnects any client device that attempts to associate with it, without analyst intervention. Which type of system provides this active response?
quizOptions: A) A WIDS, since it only alerts
C) A WIPS, since it can actively block the threat

definition: A WO is a formal document that authorizes and records a specific task to be performed, such as a maintenance activity, change, or repair, including what work is needed, who approved it, and who performed it. In security and change management, work orders provide an auditable trail connecting approved changes to the technicians who carried them out.
examContext: Exam may reference WO alongside change management documentation; know it supports accountability and non-repudiation by formally recording who authorized and who executed a given task.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya requires every firewall rule change to be tied to an approved WO documenting the business justification, the approver, and the technician who implemented it, so that during a later audit, every configuration change can be traced back to a formal, authorized request.
detail.quizQuestion: During an audit, a reviewer wants to trace a specific firewall configuration change back to who requested it, who approved it, and who implemented it. Which document should provide this trail?

items.name: SLA
items.detail: Service Level Agreement: measurable performance commitments (uptime, response time) between provider and customer, usually with penalties.

items.name: MOU
items.detail: Memorandum of Understanding: a general, usually NON-binding statement of shared intent.

items.name: MOA
items.detail: Memorandum of Agreement: more formal than an MOU, with specific responsibilities and commitments.

items.name: MSA
items.detail: Master Service Agreement: the umbrella contract with general terms; later SOWs and work orders fall under it.

items.name: SOW
items.detail: Statement of Work: the specifics of one project (deliverables, schedule, cost).

items.name: WO
items.detail: Work Order: authorization for a specific task, often under an MSA.

items.name: NDA
items.detail: Non-Disclosure Agreement: legally binds the parties to keep information confidential.

items.name: BPA
items.detail: Business Partners Agreement: how partner firms share responsibilities, profits and losses.

definition: WPA is a wireless security standard introduced to replace the deeply flawed WEP protocol, providing improved authentication and encryption for Wi-Fi networks. WPA itself was an interim improvement, using TKIP, before being superseded by the stronger WPA2 and WPA3 standards.
examContext: Exam expects you to place WPA in the evolution WEP to WPA to WPA2 to WPA3, recognizing that each generation addressed weaknesses in the one before it; know WPA used TKIP as a stopgap before WPA2 introduced AES-based CCMP.

detail.practicalScenario: While decommissioning old equipment, Sam finds a warehouse Wi-Fi network still configured for original WPA with TKIP; he upgrades the access points to support WPA2 with AES encryption, closing the gap left by TKIP's known weaknesses.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit finds a warehouse wireless network still using the original WPA standard with TKIP encryption. What is the recommended remediation?
quizOptions: A) Switch to a wired-only solution with no change to encryption
B) Downgrade further to WEP for compatibility
C) Disable encryption entirely to improve speed
D) Upgrade to WPA2 or WPA3 with AES-based encryption

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: A wireless security standard that replaced WPA, using the AES-based CCMP encryption protocol to provide strong confidentiality and integrity for Wi-Fi traffic. It remained the dominant wireless security standard for over a decade before being succeeded by WPA3, though its personal mode is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know WPA2 uses AES/CCMP, replacing WPA's TKIP, and that WPA2-Personal handshakes can be captured and attacked offline with a dictionary or brute-force attack, which WPA3 addresses with SAE.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex captures a WPA2 four-way handshake during an authorized wireless penetration test and runs it through a password-cracking tool against a common password list, successfully recovering the weak pre-shared key. He recommends the client migrate to WPA3, whose SAE handshake resists this exact offline attack.
detail.quizQuestion: During an authorized wireless assessment, a tester captures a network's authentication handshake and successfully cracks the pre-shared key offline using a wordlist. Which newer standard specifically mitigates this offline cracking technique?

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: The current generation Wi-Fi security standard that replaces WPA2's pre-shared key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), resisting offline dictionary attacks even against weak passwords, and mandates stronger encryption. It also adds individualized data encryption on open networks through Opportunistic Wireless Encryption.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know WPA3 improves on WPA2 primarily through SAE, replacing the four-way handshake vulnerable to offline attacks, and stronger mandatory encryption; it's generally the best-practice answer when securing new wireless deployments.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria upgrades the office's wireless infrastructure to WPA3, which replaces the legacy handshake with SAE so that even a captured authentication exchange can't be feasibly cracked offline. Guest visitors connecting to the open guest network also benefit from WPA3's opportunistic encryption, which protects their traffic from casual eavesdropping even without a password.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization upgrading its wireless network wants a standard that resists offline password-guessing attacks against captured handshakes, even for relatively weak passwords. Which standard should be selected?
quizOptions: D) Open authentication with no encryption

items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

definition: WPS is a feature that lets users connect devices to a Wi-Fi network easily, often using a PIN or a physical button press instead of typing a complex passphrase. The PIN-based method has a well-known brute-force vulnerability that can expose the network's actual passphrase, so security guidance generally recommends disabling WPS.
examContext: Exam may test that WPS's PIN method is vulnerable to brute-force attacks that can recover the Wi-Fi passphrase, making it a recommended setting to disable on both home and enterprise access points.

detail.practicalScenario: During a home office security review, Priya discovers the router's WPS PIN feature is still enabled and demonstrates how a free tool can brute-force the eight-digit PIN in a few hours to recover the actual Wi-Fi password; she disables WPS entirely on the router's settings page.
detail.quizQuestion: A security consultant demonstrates that a readily available tool can brute-force a router's WPS PIN within a few hours, ultimately revealing the network's actual Wi-Fi passphrase. What is the recommended remediation?
quizOptions: B) Switch from WPA2 to WEP
C) Disable WPS on the router
D) Hide the SSID broadcast only

items.name: Evil twin
items.detail: A rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it and can be eavesdropped on or phished.

items.name: Rogue access point
items.detail: ANY unauthorized AP plugged into your network, often by an employee, which creates a back door around your perimeter.

items.name: Deauthentication
items.detail: Forged deauth frames knock clients off the Wi-Fi (denial of service, or to force a reconnect so a handshake can be captured). Defeated by 802.11w protected management frames (mandatory in WPA3).

items.name: Jamming
items.detail: Transmitting noise on the same frequency to block wireless communication. A radio-frequency denial of service.

items.name: Bluejacking
items.detail: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices. An annoyance rather than data theft.

items.name: Bluesnarfing
items.detail: Stealing data (contacts, email) from a Bluetooth device without permission. Far more serious than bluejacking.

items.name: War driving
items.detail: Driving around with a laptop or phone mapping and probing Wi-Fi networks. War chalking (marking them) is the older sibling.

items.name: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.detail: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so disable WPS.

definition: WTLS was a security protocol designed to provide authentication, encryption, and data integrity for the Wireless Application Protocol (WAP) used on older mobile devices with limited processing power. It has been largely abandoned as modern smartphones now use standard TLS directly instead of a lighter-weight wireless-specific variant.
examContext: Exam may reference WTLS as a legacy protocol tied to older WAP-based mobile browsing, useful mainly for recognizing it as outdated compared to the full TLS used by modern mobile devices.

detail.practicalScenario: While reviewing a legacy inventory system that still interfaces with decade-old handheld scanners, Chen discovers the devices negotiate WTLS instead of modern TLS for their wireless data sessions; he flags the scanners for replacement since WTLS lacks the stronger cipher support of current standards.
detail.quizQuestion: An inventory of legacy handheld scanners reveals they use an older, lightweight security protocol designed for early mobile browsers with limited processing power, rather than modern TLS. Which protocol are these devices using?

definition: An umbrella term describing the broad range of IT capabilities, including software, infrastructure, platforms, security, and storage, delivered as a subscription-based cloud service rather than owned and maintained on-premises.
examContext: SY0-701 uses XaaS as a catch-all term for cloud delivery models beyond the standard IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS trio, such as security-as-a-service or disaster-recovery-as-a-service; recognize it as the general category these fall under.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization is evaluating moving its backup infrastructure, email filtering, and identity management all to subscription-based cloud offerings instead of in-house systems. Sam presents this broader shift as adopting an XaaS strategy, consolidating multiple traditionally on-premises functions into pay-as-you-go cloud services.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is subscribing to cloud-delivered backup, security monitoring, and identity management services instead of building each capability in-house. What umbrella term describes this overall consumption model?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: An XML-based language, part of NIST's SCAP, used to author standardized, machine-readable security configuration checklists and benchmarks that automated tools can process to assess a system's compliance against a baseline.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize XCCDF as a SCAP component used to express checklists and benchmarks in a structured format, often paired with OVAL, which describes how to actually check system state, to automate compliance scanning.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's team wants to automate compliance checks against a security baseline across thousands of servers instead of manually verifying settings. Chen imports an XCCDF-formatted benchmark into the organization's compliance scanner, which automatically evaluates every server against the checklist and reports which systems fail specific controls.
detail.quizQuestion: A compliance team wants to express a security configuration checklist in a standardized, machine-readable XML format that automated scanning tools can process across thousands of servers. Which SCAP component provides this format?

definition: A security platform that consolidates and correlates telemetry from multiple sources, including endpoints, network, email, and cloud, into a single detection and response system, going beyond a single-domain tool like EDR. It provides broader visibility and more automated cross-layer response than siloed point products.
examContext: SY0-701 positions XDR as an evolution beyond EDR, correlating signals across endpoints, network, and cloud rather than endpoints alone; expect it contrasted with EDR in scope-of-visibility questions.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security team replaces several disconnected point tools with an XDR platform that correlates a suspicious email attachment, the resulting endpoint process execution, and an unusual outbound cloud API call into a single linked incident. This cross-layer correlation reveals the full attack chain far faster than investigating each disconnected alert separately.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants a platform that correlates signals from endpoints, network traffic, email, and cloud services into a single unified incident view, rather than relying on endpoint telemetry alone. Which solution fits this description?

definition: XML is a markup language used to structure and exchange data between systems in a human-readable, tag-based format, widely used in web services, configuration files, and data feeds. Poorly secured XML parsers can be vulnerable to attacks like XML External Entity (XXE) injection, which can expose local files or enable server-side request forgery.
examContext: Exam may reference XML in the context of XXE injection attacks against web services; know that disabling external entity processing in the XML parser is the primary mitigation.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's security assessment of a partner's web service finds that its XML parser processes external entity references, allowing a crafted XML payload to read local server files; he recommends the development team disable external entity resolution in the parser configuration to close the XXE vulnerability.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester submits a crafted XML document containing an external entity reference to a web service and successfully retrieves the contents of a local server file. Which mitigation directly addresses this vulnerability?
quizOptions: A) Disabling external entity processing in the XML parser
B) Increasing the XML document size limit
C) Adding a Web Application Firewall signature for SQL keywords only
D) Enabling HTTPS on the web service

definition: XOR is a logical operation that outputs true only when exactly one of its two inputs is true, forming a basic building block of many cryptographic algorithms because it is reversible: applying the same key with XOR twice returns the original data. It underlies stream ciphers and the one-time pad, but using a short or reused key with XOR, as in a weak stream cipher, can allow an attacker to recover the plaintext or key through analysis.
examContext: Exam may test XOR as the mathematical operation underlying stream ciphers and one-time pads; know that a truly random, single-use key makes XOR-based encryption like a one-time pad theoretically unbreakable, while key reuse breaks that security.

detail.practicalScenario: While reviewing a legacy application's custom encryption routine, Jordan finds it simply XORs data with a short, repeating four-byte key; he flags this as cryptographically weak since the short repeating key allows an attacker to recover the key and decrypt the data through frequency analysis, and recommends replacing it with AES.
detail.quizQuestion: A code review reveals a legacy application encrypts sensitive data by XORing it with a short, four-byte key that repeats across the entire file. Why is this implementation considered cryptographically weak?
quizOptions: A) XOR operations are too slow for modern hardware
B) A short, repeating key allows an attacker to recover the key and plaintext through frequency analysis
C) XOR cannot be reversed, so the data becomes permanently unreadable
D) XOR only works on text data, not binary files

definition: An attack, also written CSRF, that tricks an authenticated user's browser into unknowingly submitting a malicious request to a web application where they're currently logged in, performing an unwanted action like changing an email address or transferring funds. It exploits the trust a site has in the user's browser session rather than stealing credentials directly.
examContext: SY0-701 tests XSRF/CSRF as a session-based web attack mitigated by anti-CSRF tokens embedded in forms, same-site cookie attributes, and verifying request origin; distinguish it from XSS, which injects script rather than forging a request.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's web application team adds a unique, unpredictable anti-CSRF token to every state-changing form, so a malicious site can no longer trick a logged-in user's browser into silently submitting a password-change request. Security testing afterward confirms that requests lacking a valid token are rejected by the server.
detail.quizQuestion: A logged-in user visits a malicious website that silently causes their browser to submit a password-change request to a banking site where they're already authenticated. Which attack does this describe?
quizOptions: D) A replay attack on a certificate

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A web application vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious client-side script into pages viewed by other users, allowing actions like session cookie theft or defacement when the victim's browser executes the injected script. It arises from insufficient input validation and output encoding of user-supplied content.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS variants, and to know that input validation/sanitization and output encoding, plus a WAF as a compensating control, are the standard mitigations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team finds a comment field on the company blog that renders raw HTML input exactly as typed, letting an attacker post a comment containing a script tag that steals other visitors' session cookies. The developers fix the flaw by encoding all user-submitted output before rendering it in the page.
detail.quizQuestion: A tester submits a comment containing a script tag on a public blog, and the script executes in every other visitor's browser who views that comment, stealing their session cookies. What vulnerability does this demonstrate?

items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Buffer overflow

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

items.name: Reflected
items.detail: The malicious script is part of the request (a crafted link or form) and is echoed straight back in the response. Non-persistent; the victim must click a booby-trapped link.

items.name: Stored (persistent)
items.detail: The script is saved on the server (a comment, forum post or profile) and served to every visitor. The most dangerous kind because it needs no click.

items.name: DOM-based
items.detail: Client-side code reads attacker-controlled data (such as the URL fragment) and writes it into the page. The payload may never reach the server.

definition: A security framework and set of technologies that grant access to applications and resources based on strict, continuous identity verification and least-privilege policy, rather than trusting a user or device simply because it's inside the network perimeter. It replaces the old implicit-trust VPN model with a never-trust, always-verify approach for every request.
examContext: SY0-701 ties ZTNA directly to Zero Trust architecture principles, including control plane/data plane and policy enforcement points; expect it contrasted with traditional perimeter-based VPN access as the modern replacement model.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya replaces the company's traditional VPN, which granted broad network access once connected, with a ZTNA solution that evaluates the user's identity, device health, and requested application on every single access attempt. A contractor's device that fails a health check is denied access to a sensitive finance application even though their VPN credentials would have previously granted full network access.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to grant access to individual applications based on continuous verification of user identity and device posture for every request, rather than broad access once connected to a VPN. Which model should it adopt?
quizOptions: C) An open wireless guest network

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.
